If you’ve been following recent Apple news, you might have heard the rumor that the company is working on a home hub that would look something like a cross between a HomePod and an iPad . Given Apple’s pedigree, it has the potential to become one of the best smart home devices around, and it now looks like the device could launch as soon as the end of 2025. That’s according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, who claimed in his Power On newsletter that we could get our hands on this product “by the end of this year at the earliest” (although that’s not yet set in stone). It could mark Apple’s attempt to both dominate the smart home and make further inroads into artificial intelligence (AI) – something it hopes its Apple Intelligence platform will be a key part of. Interested in this device? We’ve heard a few things about it already, and it's certainly shaping up to be an eye-catching addition to Apple’s product roster. That’s due in part to the fact that Apple is allegedly working on an entirely new operating system for the product, potentially named homeOS , that is based on tvOS and will prominently feature Siri and Apple Intelligence. Secondly, the key focal point of the so-called HomePad will be its display. Here, rumors have pointed to a 7-inch screen with a thick bezel, with a front-facing camera mounted on the top edge. The latter will reflect an emphasis on using the device for video calling . The third point is that Apple apps will, of course, be supported. And finally, you can expect some features from other apps, such as the iPhone’s StandBy dashboard . The focus, though, will remain on controlling your connected smart home devices. Apple has never really embraced the smart home to the extent that some rivals have. Sure, you can control connected products using HomeKit and the Home app, but these have their problems . Beyond that, there’s also a surprising lack of Apple-branded hardware in this space. That could all change in the next year or two. But the smart home isn’t Apple’s real target here – it’s artificial intelligence. AI is a huge, booming market right now, and Apple has already fallen behind due to its well-documented struggles with its Apple Intelligence platform, with a host of promised features delayed and missing altogether. Like many tech firms, Apple wants to get its AI into as many customers’ homes as possible, so launching a smart home hub makes a lot of sense in this regard: it gives Apple another way to appeal to customers who might not be convinced by Apple Intelligence so far. This isn’t the only smart home product that rumors claim Apple is working on, though. The company also has something up its sleeve that would comprise a screen on the end of a robotic arm , allowing it to be moved around at will. This more advanced product isn’t expected until “a year or two” after the HomePad launches, though, while Gurman adds that Apple has “pulled some bolder features from the device” in order to get it ready faster. Time is of the essence, and Apple is all too aware of that. With its first home hub potentially launching later this year, we’ll soon find out if Apple’s efforts have been worth the wait or need more time in the oven. That’s due in part to the fact that Apple is allegedly working on an entirely new operating system for the product, potentially named homeOS , that is based on tvOS and will prominently feature Siri and Apple Intelligence.

Secondly, the key focal point of the so-called HomePad will be its display. Here, rumors have pointed to a 7-inch screen with a thick bezel, with a front-facing camera mounted on the top edge. The latter will reflect an emphasis on using the device for video calling .

The third point is that Apple apps will, of course, be supported. And finally, you can expect some features from other apps, such as the iPhone’s StandBy dashboard . The focus, though, will remain on controlling your connected smart home devices.

Apple has never really embraced the smart home to the extent that some rivals have. Sure, you can control connected products using HomeKit and the Home app, but these have their problems . Beyond that, there’s also a surprising lack of Apple-branded hardware in this space. That could all change in the next year or two.

But the smart home isn’t Apple’s real target here – it’s artificial intelligence. AI is a huge, booming market right now, and Apple has already fallen behind due to its well-documented struggles with its Apple Intelligence platform, with a host of promised features delayed and missing altogether.

Like many tech firms, Apple wants to get its AI into as many customers’ homes as possible, so launching a smart home hub makes a lot of sense in this regard: it gives Apple another way to appeal to customers who might not be convinced by Apple Intelligence so far.

This isn’t the only smart home product that rumors claim Apple is working on, though. The company also has something up its sleeve that would comprise a screen on the end of a robotic arm , allowing it to be moved around at will. This more advanced product isn’t expected until “a year or two” after the HomePad launches, though, while Gurman adds that Apple has “pulled some bolder features from the device” in order to get it ready faster.

Time is of the essence, and Apple is all too aware of that. With its first home hub potentially launching later this year, we’ll soon find out if Apple’s efforts have been worth the wait or need more time in the oven.

We’re just days away from Apple’s ‘Awe Dropping’ event on September 9, where the company’s expected to reveal the iPhone 17 . While there’s also growing anticipation for an iPhone 17 Air to reinvent the modern flagship phone design, the event will also be a showcase opportunity for Apple to share all the other devices it’s been rumored to be working on for the last year. Last year’s event gives us clues to what to expect at the next iPhone 17 event. From go-to devices like the iPhone 17 Pro Max to a refreshed Apple Watch 11 , there’s certainly a lot that Apple could show off — along with some other surprises that might be off the radar. Perhaps we could even see a new HomePod ? You also don’t want to forget to check out our Apple iPhone 17 event live blog that will have the most up-to-date details on everything Apple-related. Using all the rumors, we’ll explain here what new products are tipped for a reveal. Even with the addition of the iPhone 16e to the lineup earlier this year, there’s still likely a fair amount of upgrades in store for the base iPhone 17 model to differentiate it enough. One of the most notable possible upgrades includes a 120Hz display , which is one of the biggest things we’ve pointed out with our iPhone 16 review . In 2025, all flagship caliber phones that start out at around $799 should have 120Hz display refresh rates. This would result in smoother animations and better responsiveness with the interface, while the gaming experience would also get a big boost. Secondly, it appears that Apple’s going to be increasing the size of its display from 6.1 inches in the current iPhone 16 to 6.3 inches with the iPhone 17 . Paired with a 120Hz refresh rate, this new display will certainly be much more inviting — but Apple will need to trim down the bezels to keep it as one-handed friendly as possible. Selfie fans will also rejoice because it’s tipped that the front-facing camera is jumping up to 24MP , which would be double the 12MP that’s been in place since the iPhone 11. Add in the possibility that it’ll also have a six-element lens, and your selfies could look better than ever before, including under low lighting conditions. Other improvements tipped for the iPhone 17 are a boost to its charging speed . Although 35W might not seem speedy compared to what some of the best Android phones offer, it would be a substantial step up over the current 20W charging speed. Out of all the devices expected to be shown off at the Apple event, the iPhone 17 Air is without question the one that everyone is anticipated to see the most. That’s because it could be a big shakeup to the way Apple designs its iPhones going forward, as it’s tipped to measure in at 5.5mm at its thinnest point — which would be ever so skinnier than the current Galaxy S25 Edge . Surely all eyes will be on its design, but the iPhone 17 Air is rumored to still get the same 24MP selfie camera and faster 35W charging speed like its siblings. Apparently, it’ll also be the only model in the lineup to lean on Apple’s C1 modem — which is reportedly due to try and save as much space as possible for the phone. Of course, it’s tipped to run the new A19 chip, but Apple will really need to optimize its chipset if it intends to offer all-day battery life from its rumored 2,900 mAh battery cell . It’ll also be interesting to see how it handles gaming, mainly because it’s reportedly getting one fewer graphics core than the Pro models. And finally, all the rumors thus far hint at just a single 48MP rear camera on the back of the iPhone 17 Air . Many are divided about this, especially given how cameras factor heavily into the decision of buying a new phone. It certainly won’t have the utility of the iPhone 17 Pros. Both the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max have a tough road ahead of themselves if they intend to earn that best phone title, but the rumors make it very promising. First and foremost, Apple’s expected to refresh their designs by introducing a new two-toned color scheme — along with stretching out the camera arrangement on the back. The main differences between the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max this time could simply come down to their sizes, which has always been the case, and their battery life. That’s because they’re both expected to be powered by Apple’s A19 Pro chip , which is reportedly being made using a new 3nm manufacturing process. The previous A18 Pro has proven to be a juggernaut, as well as power efficient, so it’ll be intriguing to see what new levels of performance the A19 Pro can achieve. Speaking of performance, Apple’s also rumored to introduce a vapor chamber to help keep its phones cool under pressure. A recent leaked diagram of this new vapor chamber shows how large this chamber is, which would transform the heat buildup around the processor and RAM to vapor, and then move away from those critical components. And finally, an upgraded 48MP telephoto camera should put the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max in a strong spot for earning that best camera phone title. However, there’s still debate around what kind of optical zoom Apple’s going to give it. So far, the rumors hint at it dropping to 3.5x because of the upgraded sensor — while another report says it could be as much as 8x . Regardless of what ends up happening, the entire iPhone 17 lineup is reportedly going to cost more, as the rumors hint at $50 price hikes across the board. Just like its iPhones, its wearables are tipped for their annual refresh, and the Apple Watch 11 is no exception. The company already announced the return of blood oxygen reading with current models that support it, but the Apple Watch 11 is tipped to get a few new hardware changes. While the physical design won’t change, it’s rumored to feature a more power-efficient display — either an LPTO or Micro-LED display . This could mean a more pixel-dense screen for the Apple Watch 11, increased brightness, and even extended battery life. Being the higher-end version, the Apple Watch Ultra 3 is expected to bring even more features than the Apple Watch 11. For starters, its display is tipped to increase to 2.12 inches — while somehow sporting a thinner chassis. That display could also be even more detailed, as leaks suggest the resolution is going up to 422 x 514 pixels. Other hardware upgrades also include the latest S10 chip to power it, satellite connectivity for messaging, and even longer battery life. The Ultra 3 is also likely to get high blood pressure detection. Of course, there are other features already with the watchOS 26 beta release , but Apple could always introduce other features, like Apple Intelligence ones tailored for the Apple Watch Ultra 3. There’s no indication yet that its price could be increased, so expect it to be at $799 just like the two past models. Apple’s last iPhone 16 event revealed an updated AirPods 4 , which gained active noise cancellation. However, Apple could introduce the AirPods Pro 3 at its upcoming ‘Awe Dropping’ event. Not only is it tipped for a new design, but this best wireless earbuds contender is reportedly going to have a touchscreen on its charging case . This would allow for quick functions such as controlling music playback and active noise cancellation, instead of having to access them on your iPhone. Those are the devices that have a strong chance of being introduced at Apple’s event in a matter of days. However, there’s still a bunch more that could also be debuted — with some having a good chance. sources.title: Apple’s Oct. 16 event: Here’s what we expect - CNET
passages: Tune back to CNET for full coverage from Apple’s event.
We’ll start things off with a live show at 8:45 a.m.
PT featuring Brian Tong, Donald Bell, Sharon Profis and Stephen Beacham.
They’ll respond to viewer calls, tweets and emails and feature live reports from Cupertino before handing it over to the reporters on site.
The company’s second event in just two months won’t have the flash from the previous affair, which saw the debut of two larger iPhones and a glimpse at the Apple Watch.
Instead, the company is expected to show off a new iPad (or two), unveil new Macs and talk more about its OS X Yosemite operating system for its desktop.
Its performance over the last two quarters, in which sales declined over a year ago and fell below Wall Street expectations , is illustrative of that kind of mentality.
Adding to the pressure are the raft of cheap tablets that have flooded the market.
Apple likely will allow the iPad to take advantage of some Apple Pay features when the service launches later in October.
That includes letting people pay for items in apps using a single touch on the fingerprint sensor.

Apple introduced its first phablet, the 5.5-inch iPhone 6 Plus, last month, and some analysts expect consumers to opt for that instead of an iPad Mini. “The iPhone 6 Plus is almost crossing over into tablet territory, and there’s a possibility that will impact … demand for the iPad Mini,” Creative Strategies analyst Tim Bajarin said.
To build customer loyalty and make sure users are accessing the most recent software, Apple last year made Mac OS X 10.9 Mavericks free for download.
Yosemite also is free for users, and it’s likely Apple will release the software to the public following its event Thursday.
Front and center will be a new version of the iPad, which faces questions over whether its declining shipments are a temporary hiccup or a troubling trend.
The question for the tablet has continued to shift from “What nifty new feature will be on the new iPad?” to “Do I really need to replace my aging — but still functional — iPad?”
Apple wasn’t the first company to create a tablet, but it was the first to make a model that really caught on with buyers.
2 moneymaker after the iPhone — and everyone from Microsoft to Xiaomi has built copycat devices.
In the second quarter, Apple shipped 13.3 million iPads, giving it a market share of 27 percent.
Apple now generates less than 15 percent of its revenue from Macs, but the devices help flesh out its family of products — which are increasingly designed to work together.
Apple in July reported Mac unit sales rose 18 percent to 4.4 million in the quarter ended June 28.
5 ranking for global PC sales in the calendar third quarter.
For the past several years, Apple has controlled a much smaller chunk of the market, but its sleek designs, such as the MacBook Air, have attracted customers.
One product long overdue for an update is the Mac Mini, which hasn’t been refreshed for two years.
Along with gold likely will be silver and space gray versions.

In this guide, we're tracking the Apple events that are on the horizon, including what we're expecting to see at each one. There won't be a full Cupertino event, but Apple could do a mini event to show off the new products. The HomePod mini 2 will feature an updated S-series chip, and Apple's N1 networking chip with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. There will be at least two new colors, including pink and sage green. Apple is planning to launch a home hub that will support smart home products, listening to music, making video calls, getting the weather, looking things up with ‌Siri‌, displaying photos, making notes, viewing calendar events, and more. The home hub has an all-display design with an iPad-like 7-inch display. There are two models, one that's designed to be mounted to the wall and one that's got an included speaker base that looks like a HomePod mini. The Apple TV will get a new Apple-designed Wi-Fi and Bluetooth chip, along with a faster A19 or A19 Pro processor that will add support for console-quality games and Apple Intelligence. No design changes are expected. Beyond the home products, there are other devices rumored for late 2026. It's possible these would be announced with a press release. The 24-inch iMac will get an update, and it'll also get the new M6 chip. No design or display changes are expected, so it'll continue to look like the current model from 2024. The iPad mini 8 is rumored to feature a major technology upgrade, with Apple set to adopt an OLED display. The iPad mini 8 could have a more water resistant design with a vibration-based speaker system that allows Apple to eliminate the device's speaker holes, plus it's expected to use the same A20 chip that Apple first used in the iPhone 18 Pro. In January 2026, Apple unveiled the second-generation AirTag. There was no event held because it was a one-off product announcement. Apple instead announced the new device via a press release. The AirTag 2 features a louder, upgraded speaker and a second-generation Ultra Wideband (UWB) chip that improves the range of Precision Finding. Apple held an "Apple Experience" in New York, London, and Shanghai on March 4, and ahead of the event, announced the MacBook Air with M5 chip, the iPad Air with M4 chip, the M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro models, a low-cost $599 MacBook Neo, and the $599 iPhone 17e. Later in March, Apple debuted the AirPods Max 2. At the WWDC 2026 keynote event on Monday, June 8, Apple introduced iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27 Golden Gate, visionOS 27, watchOS 27, and tvOS 27. The Mac mini was updated with Apple's first 2nm chip, the M6, and the higher-end version uses the M5 Pro. The Mac Studio was updated with the M5 Max and M5 Ultra chips. coreStoryFacts.text: If you’ve been following recent Apple news, you might have heard the rumor that the company is working on a home hub that would look something like a cross between a HomePod and an iPad .
Given Apple’s pedigree, it has the potential to become one of the best smart home devices around, and it now looks like the device could launch as soon as the end of 2025.

This more advanced product isn’t expected until “a year or two” after the HomePad launches, though, while Gurman adds that Apple has “pulled some bolder features from the device” in order to get it ready faster.

Like many tech firms, Apple wants to get its AI into as many customers’ homes as possible, so launching a smart home hub makes a lot of sense in this regard: it gives Apple another way to appeal to customers who might not be convinced by Apple Intelligence so far.
Time is of the essence, and Apple is all too aware of that.
The third point is that Apple apps will, of course, be supported.
Apple has never really embraced the smart home to the extent that some rivals have.
Sure, you can control connected products using HomeKit and the Home app, but these have their problems .
Beyond that, there’s also a surprising lack of Apple-branded hardware in this space.

AI is a huge, booming market right now, and Apple has already fallen behind due to its well-documented struggles with its Apple Intelligence platform, with a host of promised features delayed and missing altogether.

Given Apple’s pedigree, it has the potential to become one of the best smart home devices around, and it now looks like the device could launch as soon as the end of 2025.

That’s according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, who claimed in his Power On newsletter that we could get our hands on this product “by the end of this year at the earliest” (although that’s not yet set in stone). It could mark Apple’s attempt to both dominate the smart home and make further inroads into artificial intelligence (AI) – something it hopes its Apple Intelligence platform will be a key part of.

Interested in this device? We’ve heard a few things about it already, and it's certainly shaping up to be an eye-catching addition to Apple’s product roster. That’s due in part to the fact that Apple is allegedly working on an entirely new operating system for the product, potentially named homeOS , that is based on tvOS and will prominently feature Siri and Apple Intelligence.

Secondly, the key focal point of the so-called HomePad will be its display. Here, rumors have pointed to a 7-inch screen with a thick bezel, with a front-facing camera mounted on the top edge. The latter will reflect an emphasis on using the device for video calling .

The third point is that Apple apps will, of course, be supported. And finally, you can expect some features from other apps, such as the iPhone’s StandBy dashboard . The focus, though, will remain on controlling your connected smart home devices.

Apple has never really embraced the smart home to the extent that some rivals have. Sure, you can control connected products using HomeKit and the Home app, but these have their problems . Beyond that, there’s also a surprising lack of Apple-branded hardware in this space. That could all change in the next year or two.

But the smart home isn’t Apple’s real target here – it’s artificial intelligence. AI is a huge, booming market right now, and Apple has already fallen behind due to its well-documented struggles with its Apple Intelligence platform, with a host of promised features delayed and missing altogether.

Like many tech firms, Apple wants to get its AI into as many customers’ homes as possible, so launching a smart home hub makes a lot of sense in this regard: it gives Apple another way to appeal to customers who might not be convinced by Apple Intelligence so far.

This isn’t the only smart home product that rumors claim Apple is working on, though. The company also has something up its sleeve that would comprise a screen on the end of a robotic arm , allowing it to be moved around at will. This more advanced product isn’t expected until “a year or two” after the HomePad launches, though, while Gurman adds that Apple has “pulled some bolder features from the device” in order to get it ready faster.

Time is of the essence, and Apple is all too aware of that. With its first home hub potentially launching later this year, we’ll soon find out if Apple’s efforts have been worth the wait or need more time in the oven.

We’re just days away from Apple’s ‘Awe Dropping’ event on September 9, where the company’s expected to reveal the iPhone 17 . While there’s also growing anticipation for an iPhone 17 Air to reinvent the modern flagship phone design, the event will also be a showcase opportunity for Apple to share all the other devices it’s been rumored to be working on for the last year. Last year’s event gives us clues to what to expect at the next iPhone 17 event. From go-to devices like the iPhone 17 Pro Max to a refreshed Apple Watch 11 , there’s certainly a lot that Apple could show off — along with some other surprises that might be off the radar. Perhaps we could even see a new HomePod ? You also don’t want to forget to check out our Apple iPhone 17 event live blog that will have the most up-to-date details on everything Apple-related. Using all the rumors, we’ll explain here what new products are tipped for a reveal. Even with the addition of the iPhone 16e to the lineup earlier this year, there’s still likely a fair amount of upgrades in store for the base iPhone 17 model to differentiate it enough. One of the most notable possible upgrades includes a 120Hz display , which is one of the biggest things we’ve pointed out with our iPhone 16 review . In 2025, all flagship caliber phones that start out at around $799 should have 120Hz display refresh rates. This would result in smoother animations and better responsiveness with the interface, while the gaming experience would also get a big boost. Secondly, it appears that Apple’s going to be increasing the size of its display from 6.1 inches in the current iPhone 16 to 6.3 inches with the iPhone 17 . Paired with a 120Hz refresh rate, this new display will certainly be much more inviting — but Apple will need to trim down the bezels to keep it as one-handed friendly as possible. Selfie fans will also rejoice because it’s tipped that the front-facing camera is jumping up to 24MP , which would be double the 12MP that’s been in place since the iPhone 11. Add in the possibility that it’ll also have a six-element lens, and your selfies could look better than ever before, including under low lighting conditions. Other improvements tipped for the iPhone 17 are a boost to its charging speed . Although 35W might not seem speedy compared to what some of the best Android phones offer, it would be a substantial step up over the current 20W charging speed. Out of all the devices expected to be shown off at the Apple event, the iPhone 17 Air is without question the one that everyone is anticipated to see the most. That’s because it could be a big shakeup to the way Apple designs its iPhones going forward, as it’s tipped to measure in at 5.5mm at its thinnest point — which would be ever so skinnier than the current Galaxy S25 Edge . Surely all eyes will be on its design, but the iPhone 17 Air is rumored to still get the same 24MP selfie camera and faster 35W charging speed like its siblings. Apparently, it’ll also be the only model in the lineup to lean on Apple’s C1 modem — which is reportedly due to try and save as much space as possible for the phone. Of course, it’s tipped to run the new A19 chip, but Apple will really need to optimize its chipset if it intends to offer all-day battery life from its rumored 2,900 mAh battery cell . It’ll also be interesting to see how it handles gaming, mainly because it’s reportedly getting one fewer graphics core than the Pro models. And finally, all the rumors thus far hint at just a single 48MP rear camera on the back of the iPhone 17 Air . Many are divided about this, especially given how cameras factor heavily into the decision of buying a new phone. It certainly won’t have the utility of the iPhone 17 Pros. Both the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max have a tough road ahead of themselves if they intend to earn that best phone title, but the rumors make it very promising. First and foremost, Apple’s expected to refresh their designs by introducing a new two-toned color scheme — along with stretching out the camera arrangement on the back. The main differences between the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max this time could simply come down to their sizes, which has always been the case, and their battery life. That’s because they’re both expected to be powered by Apple’s A19 Pro chip , which is reportedly being made using a new 3nm manufacturing process. The previous A18 Pro has proven to be a juggernaut, as well as power efficient, so it’ll be intriguing to see what new levels of performance the A19 Pro can achieve. Speaking of performance, Apple’s also rumored to introduce a vapor chamber to help keep its phones cool under pressure. A recent leaked diagram of this new vapor chamber shows how large this chamber is, which would transform the heat buildup around the processor and RAM to vapor, and then move away from those critical components. And finally, an upgraded 48MP telephoto camera should put the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max in a strong spot for earning that best camera phone title. However, there’s still debate around what kind of optical zoom Apple’s going to give it. So far, the rumors hint at it dropping to 3.5x because of the upgraded sensor — while another report says it could be as much as 8x . Regardless of what ends up happening, the entire iPhone 17 lineup is reportedly going to cost more, as the rumors hint at $50 price hikes across the board. Just like its iPhones, its wearables are tipped for their annual refresh, and the Apple Watch 11 is no exception. The company already announced the return of blood oxygen reading with current models that support it, but the Apple Watch 11 is tipped to get a few new hardware changes. While the physical design won’t change, it’s rumored to feature a more power-efficient display — either an LPTO or Micro-LED display . This could mean a more pixel-dense screen for the Apple Watch 11, increased brightness, and even extended battery life. Being the higher-end version, the Apple Watch Ultra 3 is expected to bring even more features than the Apple Watch 11. New iPads and Macs, as well as an official launch of the OS X Yosemite computer operating system, should show up at Apple's event this week. Apple has the chance on Thursday to provide a few compelling reasons for consumers to upgrade or buy a new iPad. The company’s second event in just two months won’t have the flash from the previous affair, which saw the debut of two larger iPhones and a glimpse at the Apple Watch. Instead, the company is expected to show off a new iPad (or two), unveil new Macs and talk more about its OS X Yosemite operating system for its desktop. The presentation, which kicks off at 10 a.m. PT, is a lower-key affair held at Apple’s headquarters in Cupertino, Calif. While the iPhone remains Apple’s dominant revenue engine — contributing to more than half of its sales — the company is eager to bolster its other businesses. Front and center will be a new version of the iPad, which faces questions over whether its declining shipments are a temporary hiccup or a troubling trend. The question for the tablet has continued to shift from “What nifty new feature will be on the new iPad?” to “Do I really need to replace my aging — but still functional — iPad?” Its performance over the last two quarters, in which sales declined over a year ago and fell below Wall Street expectations , is illustrative of that kind of mentality. And the trend is expected to continue in the most recent quarter, which Apple will report four days after the event. Adding to the pressure are the raft of cheap tablets that have flooded the market. Apple wasn’t the first company to create a tablet, but it was the first to make a model that really caught on with buyers. The sleek design, app store and touch screen capabilities on the first iPad, introduced in 2010, attracted millions of buyers to the device. iPad grew into a huge revenue driver for Apple — the tablet’s currently its No. 2 moneymaker after the iPhone — and everyone from Microsoft to Xiaomi has built copycat devices. But Apple hasn’t made big enough changes to the iPad to compel even its most ardent fans to immediately buy the newest model. “What I’ve consistently found in research is tablets are nice to have but not something [people] need to have,” said Bob O’Donnell, chief analyst at Technalysis Research. “If the iPad Air didn’t move the needle — and it was a pretty decent upgrade — I don’t know what’s going to.” Even though the iPad will be the most anticipated news Thursday, there almost certainly will be Mac updates, as well. That includes new hardware and Apple’s latest computer operating system, Mac OS X Yosemite. Even though the Mac doesn’t make as much money as the iPad, the computers remain important to Apple’s strategy. Here’s more information on what we’re likely — and unlikely — to see at the event. More than four years (and seven models) after introducing the first iPad, Apple’s sleek device remains the king of tablets. In the second quarter, Apple shipped 13.3 million iPads, giving it a market share of 27 percent. But its position has been slipping versus rivals; a year earlier, Apple’s market share was 33 percent. The company needs a new model of its popular 9.7-inch device to revitalize iPad sales. But the updates coming Thursday are expected to be incremental changes instead of a revolution. One likely addition to the iPad Air is the TouchID fingerprint sensor, which first popped up in last year’s iPhone 5S and appeared in the new iPhone 6 and 6 Plus. It allows users to unlock their devices and purchase items in iTunes with the touch of a finger. TouchID also will soon work with Apple Pay, the company’s new mobile payments system unveiled at its September 9 iPhone 6 event. Apple likely will allow the iPad to take advantage of some Apple Pay features when the service launches later in October. That includes letting people pay for items in apps using a single touch on the fingerprint sensor. It’s less likely that the iPad will include a near field communication (NFC) chip that allows users to pay for items in retail stores by tapping their devices on a point of sale terminal — you would look pretty silly trying to wave your iPad at a cash register. Another likely update to the iPad is a gold model, also following in line with Apple’s recent iPhones. The iPhone 5S was the first device to offer that particular color. Along with gold likely will be silver and space gray versions. And the iPad undoubtedly will feature new components, such as Apple’s A8 processor. The iPad could get the same kind of storage bump as the iPhone 6, dropping the 32 GB and going straight from 16GB to 64GB and 128GB. The company already offers a 128GB iPad, but it’s a $300 premium over the $499 base model. If brought in line with Apple’s iPhone pricing, that tier could get a $100 cut in price. The company also will probably update the camera and include a higher resolution screen — a key feature as competitors have stepped up their game with display technology. The screen may include an anti-reflective coating that makes it easier to see. The new iPad Air will also likely be thinner and lighter. What’s unlikely is the appearance of a bigger screen iPad, which many have dubbed the “iPad Pro.” The device, which market watchers believe could have a 12.9-inch screen, probably won’t be announced until next year. The iPad Mini, Apple’s 7.9-inch tablet, could see some small updates, but much of the focus will be on the bigger device. Part of Apple’s iPad struggles have come from consumers replacing smaller tablets with bigger phones — typically, phone-tablet hybrids called phablets. Apple introduced its first phablet, the 5.5-inch iPhone 6 Plus, last month, and some analysts expect consumers to opt for that instead of an iPad Mini. “The iPhone 6 Plus is almost crossing over into tablet territory, and there’s a possibility that will impact … demand for the iPad Mini,” Creative Strategies analyst Tim Bajarin said. Apple’s Mac business might not be as big — or as sexy — as its mobile business, but it remains an important focus for Apple. Apple now generates less than 15 percent of its revenue from Macs, but the devices help flesh out its family of products — which are increasingly designed to work together. Apple in July reported Mac unit sales rose 18 percent to 4.4 million in the quarter ended June 28. CEO Tim Cook said the Mac boosted Apple’s overall financial results, and the company saw strong sales in some regions weak for other PC makers. Apple hasn’t yet reported its most recent quarter, but research firm IDC last week said the company moved into the No. 5 ranking for global PC sales in the calendar third quarter. For the past several years, Apple has controlled a much smaller chunk of the market, but its sleek designs, such as the MacBook Air, have attracted customers. Apple last year introduced its powerful Mac Pro, and it has continued to add Retina Displays to its various MacBooks. But there also have been some devices that haven’t been updated in years. One product long overdue for an update is the Mac Mini, which hasn’t been refreshed for two years. The device is Apple’s most affordable computer, ranging in price from $599 to $999. An owner must also purchase a display, keyboard, and mouse for the device to work, and the most expensive version of the box also works as an OS X server. It’s likely the Mac Mini will be updated with Intel’s newest processors and more internal storage. Another Apple computer in need of an update is the iMac. The all-in-one device, with the brains hidden behind a sleek display, hasn’t had a design change in two years. Most of all, its screen resolution hasn’t changed much while other devices have been bumped to Retina Displays. The iPhone 4, introduced in 2010, sported the first Retina Display, while the higher-resolution screen hit the iPad and MacBook Pro line in 2012. It’s unlikely that Apple will introduce a MacBook Air with a Retina Display, though consumers have been clamoring for such a device. The company updated its thinnest and lightest laptops with new processors and a price cut in April. It’s also unlikely that Apple will incorporate its TouchID sensor into its computers this fall, though that’s something we could see in the future. Apple unveiled the latest version of its computer software , OS X 10.10 Yosemite, in June at its Worldwide Developers Conference in San Francisco. The operating system has a new look, a refined toolbar, new notification-center features and a dark mode. In addition, Yosemite will now synchronize with Apple’s iOS mobile operating system through AirDrop file-sharing, iMessage messaging and the ability to make and take phone calls.”All in all, they come together for a gorgeous and more usable version of OS X, the best ever,” Craig Federighi, senior vice president of software engineering, told developers at the conference. Apple undoubtedly will show off Yosemite on Thursday and talk up the ways it interacts with the iPhone and iPad. The company could also discuss iCloud and other software for its devices. To build customer loyalty and make sure users are accessing the most recent software, Apple last year made Mac OS X 10.9 Mavericks free for download. Yosemite also is free for users, and it’s likely Apple will release the software to the public following its event Thursday. Tune back to CNET for full coverage from Apple’s event. We’ll start things off with a live show at 8:45 a.m. PT featuring Brian Tong, Donald Bell, Sharon Profis and Stephen Beacham. They’ll respond to viewer calls, tweets and emails and feature live reports from Cupertino before handing it over to the reporters on site. Apple’s presentation starts at 10 a.m. PT, and we’ll be bringing you all the news and commentary from inside the venue. © 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.

Apple hasn’t yet reported its most recent quarter, but research firm IDC last week said the company moved into the No. 5 ranking for global PC sales in the calendar third quarter. For the past several years, Apple has controlled a much smaller chunk of the market, but its sleek designs, such as the MacBook Air, have attracted customers.
Apple last year introduced its powerful Mac Pro, and it has continued to add Retina Displays to its various MacBooks. But there also have been some devices that haven’t been updated in years.

One product long overdue for an update is the Mac Mini, which hasn’t been refreshed for two years. The device is Apple’s most affordable computer, ranging in price from $599 to $999. An owner must also purchase a display, keyboard, and mouse for the device to work, and the most expensive version of the box also works as an OS X server. It’s likely the Mac Mini will be updated with Intel’s newest processors and more internal storage.

Another Apple computer in need of an update is the iMac. The all-in-one device, with the brains hidden behind a sleek display, hasn’t had a design change in two years. Most of all, its screen resolution hasn’t changed much while other devices have been bumped to Retina Displays. The iPhone 4, introduced in 2010, sported the first Retina Display, while the higher-resolution screen hit the iPad and MacBook Pro line in 2012.

It’s unlikely that Apple will introduce a MacBook Air with a Retina Display, though consumers have been clamoring for such a device. The company updated its thinnest and lightest laptops with new processors and a price cut in April. It’s also unlikely that Apple will incorporate its TouchID sensor into its computers this fall, though that’s something we could see in the future.

Apple unveiled the latest version of its computer software , OS X 10.10 Yosemite, in June at its Worldwide Developers Conference in San Francisco. The operating system has a new look, a refined toolbar, new notification-center features and a dark mode. In addition, Yosemite will now synchronize with Apple’s iOS mobile operating system through AirDrop file-sharing, iMessage messaging and the ability to make and take phone calls.”All in all, they come together for a gorgeous and more usable version of OS X, the best ever,” Craig Federighi, senior vice president of software engineering, told developers at the conference.
Apple undoubtedly will show off Yosemite on Thursday and talk up the ways it interacts with the iPhone and iPad. The company could also discuss iCloud and other software for its devices.

To build customer loyalty and make sure users are accessing the most recent software, Apple last year made Mac OS X 10.9 Mavericks free for download. Yosemite also is free for users, and it’s likely Apple will release the software to the public following its event Thursday.

Tune back to CNET for full coverage from Apple’s event. We’ll start things off with a live show at 8:45 a.m. PT featuring Brian Tong, Donald Bell, Sharon Profis and Stephen Beacham. They’ll respond to viewer calls, tweets and emails and feature live reports from Cupertino before handing it over to the reporters on site. Apple’s presentation starts at 10 a.m. PT, and we’ll be bringing you all the news and commentary from inside the venue.

passages: As important as some of the messages in The Social Reckoning are, the movie has been drastically underperforming at the box office.

extraction.body: As important as some of the messages in The Social Reckoning are, the movie has been drastically underperforming at the box office. Per Variety, Aaron’s Sorkin’s follow up to The Social Network only grossed a measly $5.5 million this past weekend against a budget that’s somewhere within the $30–42 million range. That would make it a certifiable flop that’s costing Columbia Pictures (and Sony) quite a bit of money — especially when you compare it to The Social Network’s $22 million opening. It’s currently got a 55% rating on Rotten Tomatoes and has widely been trashed on social media. All of this might be reflective of audiences hoping for a proper sequel to The Social Network, which won three Oscars for its screenplay (written by Sorkin), editing, and score. But it might speak to people not fully clicking with Mikey Madison’s performance as whistleblower Frances Haugen or Jeremy Allen White’s turn as Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz. (Madison, for her part, indicated to The Hollywood Reporter that it was Sorkin’s vision as director that kept from “authentically and faithfully represent[ing] a real person,” which she hopes to do in the future.) It also probably didn’t help that Jesse Eisenberg — who portrayed Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Network — had no interest in being in the film, according to Sorkin himself. Ironically, Blumhouse’s Other Mommy raked in an impressive $27.5 million this weekend, which likely suggests that people are more interested in novel horror as opposed to reminders of how social media has made everyone’s lives worse.

passages: Sixteen years ago, at the height of Facebook’s dominance over the internet, Aaron Sorkin wrote a movie called “The Social Network” that became both a box office and a critical hit.
But his companion to that Obama-era classic, “The Social Reckoning,” was DOA this weekend.

Its trailers have gone largely ignored on TikTok and Instagram, the sites that have eclipsed Facebook in terms of youth relevance, and reception has been lukewarm at best, with a B- on CinemaScore and Rotten Tomatoes scores of 55% critics and 73% audience.

But Haugen’s relationship to her boss and to a reporter looking for a big story don’t have the same pull as a personal friendship.

There were spoonfuls of sugar that helped the medicine go down, while ‘Social Reckoning’ is more of a document for our time,” said Dergarabedian. “I also think that there was more of an emotional connection to Facebook at the time because it was a new site, whereas now it feels more like a utility and not at all exciting, like turning on your coffeepot in the morning.”

extraction.body: As important as some of the messages in The Social Reckoning are, the movie has been drastically underperforming at the box office. Per Variety, Aaron’s Sorkin’s follow up to The Social Network only grossed a measly $5.5 million this past weekend against a budget that’s somewhere within the $30–42 million range. That would make it a certifiable flop that’s costing Columbia Pictures (and Sony) quite a bit of money — especially when you compare it to The Social Network’s $22 million opening. It’s currently got a 55% rating on Rotten Tomatoes and has widely been trashed on social media. All of this might be reflective of audiences hoping for a proper sequel to The Social Network, which won three Oscars for its screenplay (written by Sorkin), editing, and score. But it might speak to people not fully clicking with Mikey Madison’s performance as whistleblower Frances Haugen or Jeremy Allen White’s turn as Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz. (Madison, for her part, indicated to The Hollywood Reporter that it was Sorkin’s vision as director that kept from “authentically and faithfully represent[ing] a real person,” which she hopes to do in the future.) It also probably didn’t help that Jesse Eisenberg — who portrayed Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Network — had no interest in being in the film, according to Sorkin himself. Ironically, Blumhouse’s Other Mommy raked in an impressive $27.5 million this weekend, which likely suggests that people are more interested in novel horror as opposed to reminders of how social media has made everyone’s lives worse.

extraction.body: Aaron Sorkin’s film grossed just $5.5 million on opening weekend, continuing a trend of audiences rejecting movies about our troubled times Sixteen years ago, at the height of Facebook’s dominance over the internet, Aaron Sorkin wrote a movie called “The Social Network” that became both a box office and a critical hit. Peter Travers called it “generation-defining” and sparked a debate. Its trailers were parodied on YouTube. It made $225 million at the box office and won Sorkin an Oscar for Best Adapted Screenplay. But his companion to that Obama-era classic, “The Social Reckoning,” was DOA this weekend. With a $5.5 million domestic opening, it has earned a quarter of the $22.6 million that “The Social Network” earned. Its trailers have gone largely ignored on TikTok and Instagram, the sites that have eclipsed Facebook in terms of youth relevance, and reception has been lukewarm at best, with a B- on CinemaScore and Rotten Tomatoes scores of 55% critics and 73% audience. “The Social Reckoning” marks the latest example of audiences rejecting a film that tackles tough issues that are already monopolizing real-life headlines. Just as last week’s “Digger” is a punishing satire that focuses on the bleak potential future brought by climate change and art’s insufficiency to tackle it, “The Social Reckoning” focuses on the deleterious effects of social media on democracy and the psyches of teenagers, both issues that have been in the news as recently as this past month, when Facebook’s parent company Meta reached a $17 billion settlement in a multi-state lawsuit regarding social media addiction. In terms of financial misfires, “The Social Reckoning” is nowhere near the abject disaster that Warner Bros.’ “Digger” has turned out to be, with estimates on that bomb’s loss reaching as high as $250 million . “Social Reckoning” is a co-production with Alcon that cost a reported $30 million, and with Sony enjoying a hot streak thanks to the historic $2.5 billion run of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “Resident Evil” on pace to clear $425 million worldwide after its $40 million opening in China this weekend, the studio will be able to easily shrug off this mild flop. With horror offerings like “Resident Evil” and fellow new release “Other Mommy” in theaters this weekend – and more to come later this month with Warner Bros./DC’s “Clayface” – the prospect of supernatural frights will always be more tantalizing for the majority of moviegoers than films about the frights of real life. “It’s almost an exact replica of last week with ‘Verity’ and ‘Digger’ where the cinematic equivalent of fast food is outperforming the cinematic equivalent of fine dining,” said Rentrak analyst Paul Dergarabedian. A deeper look at “The Social Reckoning” shows that it lacked any of the dramatic hooks that made “The Social Network” so intriguing to mature audiences and such a magnet for parodies back in 2010. Take a look back at some of the crackerjack trailers that were cut for “The Social Network,” including a teaser where lines from the film are typed out as Facebook status updates and the famous trailer that used Scala & Kolacny Brothers’ cover of Radiohead’s “Creep” (director David Fincher famously had a heavy hand in the film’s marketing). In those trailers, “The Social Network” promised a look inside the proto-tech-bro culture that gave rise to what was at the time the world’s most popular website and the lawsuits that spawned around its founding. But more than that, it hinged on a personal conflict with Jesse Eisenberg and Andrew Garfield as Mark Zuckerberg and Eduardo Saverin, best friends and Harvard roommates whose friendship would be destroyed by their world-changing creation. The dissolution of that friendship led to some of the most famous lines Sorkin has ever written, and Sony Pictures used them as the core of the film’s trailers: “A million dollars isn’t cool. You know what’s cool? A billion dollars.” “Your best friend is suing you for $600 million.” “You better lawyer up, because I am coming back for everything.” The film also came out at a time when there was a mystique and luster around tech wunderkinds like Zuckerberg that “The Social Network” promised to pierce. Wrapping it in a personal story about Zuck’s original sin in founding his billion-dollar company gave it an irresistible hook for audiences. At the time, Facebook itself was still considered a force for good in society. “‘The Social Network’ was a story of betrayal. It had Justin Timberlake in it. There were spoonfuls of sugar that helped the medicine go down, while ‘Social Reckoning’ is more of a document for our time,” said Dergarabedian. “I also think that there was more of an emotional connection to Facebook at the time because it was a new site, whereas now it feels more like a utility and not at all exciting, like turning on your coffeepot in the morning.” Sorkin asked the media to refer to “The Social Reckoning” as a “companion” to “The Social Network” rather than a sequel, and while Sony’s marketing might have suggested otherwise with posters that alluded to the 2010 film, it becomes clear upon viewing the film why that request was made. In “The Social Reckoning,” Zuckerberg, now played by Jeremy Strong, is a supporting character in the film. While a good portion of the movie is devoted to the CEO’s denial of the negative effects of Facebook’s failure to handle misinformation and his shocked response to the Jan. 6 Capitol riots, the core of the movie is focused on Frances Haugen, the data engineer at Facebook played by Mikey Madison, who risks her career by leaking secret files from Meta to Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz, played by Jeremy Allen White. In other words, the core of “The Social Reckoning” is a legal thriller exploring how a whistleblower is pushed to expose wrongdoing to the world. But Haugen’s relationship to her boss and to a reporter looking for a big story don’t have the same pull as a personal friendship. With a more didactic screenplay that explicitly outlines how Facebook’s algorithm throws facts and mental well-being to the wind in the name of keeping users engaged, “The Social Reckoning” failed the “what have you got that’s new” test for moviegoers. “The Social Reckoning” also found itself in that awkward place where it was both too soon and too late to tell this story. The Wall Street Journal investigations began in 2021, and nothing in the film will shock anyone even remotely familiar with the charges leveled at Facebook, with its recent settlement and a host of other related lawsuits still flooding the headlines this year. At the same time, there isn’t enough distance from the controversy to allow people to rediscover it like audiences did with Robert Pattinson’s Chris Hansen in “Primetime,” a film that is two decades removed from the cultural zenith of “To Catch a Predator.” Beyond the satisfaction of seeing Zuckerberg get skewered – the hollowness of which “Digger” aimed for – there wasn’t much to get people interested. But there may be some films on the horizon that, at least on a lower budget and more limited release scale, could get audiences interested in tougher issues. Next weekend, A24’s cryptic and wildly acclaimed Noah Oppenheim documentary, “You Can See Everything,” hits theaters, and later this winter, Luca Guadagnino’s Sam Altman-ChatGPT-focused “Artificial,” which will be released by Neon after Amazon MGM dropped the film. “You Can See Everything” is follows Elizabeth Holmes, the infamous creator of health technology startup Theranos, who went to prison in one of the most high-profile fraud cases of the past decade. With headlines, podcasts and a Hulu miniseries made about her, Holmes has been in the public consciousness as much as Zuckerberg. But “You Can See Everything” is passing the “what’s new” test with its premise: Holmes herself invited A24 to shoot a documentary in her house before she began her sentence, and “The Rehearsal” creator Nathan Fielder is the one who gets to ask her questions. “You Can See Everything” has become one of the buzziest films of the year within Hollywood and among cinephiles, and its limited release could yield the highest per theater average of 2026. If that word-of-mouth spreads to the point that A24 is willing to try a wide release – there are no details on such an expansion yet – it could be a breakthrough for non-music documentaries, which have struggled outside of the Amazon MGM-boosted “Melania” earlier this year. Meanwhile, “Artificial” has been hailed by critics as a film that feels closer in spirit to “The Social Network,” taking viewers inside the creation of an AI model that has the potential to end civilization. Like “You Can See Everything,” Neon is starting with a limited release on Christmas Day with a likely steady nationwide rollout in January 2027. It remains to be seen if Andrew Garfield’s performance as OpenAI founder Altman – which has been hailed as awards-worthy for its creepiness – will be enough to sell a wide audience on a grim film about a new technology that, like Facebook, is all over the news for all the wrong reasons.

extraction.body: On Monday, CBS News reported that federal agents searched the Washington, D.C., home of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar (D–Minn.), as part of an ongoing investigation that "centers on Omar's immigration paperwork." In a statement to the Associated Press, the Justice Department said agents from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI)—an office within the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) that conducts federal criminal investigations into immigration fraud and identity and benefits fraud—"executed a judicially authorized search warrant" as "part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation." The search warrant reportedly "lists a series of potential immigration crimes under investigation, including false statements and fraud in immigration paperwork, as well as a general conspiracy charge," according to The New York Times . The Times reported that federal officials are also investigating "whether Ms. Omar derived citizenship from a father who may have been ineligible to obtain naturalized status." In a statement, Omar called the investigation an "outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies," stating she did "nothing wrong." Omar has been in the Justice Department's crosshairs since January, when President Donald Trump announced that the department and Congress were "looking at 'Congresswoman' Illhan Omar, who left Somalia with NOTHING, and is now reportedly worth more than 44 Million Dollars." Trump was referencing an investigation by the House Ethics Committee, based on a 2025 financial disclosure form showing she and her husband held assets worth between $6 million and $30 million, a notable increase from her previous filings. Omar later filed an amended disclosure form that showed the assets were worth $18,004 to $95,000 after accounting for liabilities. However, in September, the Wall Street Journal reported that the Office of Congressional Conduct—which reviews allegations against House members and their staff—voted 5–1 to recommend that the House Ethics Committee dismiss the allegations. Per the Journal , investigators found no "substantial reason to believe that Rep. Omar reported false or incomplete information in her financial disclosures." Omar's office told the Journal she didn't catch the errors, which stemmed from erroneous valuations of her husband's businesses, because she "isn't involved in her husband's businesses and trusted the accountant involved." The investigation into Omar appears to be part and parcel of the Trump administration's weaponization of government—which the president vowed to end—adding to a list of cases that includes former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson , former FBI Director James Comey , and former National Security Adviser John Bolton . Omar's opposition to the Trump administration's immigration enforcement efforts, particularly in her home state of Minnesota, and her Somali heritage have made her a frequent target of the president and his allies. Last December, a federal indictment revealed a nearly $9 billion fraud scandal in Minnesota, much of it tied to the state's Somali immigrants. In March, Vice President J.D. Vance—who leads the Trump administration's anti-fraud task force — told right-wing commentator Benny Johnson that Omar "definitely committed immigration fraud against the United States of America." Vance accused Omar of "being at the center of a lot of the worst fraudsters in the Somali community." Vance doubled down in May, telling White House reporters the immigration fraud allegations were "something that the Department of Justice is looking at right now." He appeared to pull back from his March claim that he was certain Omar had committed immigration fraud, instead stating that while he didn't want to "prejudge an investigation," it "certainly seems like something fishy is there." In September, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin told Johnson that the investigation into Omar was still "ongoing," and that the department knew she had "married her brother to try to bring him into the United States." Omar's office has denied the accusations, which were first levied against her in 2016. Mullin claims the investigation into Omar is "not political." He could be telling the truth; federal investigators have scrutinized Omar before. In 2024, the Biden administration's Justice Department opened an investigation into Omar's "finances, campaign spending and interactions with a foreign citizen," according to The New York Times . Per the Times , the investigation eventually "stalled for lack of evidence." But Mullin's words are also hard to take at face value. Despite denying accusations of weaponizing the justice system, the Trump administration has time and again used dubious legal reasoning to investigate the president's political enemies. This includes New York Attorney General Letitia James, who, after successfully suing Trump for financial fraud, was indicted for mortgage fraud by Trump's Justice Department, which used the same petty justification on her. The president has also continued a campaign to indict Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, announcing last week that the White House would hold in-person hearings to look into claims she committed mortgage fraud. Ousting Cook would ostensibly allow the president to install a Fed governor aligned with his priorities. It's a tactic that failed Trump once before, when his Justice Department opened a criminal investigation into former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell for his handling of renovations at the central bank's headquarters. Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, dropped the probe in April, and the department ultimately found nothing criminal in Powell's conduct. An investigation will reveal whether Omar broke the law. Still, if it's anything like the Trump administration's previous efforts, the investigation is likely driven by political animus, not criminal behavior. Start your day with Reason . Get a daily brief of the most important stories and trends every weekday morning when you subscribe to Reason Roundup . NEXT: Are Warrantless Phone Searches at the Border Constitutional? The Supreme Court May Soon Decide. Tosin Akintola is an assistant editor at Reason . Celebrate your independence with a subscription to Reason magazine, your most trusted source of honest, insightful news and analysis. extraction.body: Ask your smart speaker to play K C B S Radio on Audacy WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal agents on Monday searched the home of Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar , a startling escalation in a criminal investigation that brings renewed focus to the frequent target of Trump administration derision in the final weeks of her reelection bid . The search of the Minnesota congresswoman's home so close to next month's midterm contests that will determine control of the House and the Senate was swiftly condemned by top Democrats in Congress, who raised questions about the timing given longstanding Justice Department protocol to avoid overt investigative steps involving political candidates in the direct run-up to an election. Omar, an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, said she was being targeted as one of the Republican's “political enemies.” The scope of the investigation was unclear, though Trump and officials in his administration have repeatedly referred in recent months to the existence of an inquiry into Omar, a Somali-born Democrat whose status as an immigrant to the U.S. and left-wing views have drawn scrutiny from the White House and other Republicans. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin last month cited an “ongoing investigation” that he suggested was examining potential fraud in her family's immigration paperwork. “Something's going to happen,” he said in a potential foreshadowing of the search. In a statement on X on Monday, Omar called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. extraction.body: On Monday, CBS News reported that federal agents searched the Washington, D.C., home of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar (D–Minn.), as part of an ongoing investigation that "centers on Omar's immigration paperwork." In a statement to the Associated Press, the Justice Department said agents from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI)—an office within the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) that conducts federal criminal investigations into immigration fraud and identity and benefits fraud—"executed a judicially authorized search warrant" as "part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation." The search warrant reportedly "lists a series of potential immigration crimes under investigation, including false statements and fraud in immigration paperwork, as well as a general conspiracy charge," according to The New York Times . The Times reported that federal officials are also investigating "whether Ms. Omar derived citizenship from a father who may have been ineligible to obtain naturalized status." In a statement, Omar called the investigation an "outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies," stating she did "nothing wrong." Omar has been in the Justice Department's crosshairs since January, when President Donald Trump announced that the department and Congress were "looking at 'Congresswoman' Illhan Omar, who left Somalia with NOTHING, and is now reportedly worth more than 44 Million Dollars." Trump was referencing an investigation by the House Ethics Committee, based on a 2025 financial disclosure form showing she and her husband held assets worth between $6 million and $30 million, a notable increase from her previous filings. Omar later filed an amended disclosure form that showed the assets were worth $18,004 to $95,000 after accounting for liabilities. However, in September, the Wall Street Journal reported that the Office of Congressional Conduct—which reviews allegations against House members and their staff—voted 5–1 to recommend that the House Ethics Committee dismiss the allegations. Per the Journal , investigators found no "substantial reason to believe that Rep. Omar reported false or incomplete information in her financial disclosures." Omar's office told the Journal she didn't catch the errors, which stemmed from erroneous valuations of her husband's businesses, because she "isn't involved in her husband's businesses and trusted the accountant involved." The investigation into Omar appears to be part and parcel of the Trump administration's weaponization of government—which the president vowed to end—adding to a list of cases that includes former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson , former FBI Director James Comey , and former National Security Adviser John Bolton . Omar's opposition to the Trump administration's immigration enforcement efforts, particularly in her home state of Minnesota, and her Somali heritage have made her a frequent target of the president and his allies. Last December, a federal indictment revealed a nearly $9 billion fraud scandal in Minnesota, much of it tied to the state's Somali immigrants. In March, Vice President J.D. Vance—who leads the Trump administration's anti-fraud task force — told right-wing commentator Benny Johnson that Omar "definitely committed immigration fraud against the United States of America." Vance accused Omar of "being at the center of a lot of the worst fraudsters in the Somali community." Vance doubled down in May, telling White House reporters the immigration fraud allegations were "something that the Department of Justice is looking at right now." He appeared to pull back from his March claim that he was certain Omar had committed immigration fraud, instead stating that while he didn't want to "prejudge an investigation," it "certainly seems like something fishy is there." In September, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin told Johnson that the investigation into Omar was still "ongoing," and that the department knew she had "married her brother to try to bring him into the United States." Omar's office has denied the accusations, which were first levied against her in 2016. Mullin claims the investigation into Omar is "not political." He could be telling the truth; federal investigators have scrutinized Omar before. In 2024, the Biden administration's Justice Department opened an investigation into Omar's "finances, campaign spending and interactions with a foreign citizen," according to The New York Times . Per the Times , the investigation eventually "stalled for lack of evidence." But Mullin's words are also hard to take at face value. Despite denying accusations of weaponizing the justice system, the Trump administration has time and again used dubious legal reasoning to investigate the president's political enemies. This includes New York Attorney General Letitia James, who, after successfully suing Trump for financial fraud, was indicted for mortgage fraud by Trump's Justice Department, which used the same petty justification on her. The president has also continued a campaign to indict Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, announcing last week that the White House would hold in-person hearings to look into claims she committed mortgage fraud. Ousting Cook would ostensibly allow the president to install a Fed governor aligned with his priorities. It's a tactic that failed Trump once before, when his Justice Department opened a criminal investigation into former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell for his handling of renovations at the central bank's headquarters. Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, dropped the probe in April, and the department ultimately found nothing criminal in Powell's conduct. An investigation will reveal whether Omar broke the law. Still, if it's anything like the Trump administration's previous efforts, the investigation is likely driven by political animus, not criminal behavior. Start your day with Reason . Get a daily brief of the most important stories and trends every weekday morning when you subscribe to Reason Roundup . NEXT: Are Warrantless Phone Searches at the Border Constitutional? The Supreme Court May Soon Decide. Tosin Akintola is an assistant editor at Reason . Celebrate your independence with a subscription to Reason magazine, your most trusted source of honest, insightful news and analysis. extraction.body: Ask your smart speaker to play K C B S Radio on Audacy WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal agents on Monday searched the home of Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar , a startling escalation in a criminal investigation that brings renewed focus to the frequent target of Trump administration derision in the final weeks of her reelection bid . The search of the Minnesota congresswoman's home so close to next month's midterm contests that will determine control of the House and the Senate was swiftly condemned by top Democrats in Congress, who raised questions about the timing given longstanding Justice Department protocol to avoid overt investigative steps involving political candidates in the direct run-up to an election. Omar, an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, said she was being targeted as one of the Republican's “political enemies.” The scope of the investigation was unclear, though Trump and officials in his administration have repeatedly referred in recent months to the existence of an inquiry into Omar, a Somali-born Democrat whose status as an immigrant to the U.S. and left-wing views have drawn scrutiny from the White House and other Republicans. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin last month cited an “ongoing investigation” that he suggested was examining potential fraud in her family's immigration paperwork. “Something's going to happen,” he said in a potential foreshadowing of the search. In a statement on X on Monday, Omar called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said. “I will not be silenced.” Though the Republican focus on Omar's background dates back years, the search notably took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking reelection. The Justice Department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election. Top Democrats seized on the timing as the latest instance in what they said was the “continued corrupt weaponization” against Trump's perceived adversaries. “For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations,” said a joint statement from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and other top congressional Democrats. “Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.” The search was carried out by agents with Homeland Security Investigations, which is part of the Department of Homeland Security. A DHS spokesperson referred questions to the Justice Department, which said in a statement that HSI agents had executed a judicially authorized search warrant in the Washington, D.C., area related to an ongoing federal criminal investigation but provided no other details. The street around Omar's home was blocked off Monday morning as some HSI agents removed boxes labeled “Seized Property Evidence.” The operation came just days after Trump referred pejoratively to Omar at a rally in Tennessee as coming from a country of “crime and squalor" and suggested that Vice President JD Vance “and our people” were investigating her. Hours after the search, Trump told reporters he had “nothing to do” with it and it's “really up to the DOJ.” Vance has in the past accused Omar of committing immigration fraud, an allegation she has denied, and has said the administration was looking for pathways to investigate her. Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota’s 5th District, including Minneapolis. She is part of The Squad of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim-American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress. When Republicans swept control of the House in 2023, they voted to oust Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee, citing her anti-Israel remarks. In January, Trump lashed out at Omar during a rally in Iowa hours before an assailant sprayed the congresswoman during her own town hall meeting in Minneapolis with a substance that turned out to be vinegar. The attacker was sentenced to 14 months in prison. Omar has repeatedly refuted allegations about her marriage and immigration status raised by conservative critics, even before she joined Congress. According to her House biography, Omar has said she and her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was 8: “The family spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya before coming to the United States in 1990s. In 1997, she moved to Minneapolis with her family.” Conservative online sites have alleged that Omar married a brother to commit immigration fraud. Omar has broadly denied the allegations as “disgusting lies" and called the insinuation “absurd and offensive.” “It certainly seems like something fishy is there, but everybody's entitled to equal justice under the laws,” Vance told reporters in May. “So we're going to investigate it. We're going to take a look at it. If we think there's a crime, we're going to prosecute that crime. And that's something the Department of Justice is looking at right now." In an interview last March with conservative podcaster Benny Johnson, Vance said without offering evidence that “we actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud against the United States of America.” Omar’s office at the time dismissed Vance’s claims as fabricated and defamatory. Last month, when the podcaster Johnson reminded Mullin about Vance's comments on Omar and asked whether anything would happen from that investigation, the Homeland Security secretary responded, “Something's going to happen.” He cited an “ongoing investigation” that he suggested was examining potential fraud in the family's immigration paperwork. “If we actually move a case forward, it's not a political case. It's actually a case because they did things wrong,” Mullin said. “If you decided to break the law or lie on the information that you gave to the United States, to be able to come into the United States ... there's no expiration to that.”
