Though the Republican focus on Omar's background dates back years, the search notably took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking reelection. The Justice Department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election. Top Democrats seized on the timing as the latest instance in what they said was the “continued corrupt weaponization” against Trump's perceived adversaries.

“For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations,” said a joint statement from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and other top congressional Democrats. “Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.”
The search was carried out by agents with Homeland Security Investigations, which is part of the Department of Homeland Security.

A DHS spokesperson referred questions to the Justice Department, which said in a statement that HSI agents had executed a judicially authorized search warrant in the Washington, D.C., area related to an ongoing federal criminal investigation but provided no other details.
The street around Omar's home was blocked off Monday morning as some HSI agents removed boxes labeled “Seized Property Evidence.”

The operation came just days after Trump referred pejoratively to Omar at a rally in Tennessee as coming from a country of “crime and squalor" and suggested that Vice President JD Vance “and our people” were investigating her. Hours after the search, Trump told reporters he had “nothing to do” with it and it's “really up to the DOJ.”
Vance has in the past accused Omar of committing immigration fraud, an allegation she has denied, and has said the administration was looking for pathways to investigate her.

Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota’s 5th District, including Minneapolis. She is part of The Squad of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim-American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress.
When Republicans swept control of the House in 2023, they voted to oust Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee, citing her anti-Israel remarks.

In January, Trump lashed out at Omar during a rally in Iowa hours before an assailant sprayed the congresswoman during her own town hall meeting in Minneapolis with a substance that turned out to be vinegar. The attacker was sentenced to 14 months in prison.
Omar has repeatedly refuted allegations about her marriage and immigration status raised by conservative critics, even before she joined Congress.

According to her House biography, Omar has said she and her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was 8: “The family spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya before coming to the United States in 1990s. In 1997, she moved to Minneapolis with her family.”

Conservative online sites have alleged that Omar married a brother to commit immigration fraud. Omar has broadly denied the allegations as “disgusting lies" and called the insinuation “absurd and offensive.”

“It certainly seems like something fishy is there, but everybody's entitled to equal justice under the laws,” Vance told reporters in May. “So we're going to investigate it. We're going to take a look at it. If we think there's a crime, we're going to prosecute that crime. And that's something the Department of Justice is looking at right now."

In an interview last March with conservative podcaster Benny Johnson, Vance said without offering evidence that “we actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud against the United States of America.” Omar’s office at the time dismissed Vance’s claims as fabricated and defamatory.

Last month, when the podcaster Johnson reminded Mullin about Vance's comments on Omar and asked whether anything would happen from that investigation, the Homeland Security secretary responded, “Something's going to happen.”
He cited an “ongoing investigation” that he suggested was examining potential fraud in the family's immigration paperwork.

“If we actually move a case forward, it's not a political case. It's actually a case because they did things wrong,” Mullin said. “If you decided to break the law or lie on the information that you gave to the United States, to be able to come into the United States ... there's no expiration to that.”

Additionally, FFR and FFAI will host a joint new product launch event on October 14, 2026, featuring four major launches focused on embodied AI robotics, Physical AI education, and developer enablement. The event will feature FF Nova, FF's first embodied AI humanoid robot designed for developers and educational institutions, through an exclusive, invitation-only launch. FFAI has also announced that FF will introduce FF Nova Mini, a humanoid robot designed for foundational Physical AI education, along with the EAI Education Ecosystem Brain and Curriculum Skills 2.0. In addition, FF will launch the FF Nova Developer Reinforcement Learning Platform and open exclusive early access to the developer community. FF EAI Robotics Ecosystem Inc. The FF EAI Robotics business has already achieved commercial deliveries of humanoid and biomimetic robotic products. Through its multi-form-factor robotic products, EAI technology platform, closed-loop data capabilities, and industry solutions, the business continues to advance the scaled adoption of robotics across real-world applications. extraction.body: Without a cause of death, it’s unclear if Russia’s precautions were the right ones. Over the weekend, the World Health Organization released a disease outbreak report on the events surrounding the death of a Russian infectious disease researcher earlier this month, highlighting that Russia has yet to report a confirmed cause of death. With that “key uncertainty,” the United Nations health agency said it remains impossible to assess the risk of the event or whether the public health measures Russia took were adequate to prevent spread of the unknown disease. The WHO reported that, so far, it has seen no evidence of ongoing transmission of the mystery disease. “However, confidence in the assessment remains limited by the absence of a confirmed etiological diagnosis, and the remaining uncertainty regarding the source and mode of exposure,” the agency wrote in its report. The agency laid out the order of events as information trickled out from Russian authorities, noting that it only became aware of the death via media reports on October 2. The WHO subsequently made contact with Russian authorities and requested information on October 3, 6, 7, and 8. Early media reports indicated that the lab worker had become ill on September 29, possibly following an incident at the lab, the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute (APRI) of Siberia and the Far East. Some early reports suggested that the researcher—who was identified by media as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova—died of the plague after breaking a test tube. On October 2, the Irkutsk branch of Russian health agency Rospotrebnadzor (RPN) said in a statement that a “special sanitary-epidemiological expert commission” had already met over a suspected case of a high-threat pathogen. Sanitary and epidemic control measures were put in place, including identifying, monitoring, and testing all contacts. At the time, RPN said that all contacts had tested negative for high-threat pathogens. On October 6, Russia’s National Focal Point for the International Health Regulations (NFP) first responded to the WHO’s information requests, saying that no case of plague had been recorded in Irkutsk Oblast. The NFP confirmed that an APRI lab worker had died from a severe case of pneumonia after developing symptoms compatible with an acute respiratory viral infection. The worker was tested for a number of high-threat pathogens, but all the tests had come back negative. Doctors categorized the cause of death as being from pneumonia of undetermined etiology. The NFP also reiterated information from RPN about the public health measures taken and that people in contact with the lab worker all tested negative for high-threat pathogens. The NFP added that the widest range of possible contacts were identified and tested in accordance with Russia’s public health laws. In follow-up responses, the NFP gave more details about testing and some results that weren’t concerning. It said authorities conducted 5,500 laboratory tests on contacts. They tested for a range of pathogens, including influenza, SARS-CoV-2, other respiratory infections, and bacterial infections, including plague and Streptococcus. Among the contacts, they identified two cases of COVID-19, three cases of rhinovirus, and one case of Haemophilus spp., a common bacteria group that includes those that can cause respiratory infections and pneumonia. They also found a few opportunistic infections. As of October 9, Russian authorities told WHO that they had not detected any high-threat pathogens in the laboratory’s research portfolio in any of the contacts, and they were no longer being monitored. The monitoring period was set for seven days for all the contacts. Authorities also added that the worker who died was not infected with plague bacteria, Yersinia pestis, and the worker had been vaccinated against the infection due to the occupational hazard. They added that no lab biosafety or biosecurity incident had occurred at APRI, and the deceased worker had not traveled outside the region within the two weeks before becoming ill. Reviewing all the information coming out of Russia, the WHO was largely at a loss as to what happened and what risk the event posed, concluding: “A key uncertainty for this event is the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker.” Without the cause of death, the agency can’t “independently assess whether the duration of the reported monitoring period for contacts was sufficient to exclude all plausible causes of the fatal illness.” They also aren’t ruling out the possibility of a laboratory-associated exposure. The global health body has not confirmed plague as the cause of death and says it has not identified evidence of ongoing transmission associated with the event. Pneumonia Of Unknown Etiology According to information provided by Russian authorities, testing did not identify plague or other tested high-threat pathogens. The death has been classified as pneumonia of undetermined etiology, while WHO says it has not received information identifying the causative agent responsible for the fatal illness. 'No Confirmation On Cause' A key uncertainty in the assessment is the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the dead laboratory worker. WHO has stated that it cannot independently assess whether the reported monitoring period for contacts was sufficient to exclude all plausible causes of the fatal illness without a confirmed diagnosis. The absence of an identified pathogen means that the source of the illness remains unclear, and further clinical, epidemiological and laboratory information is needed to establish the cause. extraction.body: Without a cause of death, it’s unclear if Russia’s precautions were the right ones. Over the weekend, the World Health Organization released a disease outbreak report on the events surrounding the death of a Russian infectious disease researcher earlier this month, highlighting that Russia has yet to report a confirmed cause of death. With that “key uncertainty,” the United Nations health agency said it remains impossible to assess the risk of the event or whether the public health measures Russia took were adequate to prevent spread of the unknown disease. The WHO reported that, so far, it has seen no evidence of ongoing transmission of the mystery disease. “However, confidence in the assessment remains limited by the absence of a confirmed etiological diagnosis, and the remaining uncertainty regarding the source and mode of exposure,” the agency wrote in its report. The agency laid out the order of events as information trickled out from Russian authorities, noting that it only became aware of the death via media reports on October 2. The WHO subsequently made contact with Russian authorities and requested information on October 3, 6, 7, and 8. Early media reports indicated that the lab worker had become ill on September 29, possibly following an incident at the lab, the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute (APRI) of Siberia and the Far East. Some early reports suggested that the researcher—who was identified by media as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova—died of the plague after breaking a test tube. On October 2, the Irkutsk branch of Russian health agency Rospotrebnadzor (RPN) said in a statement that a “special sanitary-epidemiological expert commission” had already met over a suspected case of a high-threat pathogen. Sanitary and epidemic control measures were put in place, including identifying, monitoring, and testing all contacts. At the time, RPN said that all contacts had tested negative for high-threat pathogens. On October 6, Russia’s National Focal Point for the International Health Regulations (NFP) first responded to the WHO’s information requests, saying that no case of plague had been recorded in Irkutsk Oblast. The NFP confirmed that an APRI lab worker had died from a severe case of pneumonia after developing symptoms compatible with an acute respiratory viral infection. The worker was tested for a number of high-threat pathogens, but all the tests had come back negative. Doctors categorized the cause of death as being from pneumonia of undetermined etiology. The NFP also reiterated information from RPN about the public health measures taken and that people in contact with the lab worker all tested negative for high-threat pathogens. The NFP added that the widest range of possible contacts were identified and tested in accordance with Russia’s public health laws. In follow-up responses, the NFP gave more details about testing and some results that weren’t concerning. It said authorities conducted 5,500 laboratory tests on contacts. They tested for a range of pathogens, including influenza, SARS-CoV-2, other respiratory infections, and bacterial infections, including plague and Streptococcus. Among the contacts, they identified two cases of COVID-19, three cases of rhinovirus, and one case of Haemophilus spp., a common bacteria group that includes those that can cause respiratory infections and pneumonia. They also found a few opportunistic infections. As of October 9, Russian authorities told WHO that they had not detected any high-threat pathogens in the laboratory’s research portfolio in any of the contacts, and they were no longer being monitored. The monitoring period was set for seven days for all the contacts. Authorities also added that the worker who died was not infected with plague bacteria, Yersinia pestis, and the worker had been vaccinated against the infection due to the occupational hazard. They added that no lab biosafety or biosecurity incident had occurred at APRI, and the deceased worker had not traveled outside the region within the two weeks before becoming ill. Reviewing all the information coming out of Russia, the WHO was largely at a loss as to what happened and what risk the event posed, concluding: “A key uncertainty for this event is the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker.” Without the cause of death, the agency can’t “independently assess whether the duration of the reported monitoring period for contacts was sufficient to exclude all plausible causes of the fatal illness.” They also aren’t ruling out the possibility of a laboratory-associated exposure. The World Health Organisation (WHO) says it has found no evidence of ongoing transmission linked to the death of a laboratory worker in Russia, following reports that pneumonic plague was suspected as the cause. In a Disease Outbreak News update published on Saturday, 10 October 2026, the WHO said it was informed of the death of an employee of the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East on 2 October. According to reports, the worker died on the same day after being hospitalised on 29 September with severe pneumonia. Pneumonic plague was suspected following possible occupational exposure in a laboratory setting. However, the Russian Federation’s National Focal Point for the International Health Regulations confirmed the death to the WHO and reported that no recent cases of plague had been registered in Irkutsk Oblast. The authorities also said investigations found no evidence of a laboratory biosecurity incident, contrary to media reports. The WHO said laboratory tests conducted on the deceased worker and contacts were negative for the high-threat pathogens tested, while no additional cases of severe pneumonia linked to the incident had been reported. All identified contacts were medically monitored in healthcare facilities or at home and remained asymptomatic throughout the follow-up period. Quarantine measures were also introduced at the hospital where the worker had been treated. “Based on the information provided by NFP, WHO has not identified evidence of ongoing transmission associated with this event,” the organisation said. However, the global health agency noted that a key uncertainty remained because the cause of the worker’s death had not been conclusively established. The WHO said it would continue monitoring the situation and assess any potential public health implications as further information becomes available. Pneumonic plague is a severe form of plague that affects the lungs and can spread between people through infectious respiratory droplets. However, the suspected diagnosis in this case has not been confirmed. The WHO’s update is based on information supplied by Russian health authorities and does not establish a confirmed plague outbreak. © 2026 TVC Communications - Owner of TVC News Get a curated selection of the latest Nigeria and global news, right in your email.

It's not just the debt that many tech companies are piling on that is a concern, but as AI advances and tech is doing more for people and businesses than it did before, there are also significant risks related to automation. With stocks like Nvidia ( Nasdaq: NVDA ) posting moonshot growth over the past year, Canadian investors are no doubt wondering — should I be investing in “AI stocks?”

It’s easy to lose sight of this in all the buzz, but artificial intelligence (AI) stocks are simply tech companies that are making incredibly smart machines. Whether it’s using face recognition to unlock your phone or “auto-correcting” your grammatical errors, artificial intelligence has already infiltrated our daily lives.

And the technology is only getting started: The worldwide AI market is forecasted to grow immensely before the end of this decade. PWC sees AI technology contributing up to $15.7 trillion to the global economy by 2030. 1
So if you believe artificial intelligence will play a growing role in our lives, investing in AI stocks could be a smart way to benefit from that prediction.
Here, we’ll break down the ins and outs of AI investing in Canada to help you decide if it’s the right investment for you in 2026.

When our analyst team has a stock tip, it can pay to listen. After all, Stock Advisor Canada's total average return is 103% - a market-crushing outperformance compared to 88% for the S&P/TSX Composite Index.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is a branch of computer science tasked with making machines that emulate human intelligence. These machines make decisions without human interference, and they can learn from past experiences to make better decisions in the future.
Generally speaking, AI stocks can be broken down into two groups

This list of Canadian AI stocks to invest in will no doubt evolve as the technology continues to grow at a furious pace. Already, there are dozens of startups that could one day hit the public markets.
For now, let’s look at a few of the top artificial intelligence companies already trading on the Toronto Stock Exchange .

Kinaxis ( TSX: KXS ) remains one of the most compelling Canadian names at the intersection of SaaS (software-as-a-service) and AI, offering mission-critical supply chain management tools that global enterprises rely on daily. Its RapidResponse platform enables real-time simulation, planning, and problem detection across complex logistics networks – capabilities that became indispensable during the pandemic and remain essential amid ongoing supply disruptions and the shift toward AI-driven efficiency. While the stock doesn’t pay a dividend, its value proposition lies squarely in growth, recurring revenue, and long-term compounding.

The company continues to post strong momentum though 2025. In its most recent quarter, SaaS recurring revenue grew more than 17%, supporting a broader trend of consistent double-digit annual revenue gains. Net profit jumped 150% year over year, highlighting the scalability of its model. Despite these results, the share price has remained in a relatively tight range, suggesting the market hasn’t yet fully recognized the company’s strength.

What sets Kinaxis apart is the “stickiness” of its customer base. With blue-chip clients in sectors like automotive, healthcare, and consumer goods, multi-year contracts and mission-critical integrations create a high barrier to switching. This stability fuels predictable subscription income, strong gross margins, and a healthy flow of cash that Kinaxis uses to reinvest in innovation rather than risky expansion. The company also maintains a debt-free balance sheet, an advantage few tech peers can claim.

With enterprise demand rising for AI-enhanced planning tools this year, and financial performance strengthening quarter after quarter, Kinaxis looks well positioned for a breakout if sentiment shifts. For investors seeking high-quality, profitable tech exposure into 2026, this remains a standout candidate.

Celestica ( TSX: CLS ) has emerged as one of Canada’s most explosive growth stories in 2025, powered by its deep exposure to AI data-center hardware and hyperscaler infrastructure. Once known primarily as a contract manufacturer, the company has transformed into a central supplier for next-generation compute and cloud systems. That shift has unlocked extraordinary shareholder returns: Celestica is up more than 350% over the past year and nearly 3,000% since late 2022, making it the best-performing large-cap tech stock in the country.

Momentum remains strong this year. In Q3 2025, Celestica delivered 28% revenue growth, a record operating margin, and rising contributions from hyperscaler clients—its most important growth engine as AI/ML compute demand accelerates. With cloud providers racing to expand capacity for high-performance servers, networking gear, and storage systems, Celestica has secured a multiyear runway of orders tied directly to the global AI buildout. Analysts now expect the company’s earnings to more than double by 2028, reflecting both margin expansion and aggressive production scaling.

Celestica’s positioning within the AI hardware stack is what sets it apart. The company supplies critical components needed for AI workloads, training clusters, and massive cloud deployments, making it a direct beneficiary of capex cycles led by Meta, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and other hyperscalers. Demand for compute and storage capacity continues to climb sharply in 2025 as AI rollouts intensify, driving consistently strong backlogs and repeated quarterly earnings beats.

OpenText ( TSX: OTEX ) is one of the more intriguing value opportunities in Canadian tech heading into 2025, with its transformation efforts now gaining traction after several reset years. The Waterloo-based enterprise software company focuses on information management, cybersecurity, and AI-enhanced cloud solutions. Its Aviator platform — which integrates generative AI, predictive analytics, and conversational search — has become central to its strategy as customers shift toward higher-margin cloud subscriptions.

After a difficult start to last year, OpenText has staged a meaningful rebound. Shares have climbed more than 40% over the past six months, boosted by improving financial execution and clearer integration progress following the Micro Focus acquisition. In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025, revenue rose 4.5% sequentially to US$1.3 billion, while adjusted EBITDA jumped more than 12% to US$443.9 million. That pushed the EBITDA margin to 33.9%, up from 32.7% a year earlier. The stock offers a dividend yield near 2.8%, making it a rare total-return play within Canada’s AI sector.

A key driver of the recent rally has been OpenText’s strategic shift toward cloud and AI, supported by a multiyear effort to streamline operations. To reduce debt and concentrate capital on cloud innovation, the OpenText divested non-core assets including the AMC business in 2024 and just recently, eDOCS. With fresh guidance calling for 1–2% revenue growth in fiscal 2026, investors have taken the return to forward visibility as a sign that the balance-sheet cleanup and product consolidation are working.

Momentum into late 2025 remains strong, with the stock breaking above the $50 level for the first time since early 2024. For investors seeking a stable, cash-flow-rich way to participate in the rise of AI and enterprise cloud, OTEX stands out as a compelling, under-the-radar option.

Another SaaS company, Docebo ( TSX: DCBO ) remains one of the more compelling long-term growth stories in Canada’s tech sector, even if its recent share-price performance suggests otherwise. The stock has fallen sharply in 2025 pressured by leadership turnover, tougher competition, and a broader market debate around the profitability of AI-aligned software firms. That decline has pushed Docebo’s valuation down to appealing levels, with its forward earnings multiple now below 20. As a pure growth name, the company does not pay a dividend, so returns are entirely tied to business execution and share-price appreciation.

Operationally, the company continues to deliver. Docebo’s most recent quarterly report showed revenue up 11% to more than $61 million, ahead of expectations, with profitability rising more than 20% year over year. Earlier quarters also exceeded guidance, including second-quarter increases of 14.5% in revenue and 15.4% in adjusted EPS. Multi-year customer agreements help support revenue stability, even as the broader learning-software landscape becomes more competitive.

The AI market has evolved from the “hype” phase of previous years into a period of massive commercial deployment. By the start of 2026, AI has become a fundamental driver of corporate earnings, with the Canadian AI market projected to surpass $40 billion (USD) in revenue this year.
While the sector offers immense growth, the investment landscape has become more discerning:

Canadian investors should remain cautious of micro-cap “pure-play” AI stocks, which often exhibit extreme volatility. Instead, the focus for 2026 is on companies with established competitive moats and proprietary data.

Canada’s AI landscape offers diverse opportunities beyond the global mega-caps. Conservative investors can look to blue-chip giants like CGI Inc. and OpenText, which provide stability by integrating AI into massive existing service contracts. Growth-focused investors may prefer specialized SaaS leaders like Kinaxis or Docebo, which are leveraging AI to dominate supply chain and e-learning niches. For high-reward infrastructure plays, Celestica remains a standout, benefiting from the global surge in demand for AI data center hardware.

The Bottom Line: AI stocks remain a strong buy for those with a long-term horizon. However, success in 2026 requires moving past the buzzwords to evaluate a company’s fundamental business model and its ability to turn AI integration into bottom-line profit.

If you don’t want to invest in individual AI stocks, you can always buy an AI-focused exchange-traded fund (ETF) . ETFs are an easy way to invest in a bunch of companies at the same time, so you get more diversification and potentially take on less risk than you would by investing in any single stock.

extraction.body: Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks have been soaring in value in recent years, with Nvidia ( NVDA -1.29% ) leading the charge. The chip giant is worth a massive $5.4 trillion, as its products are crucial for many tech companies looking to stay ahead of the competition. The opportunities are enormous, but what doesn't get nearly as much attention are the risks. It's not just the debt that many tech companies are piling on that is a concern, but as AI advances and tech is doing more for people and businesses than it did before, there are also significant risks related to automation. What could derail AI stocks is the risk that AI agents pose to both the companies that develop them and the customers relying on them. There have been multiple reports about AI agents not staying within their confines, which is a growing issue in the tech sector . One of the most high-profile events included OpenAI agents launching a cyberattack against Hugging Face a few months ago. The company is now facing a lawsuit due to that. There are multiple issues stemming from this type of risk. First is the obvious one -- a company can face high legal costs if its agents go rogue and cause harm. In addition, OpenAI will need to spend more time and money to develop agents more carefully to ensure the risks are minimal in the future. And even then, there may still be concerns if it has done enough. The second issue is that companies may be less willing to deploy agents if there is the potential for these types of situations. Even if an agent doesn't attack another company, it may still improperly use or share confidential data. If a company has to spend additional efforts on safeguarding its assets, it would make investments in AI even more costly. At a time when spending on AI is already under scrutiny, companies may balk at the idea, especially if there are doubts about the potential payoff. The result could be a slowdown of demand, which could derail the bull story around not only Nvidia but also other AI stocks . Nvidia is a top growth stock to own, so long as the AI growth story is a promising one. But if there are any cracks in it, or if there are signs that companies are beginning to pull back on AI-related spending, that can wreak havoc on Nvidia's growth and its valuation. Currently, the stock looks cheap as it's trading at just 25 times its estimated future profits. But that's based on analyst expectations of how it will do in the future. If those expectations unravel, the stock may not look nearly as cheap and attractive anymore, and that may be the case for many other stocks as well. Investors should consider the risks related to AI before deciding whether to buy Nvidia or any other stock, as ignoring them could prove costly down the road. Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks have been soaring in value in recent years, with Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) leading the charge. The chip giant is worth a massive $5.4 trillion, as its products are crucial for many tech companies looking to stay ahead of the competition.

The opportunities are enormous, but what doesn't get nearly as much attention are the risks. It's not just the debt that many tech companies are piling on that is a concern, but as AI advances and tech is doing more for people and businesses than it did before, there are also significant risks related to automation. What could derail AI stocks is the risk that AI agents pose to both the companies that develop them and the customers relying on them.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

There have been multiple reports about AI agents not staying within their confines, which is a growing issue in the tech sector . One of the most high-profile events included OpenAI agents launching a cyberattack against Hugging Face a few months ago. The company is now facing a lawsuit due to that.

There are multiple issues stemming from this type of risk. First is the obvious one -- a company can face high legal costs if its agents go rogue and cause harm. In addition, OpenAI will need to spend more time and money to develop agents more carefully to ensure the risks are minimal in the future. And even then, there may still be concerns if it has done enough.

The second issue is that companies may be less willing to deploy agents if there is the potential for these types of situations. Even if an agent doesn't attack another company, it may still improperly use or share confidential data. If a company has to spend additional efforts on safeguarding its assets, it would make investments in AI even more costly. At a time when spending on AI is already under scrutiny, companies may balk at the idea, especially if there are doubts about the potential payoff.
The result could be a slowdown of demand, which could derail the bull story around not only Nvidia but also other AI stocks .

Nvidia is a top growth stock to own, so long as the AI growth story is a promising one. But if there are any cracks in it, or if there are signs that companies are beginning to pull back on AI-related spending, that can wreak havoc on Nvidia's growth and its valuation.

Currently, the stock looks cheap as it's trading at just 25 times its estimated future profits. But that's based on analyst expectations of how it will do in the future. If those expectations unravel, the stock may not look nearly as cheap and attractive anymore, and that may be the case for many other stocks as well.
Investors should consider the risks related to AI before deciding whether to buy Nvidia or any other stock, as ignoring them could prove costly down the road.

passages: Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks have been soaring in value in recent years, with Nvidia ( NVDA -1.29% ) leading the charge. The chip giant is worth a massive $5.4 trillion, as its products are crucial for many tech companies looking to stay ahead of the competition.

The opportunities are enormous, but what doesn't get nearly as much attention are the risks. It's not just the debt that many tech companies are piling on that is a concern, but as AI advances and tech is doing more for people and businesses than it did before, there are also significant risks related to automation. What could derail AI stocks is the risk that AI agents pose to both the companies that develop them and the customers relying on them.

There have been multiple reports about AI agents not staying within their confines, which is a growing issue in the tech sector . One of the most high-profile events included OpenAI agents launching a cyberattack against Hugging Face a few months ago. The company is now facing a lawsuit due to that.

There are multiple issues stemming from this type of risk. First is the obvious one -- a company can face high legal costs if its agents go rogue and cause harm. In addition, OpenAI will need to spend more time and money to develop agents more carefully to ensure the risks are minimal in the future. And even then, there may still be concerns if it has done enough.

The second issue is that companies may be less willing to deploy agents if there is the potential for these types of situations. Even if an agent doesn't attack another company, it may still improperly use or share confidential data. If a company has to spend additional efforts on safeguarding its assets, it would make investments in AI even more costly. At a time when spending on AI is already under scrutiny, companies may balk at the idea, especially if there are doubts about the potential payoff.
The result could be a slowdown of demand, which could derail the bull story around not only Nvidia but also other AI stocks .

Nvidia is a top growth stock to own, so long as the AI growth story is a promising one. But if there are any cracks in it, or if there are signs that companies are beginning to pull back on AI-related spending, that can wreak havoc on Nvidia's growth and its valuation.

sources.title: Epic Delays Disney Game, Goes AI First [2026] - shattered.io
passages: Epic Games has pushed back the release of its long-awaited collaboration with Walt Disney Co., and the reason has nothing to do with a bug list or a missing boss fight.

According to reporting from Bloomberg and GamesIndustry.biz, Epic told the development team working on the project to rebuild its workflow around an “AI first” model, trading hand-written code and traditional art pipelines for generative tools including Anthropic’s Claude.
Claude’s presence in a flagship Epic production is notable on its own.

Anthropic has spent much of 2026 pushing its models deeper into coding and agentic workflows, and Claude Opus 5.5’s expanded context window has made it a popular choice for large, sprawling codebases, exactly the kind a live-service multiplayer shooter accumulates.
Using it for both code and creative asset direction on a Disney-licensed title signals a level of institutional confidence from Epic that goes beyond a pilot program.

Epic’s own engine business has repeatedly used technical superiority as a competitive weapon against Unity, and the two companies have traded market share in recent quarters, with Unreal Engine 6 reportedly holding roughly 42% share against Unity’s 30% .
An AI-first production pipeline, if it proves faster without compromising quality, would be another point Epic could use to recruit studios away from competing engines.

If it instead produces a visibly rough, delayed game built on one of the most recognizable entertainment properties in the world, it becomes a cautionary tale that rival engine makers will be happy to cite.

For Anthropic, the exposure is reputational in the opposite direction, a positive one if the eventual game ships well, a negative one if critics trace production problems back to AI-generated code or art.
The takeaway: this delay is not proof that AI-first game development fails, nor is it proof that it works.
It had been positioned internally for a March launch.
That timeline has now slipped, and as of October 12, 2026, Epic has not communicated a new date publicly or internally, according to the reporting reviewed for this story.
Did Epic confirm the AI shift caused the delay?

Against that backdrop, Epic retooling a flagship Disney collaboration around generative workflows looks less like an outlier bet and more like catching up to an industry-wide shift that is already underway.
For Epic, the immediate financial exposure from a single delayed title is limited.

There is also a simpler explanation worth taking seriously: Epic may have concluded that shipping in March with the original pipeline would have produced a worse game than shipping later with a retooled one.

What distinguishes this moment is the specificity of the claim: not “we upgraded our engine” or “we built an AI tool,” but “we rebuilt our production process around AI mid-development on a named, dated, licensed product.” That is a much higher-stakes bet than anything on the list above, and it is why the Disney delay is drawing more scrutiny than a typical engine migration story would.
Disney licenses its characters across dozens of partners every year and has weathered delays on games before without major fallout, provided the eventual product meets brand standards.

extraction.body: Epic Games has pushed back the release of its long-awaited collaboration with Walt Disney Co., and the reason has nothing to do with a bug list or a missing boss fight. According to reporting from Bloomberg and GamesIndustry.biz, Epic told the development team working on the project to rebuild its workflow around an “AI first” model, trading hand-written code and traditional art pipelines for generative tools including Anthropic’s Claude. The game, a multiplayer shooter built around Marvel and Star Wars characters, was slated for a March release. That date is gone, and Epic has not named a replacement. The story lands at an awkward moment for the games industry, which is already bracing for a wave of AI-driven production changes. Epic is not a scrappy startup experimenting on a side project. It is the company behind Fortnite, the Unreal Engine that powers a huge share of AAA development, and a decade of public fights over app store economics. When Epic changes how it builds games, other studios take notice, and this delay is becoming a case study in what “AI first” actually means when it collides with a licensed, high-profile project tied to two of the most valuable entertainment brands on the planet. The project in question is described across multiple outlets, including GamesIndustry.biz , as a multiplayer shooter drawing characters and settings from Marvel and Star Wars, two franchises Disney owns outright. It had been positioned internally for a March launch. That timeline has now slipped, and as of October 12, 2026, Epic has not communicated a new date publicly or internally, according to the reporting reviewed for this story. What makes this delay different from a routine schedule slip is the instruction that reportedly came with it. Developers on the project were told to adopt an AI first production model, a phrase that, per the internal messaging described in the reporting, meant leaning on generative tools for both code and art rather than treating AI as a supplementary tool. One of the game’s directors reportedly wrote in an internal message that there would be “no more hand-written code,” and that the game’s art would be “generated with full AI workflows.” Those are striking lines for a licensed project built on characters as tightly controlled as Spider-Man or Darth Vader, where visual consistency with decades of established designs typically matters as much as gameplay feel. Epic’s communications director, Jake Jones, addressed the shift in a statement to Ars Technica , saying the company is “embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do.” The framing is deliberate: Epic wants the story to read as developers directing AI tools, not AI tools replacing developers. Whether that distinction holds up once the game actually ships is a separate question, and one the industry will be watching closely. Human developers were still instructed to manage and guide the AI-generated output rather than being removed from the loop entirely, based on the available reporting. That detail matters because it suggests Epic is not attempting to automate the project end to end without oversight, but rather restructuring what human developers spend their time doing, shifting them from production tasks toward direction, curation, and quality control. It is tempting to draw a straight line from “AI first mandate” to “project delayed,” but the reporting does not actually confirm that causation. Alongside the AI shift, reports also point to underestimated staffing needs and development time as contributing factors, a far more ordinary explanation that shows up in postmortems for licensed games going back decades. Disney properties come with extensive approval processes, legal review, and brand guidelines that can slow any studio regardless of its tooling. Still, the optics are hard to ignore. A studio pivots to AI-generated art and code on a project, and the same project misses its date. Readers and competitors will draw their own conclusions, and some of those conclusions will be unfair to the engineers and artists who had no say in the production strategy. The more useful question is whether retooling a project mid-development around generative tools is itself a schedule risk, independent of whether the underlying technology works. Switching pipelines partway through any game’s production cycle has historically been one of the most reliable ways to blow a deadline, long before generative AI entered the picture. There is also a simpler explanation worth taking seriously: Epic may have concluded that shipping in March with the original pipeline would have produced a worse game than shipping later with a retooled one. Delays framed around quality are common in games marketing, but they are not automatically false. Without an official release date or a direct comment from Epic on root cause, both readings remain live possibilities, and this article treats them as such rather than asserting one as fact. “AI first” is quickly becoming one of those phrases every tech company wants to claim and few define consistently. For Epic’s Disney project, the reporting indicates it meant generative tools, including Anthropic’s Claude, handling first-pass code generation and full AI workflows producing art assets, with human staff reviewing, directing, and refining the output rather than originating it from scratch. That is a meaningfully different workflow from using AI as autocomplete inside an IDE, which is how most studios have deployed these tools so far. Claude’s presence in a flagship Epic production is notable on its own. Epic Games is shifting to an “AI first” development strategy for its collaboration with the Walt Disney Company, letting AI models write all the code and guide all the artwork for an upcoming shooter. That’s according to a Bloomberg report , which cites unnamed people familiar with the project who commented on the significant pivot in internal development at the Unreal Engine maker. Human developers will be tasked with managing and guiding code and art assets generated by models such as Anthropic’s Claude, according to internal Epic employee messages viewed by Bloomberg. That means “no more hand-written code” and art assets “generated with full AI workflows,” according to the report. The $1.5 billion collaboration between Epic and Disney, announced in early 2024 , was slated to release a Marvel- and Star Wars-themed shooter in March 2027. That project has now been delayed indefinitely amid the AI-related shakeup and understaffed, slower-than-expected development thus far, according to the report. “We’re embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do,” an Epic spokesperson said in a statement. “We have a huge pivot underway here at Epic, moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration,” Epic CEO Tim Sweeney wrote on social media shortly after the Bloomberg story was posted. “The aim isn’t to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal.” Sweeney and Epic have long been bullish on what they see as an impending game development revolution spurred by AI. In an interview with IGN in June , Sweeney saw the technology resulting in games with “the possibility of infinite dialogue with a really simple setup for creators,” leading to situations where “small teams will be able to create games with immense amounts of characters and immense and interactive worlds.” Sweeney said last November that AI usage disclosure tags such as those required by Valve’s Steam platform “make no sense” because AI tools “will be involved in nearly all future production.” Epic laid off over 1,000 employees in March , citing a “downturn in Fortnite engagement” as the main reason behind the move. Months later, Fortnite Senior External Development Manager Stephanie Arnette said that “I know everyone’s biggest fear is, ‘Oh my god, AI is going to take all our jobs.’ That’s not our goal. The goal is to make us more efficient.” Last May, Epic and Disney faced some embarrassment when an AI-voiced Darth Vader character added to Fortnite started repeating curse words and uttering some baffling opinions before a hotfix was rolled out. A survey of over 2,300 game industry professionals ahead of this year’s Game Developers Conference found that 36 percent used generative AI tools as part of their jobs, including 30 percent of those at game development studios. But those AI tools were used for tasks like research and brainstorming (by 81 percent of AI-using respondents) much more than for code assistance (47 percent) and prototyping (35 percent). extraction.body: Epic Games has pushed back the release of its long-awaited collaboration with Walt Disney Co., and the reason has nothing to do with a bug list or a missing boss fight. According to reporting from Bloomberg and GamesIndustry.biz, Epic told the development team working on the project to rebuild its workflow around an “AI first” model, trading hand-written code and traditional art pipelines for generative tools including Anthropic’s Claude. The game, a multiplayer shooter built around Marvel and Star Wars characters, was slated for a March release. That date is gone, and Epic has not named a replacement. The story lands at an awkward moment for the games industry, which is already bracing for a wave of AI-driven production changes. Epic is not a scrappy startup experimenting on a side project. It is the company behind Fortnite, the Unreal Engine that powers a huge share of AAA development, and a decade of public fights over app store economics. When Epic changes how it builds games, other studios take notice, and this delay is becoming a case study in what “AI first” actually means when it collides with a licensed, high-profile project tied to two of the most valuable entertainment brands on the planet. The project in question is described across multiple outlets, including GamesIndustry.biz , as a multiplayer shooter drawing characters and settings from Marvel and Star Wars, two franchises Disney owns outright. It had been positioned internally for a March launch. That timeline has now slipped, and as of October 12, 2026, Epic has not communicated a new date publicly or internally, according to the reporting reviewed for this story. What makes this delay different from a routine schedule slip is the instruction that reportedly came with it. Developers on the project were told to adopt an AI first production model, a phrase that, per the internal messaging described in the reporting, meant leaning on generative tools for both code and art rather than treating AI as a supplementary tool. One of the game’s directors reportedly wrote in an internal message that there would be “no more hand-written code,” and that the game’s art would be “generated with full AI workflows.” Those are striking lines for a licensed project built on characters as tightly controlled as Spider-Man or Darth Vader, where visual consistency with decades of established designs typically matters as much as gameplay feel. Epic’s communications director, Jake Jones, addressed the shift in a statement to Ars Technica , saying the company is “embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do.” The framing is deliberate: Epic wants the story to read as developers directing AI tools, not AI tools replacing developers. Whether that distinction holds up once the game actually ships is a separate question, and one the industry will be watching closely. Human developers were still instructed to manage and guide the AI-generated output rather than being removed from the loop entirely, based on the available reporting. That detail matters because it suggests Epic is not attempting to automate the project end to end without oversight, but rather restructuring what human developers spend their time doing, shifting them from production tasks toward direction, curation, and quality control. It is tempting to draw a straight line from “AI first mandate” to “project delayed,” but the reporting does not actually confirm that causation. Alongside the AI shift, reports also point to underestimated staffing needs and development time as contributing factors, a far more ordinary explanation that shows up in postmortems for licensed games going back decades. Disney properties come with extensive approval processes, legal review, and brand guidelines that can slow any studio regardless of its tooling. Still, the optics are hard to ignore. A studio pivots to AI-generated art and code on a project, and the same project misses its date. Readers and competitors will draw their own conclusions, and some of those conclusions will be unfair to the engineers and artists who had no say in the production strategy. The more useful question is whether retooling a project mid-development around generative tools is itself a schedule risk, independent of whether the underlying technology works. Switching pipelines partway through any game’s production cycle has historically been one of the most reliable ways to blow a deadline, long before generative AI entered the picture. There is also a simpler explanation worth taking seriously: Epic may have concluded that shipping in March with the original pipeline would have produced a worse game than shipping later with a retooled one. Delays framed around quality are common in games marketing, but they are not automatically false. Without an official release date or a direct comment from Epic on root cause, both readings remain live possibilities, and this article treats them as such rather than asserting one as fact. “AI first” is quickly becoming one of those phrases every tech company wants to claim and few define consistently. For Epic’s Disney project, the reporting indicates it meant generative tools, including Anthropic’s Claude, handling first-pass code generation and full AI workflows producing art assets, with human staff reviewing, directing, and refining the output rather than originating it from scratch. That is a meaningfully different workflow from using AI as autocomplete inside an IDE, which is how most studios have deployed these tools so far. Claude’s presence in a flagship Epic production is notable on its own. Anthropic has spent much of 2026 pushing its models deeper into coding and agentic workflows, and Claude Opus 5.5’s expanded context window has made it a popular choice for large, sprawling codebases, exactly the kind a live-service multiplayer shooter accumulates. Using it for both code and creative asset direction on a Disney-licensed title signals a level of institutional confidence from Epic that goes beyond a pilot program. The internal line about “no more hand-written code” is the most quoted detail from the reporting, and for good reason. Most studios that have adopted AI coding assistants still describe the tools as accelerants, something that drafts boilerplate or suggests fixes while engineers remain the primary authors. A directive suggesting the reverse, that AI generates the code and engineers primarily review and steer it, represents a different division of labor. It is closer to how some teams already use Claude Code for scaffolding entire features, just scaled up to a full production title rather than a side project or prototype. Art generation carries its own set of complications that code generation does not. Marvel and Star Wars characters are governed by brand bibles that specify exact silhouettes, color palettes, and proportions. Generative art tools are good at producing plausible-looking content quickly, but matching decades-old brand guidelines with pixel-level consistency across hundreds of assets is a harder bar to clear than writing functional code. If Disney’s approval process rejected early AI-generated assets for failing to match established character designs, that alone could account for schedule slippage independent of any coding issues. Epic did not arrive at this decision in a vacuum. The broader game engine market has been racing toward AI-assisted tooling for more than a year. Google and Unity launched Spark, an AI game maker aimed at adult creators , and Unity’s own roadmap for Unity 7 includes AI-assisted shader work promising dramatic speed gains. Capcom has gone even further on the content side, building a suite of six internal AI programs under its REX initiative to help remake assets in its RE Engine. Against that backdrop, Epic retooling a flagship Disney collaboration around generative workflows looks less like an outlier bet and more like catching up to an industry-wide shift that is already underway. Epic’s own engine business has repeatedly used technical superiority as a competitive weapon against Unity, and the two companies have traded market share in recent quarters, with Unreal Engine 6 reportedly holding roughly 42% share against Unity’s 30% . An AI-first production pipeline, if it proves faster without compromising quality, would be another point Epic could use to recruit studios away from competing engines. If it instead produces a visibly rough, delayed game built on one of the most recognizable entertainment properties in the world, it becomes a cautionary tale that rival engine makers will be happy to cite. Reaction across gaming press and developer communities, including outlets like Dexerto , has split along predictable lines. Some read the delay as validation that AI-generated code and art still need more runway before they can anchor a major licensed release. Others see it as evidence that studios willing to absorb short-term schedule pain for structural workflow change will come out ahead once the tools mature. Both camps are, in effect, making predictions about technology that is evolving month to month, which is exactly why a single delayed game should not be treated as definitive proof of either position. The comparison makes Epic’s situation look distinct for one reason: it is the only entry on this list where AI tooling was applied directly to a specific, dated, licensed product rather than to an engine feature, an internal catalog project, or a standalone consumer app. That distinction is exactly why the delay carries more weight than it otherwise would. A missed internal roadmap milestone is routine. A missed date on a co-branded Marvel and Star Wars title, attached publicly to an AI production method, becomes a referendum on the method itself, fairly or not. Generative AI’s march into game production did not start with Epic’s Disney project, and it is worth placing this story on a timeline rather than treating it as an isolated event. Jagex leaned on modern engine tooling, including a jump to Unreal Engine, for its RS4 relaunch of RuneScape, a title reportedly ending a 25-year wait for a new entry in the MMO’s core lineage . Rocket League’s developers took an even bigger technical leap, skipping two engine generations entirely to jump from Unreal Engine 3 straight to Unreal Engine 6 , a move that reflects how aggressively studios are willing to overhaul foundational tooling when the payoff looks big enough. What distinguishes this moment is the specificity of the claim: not “we upgraded our engine” or “we built an AI tool,” but “we rebuilt our production process around AI mid-development on a named, dated, licensed product.” That is a much higher-stakes bet than anything on the list above, and it is why the Disney delay is drawing more scrutiny than a typical engine migration story would. For Epic, the immediate financial exposure from a single delayed title is limited. Epic is privately held and does not disclose per-project revenue, so there is no stock reaction to track the way there would be for a public company. The bigger stake is reputational and strategic: Epic has spent years positioning Unreal Engine as the technically superior choice for AAA and licensed development, competing directly against Unity for engine market share. A high-profile stumble on a Disney collaboration, even one eventually resolved, gives ammunition to studios weighing whether to commit to Epic’s AI-forward production philosophy for their own licensed projects. For Disney, the calculus is different. Disney licenses its characters across dozens of partners every year and has weathered delays on games before without major fallout, provided the eventual product meets brand standards. The bigger risk for Disney is not the delay itself but the possibility that AI-generated likenesses of Spider-Man, Darth Vader, or other closely guarded characters drift even slightly from established designs in ways fans notice immediately. Brand consistency, not ship dates, is typically Disney’s highest priority in licensing deals of this scale. For Anthropic, the exposure is reputational in the opposite direction, a positive one if the eventual game ships well, a negative one if critics trace production problems back to AI-generated code or art. Anthropic has been aggressively marketing Claude’s coding capabilities throughout 2026, and a visible win inside a Disney-branded, Epic-published title would be a significant proof point for enterprise and studio customers evaluating whether to adopt similar workflows. For engineers and artists working inside Epic or watching from competing studios, the practical question is what “managing and guiding AI-generated work” actually looks like day to day. Reviewing AI output at scale, catching subtle art inconsistencies, and debugging code you did not write yourself are different skills than originating that work from scratch, and they are not skills every studio has systematically trained its staff to use. Studios considering a similar pivot would be wise to treat this less as a tooling swap and more as a role redefinition that needs its own onboarding and quality assurance processes. There is also a morale dimension that rarely shows up in corporate statements. Developers who spent months building systems for a shooter under one production model, then were told midstream to shift toward reviewing AI output instead of writing it, are absorbing a significant change in how they spend their working hours. Jones’s statement that Epic developers remain “the visionaries and creative drivers” is Epic’s attempt to reassure that workforce, but whether that framing matches the day-to-day experience on the ground is something only the people on the project can really judge. Strip away the Disney and Marvel names, and this story is really about whether “AI first” is a production philosophy mature enough to survive contact with a real, dated, high-stakes commercial release. Plenty of studios have used AI tools successfully on smaller, lower-visibility features. Far fewer have attempted to rebuild an entire project’s code and art pipeline around generative tools mid-development, on a licensed product, with a named external partner watching the outcome. Epic’s experience, whatever the eventual verdict, will be one of the most closely studied case studies the industry has for judging that question. The takeaway: this delay is not proof that AI-first game development fails, nor is it proof that it works. It is one data point from one studio on one project, wrapped in a licensing relationship that adds pressure the typical AI pilot program never faces. The next real signal will come when Epic actually sets, and hits or misses, a new date, and when players finally get to judge whether “full AI workflows” produced art that looks and feels like the Marvel and Star Wars they already know. According to reporting from Bloomberg and GamesIndustry.biz, Epic told the development team working on the project to rebuild its workflow around an “AI first” model, trading hand-written code and traditional art pipelines for generative tools including Anthropic’s Claude.
Claude’s presence in a flagship Epic production is notable on its own.

Anthropic has spent much of 2026 pushing its models deeper into coding and agentic workflows, and Claude Opus 5.5’s expanded context window has made it a popular choice for large, sprawling codebases, exactly the kind a live-service multiplayer shooter accumulates.
Using it for both code and creative asset direction on a Disney-licensed title signals a level of institutional confidence from Epic that goes beyond a pilot program.

Epic’s own engine business has repeatedly used technical superiority as a competitive weapon against Unity, and the two companies have traded market share in recent quarters, with Unreal Engine 6 reportedly holding roughly 42% share against Unity’s 30% .
An AI-first production pipeline, if it proves faster without compromising quality, would be another point Epic could use to recruit studios away from competing engines.

If it instead produces a visibly rough, delayed game built on one of the most recognizable entertainment properties in the world, it becomes a cautionary tale that rival engine makers will be happy to cite.

For Anthropic, the exposure is reputational in the opposite direction, a positive one if the eventual game ships well, a negative one if critics trace production problems back to AI-generated code or art.
The takeaway: this delay is not proof that AI-first game development fails, nor is it proof that it works.
It had been positioned internally for a March launch.
That timeline has now slipped, and as of October 12, 2026, Epic has not communicated a new date publicly or internally, according to the reporting reviewed for this story.
Did Epic confirm the AI shift caused the delay?

Against that backdrop, Epic retooling a flagship Disney collaboration around generative workflows looks less like an outlier bet and more like catching up to an industry-wide shift that is already underway.
For Epic, the immediate financial exposure from a single delayed title is limited.

There is also a simpler explanation worth taking seriously: Epic may have concluded that shipping in March with the original pipeline would have produced a worse game than shipping later with a retooled one.

What distinguishes this moment is the specificity of the claim: not “we upgraded our engine” or “we built an AI tool,” but “we rebuilt our production process around AI mid-development on a named, dated, licensed product.” That is a much higher-stakes bet than anything on the list above, and it is why the Disney delay is drawing more scrutiny than a typical engine migration story would.
Disney licenses its characters across dozens of partners every year and has weathered delays on games before without major fallout, provided the eventual product meets brand standards.

Geneva, Switzerland, Oct. 06, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Investment to support next-generation satellites and integration of SEALSQ’s post-quantum security technologies across space and ground infrastructure SEALSQ Corp (NASDAQ: LAES) ("SEALSQ" or "Company"), a company that focuses on developing and selling Semiconductors, PKI, and Post-Quantum technology hardware and software products, today announced that it led a $10 million private investment in public equity (PIPE) in WISeSat.Space Holdings Corp. (Nasdaq: SAIQ) (“WISeSat.Space”), a space technology company. The investment closed on October 1, 2026. WISeSat.Space and SEALSQ are subsidiaries of WISeQey Corp. (formerly known as WISeKey International Holding AG, “WISeQey”) (Nasdaq/SIX: WQEY), a global quantum cybersecurity and space IoT company. The PIPE Investment closed on October 1, 2026, concurrently with the closing of the Business Combination. The purchase price per share, equal to the redemption price, was $10.79 per share. The Subscription Agreement includes a price-protection mechanism that may result in the issuance of additional WISeSat Ordinary Shares to SEALSQ under certain conditions if the volume-weighted average price of WISeSat Ordinary Shares for the 10 consecutive trading days ending on the 60th calendar day after Closing is below the purchase price, subject to a maximum issuance of an additional 1,073,216 shares. SEALSQ is also subject to customary lock-up restrictions under the Subscription Agreement. The investment provides WISeSat.Space with additional equity capital as it advances its space cybersecurity strategy, including the planned expansion of its satellite infrastructure, and the integration of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) security technologies into its satellites, ground and user-segment architectures. WISeSat.Space is engaged in the development of a new generation of WISeSat.Space satellites , intended to support trusted communications, digital identity, and data exchange through space-based infrastructure. The planned architecture is intended to integrate advanced cybersecurity capabilities with satellite communications, creating a foundation for trusted and resilient communications across space and ground infrastructure. A key focus of the program is expected to be the development of quantum-resilient secure communications capabilities , designed to address emerging cybersecurity threats associated with the future evolution of quantum computing. By incorporating post-quantum security into the satellite communications architecture, WISeSat aims to strengthen device authentication, data integrity, and secure communications across space and ground infrastructure. The collaboration with SEALSQ is also expected to support the development of a broader trusted space infrastructure , under which WISeSat.Space would provide satellite capacity and related space and ground infrastructure, while SEALSQ would use that capacity to support the development and delivery of planned quantum and post-quantum services using its secure semiconductor, cryptographic and trusted identity technologies. Carlos Moreira, CEO of SEALSQ, WISeSat.Space and WISeQey noted, “This investment brings together two companies within the WISeQey group around a shared goal: making space infrastructure secure against both current and future cyber threats. For WISeSat.Space, it provides capital to advance our next generation of satellites and to build post-quantum security into our space, ground and user segments. For SEALSQ, it opens a path to deliver quantum and post-quantum services using WISeSat.Space's satellite capacity. Together, secure semiconductors, cryptography and satellite connectivity have the potential to help set new standards for trust and security across the emerging space economy.” John O’Hara, CFO of SEALSQ, added, “This investment supports SEALSQ’s strategy to extend the application of our secure semiconductor, cryptographic and trusted identity technologies into space-based communications. By supporting the development of WISeSat.Space’s infrastructure, we aim to create a foundation for delivering post-quantum security services across satellite and ground networks. Our focus is on translating this collaboration into commercial opportunities that support long-term value for SEALSQ shareholders.” The new satellite program is expected to contribute to WISeSat.Space’s broader vision of bringing trust and sovereignty to space transactions , enabling secure interactions among independently operated space and terrestrial systems while strengthening the protection of critical digital assets. The WISeQey Root of Trust ensures the integrity of online transactions between objects and people. For more information on WISeQey’s strategic direction and its subsidiary companies, please visit www.wisekey.com. WISeSat is a space technology company focused on secure satellite communications for Internet of Things applications. passages: Geneva, Switzerland – May 5, 2026 — WISeKey International Holding Ltd (SIX: WIHN; NASDAQ: WKEY ), a global leader in cybersecurity, digital identity and IoT, today provides an update on the strategic progress of its space subsidiary WISeSat.Space ("WISeSat"), from its initial secure satellite communications pilot missions launched in 2021 to advancing its positioning as "WISE Space Advanced Technologies," a European quantum-secure space-technology company.

By integrating post‑quantum payloads developed with SEALSQ and aligning with its QSOC roadmap, WISeSat is building a differentiated, defensible platform that can support new revenue streams in secure data services, edge processing, and trusted connectivity for both governmental and commercial customers.

The subsidiaries include (i) SEALSQ Corp (Nasdaq: LAES), which focuses on semiconductors, PKI, and post-quantum technology products, (ii) WISeKey SA, which specializes in RoT and PKI solutions for secure authentication and identification in IoT, blockchain, and AI, (iii) WISeSat AG which focuses on space technology for secure satellite communication, specifically for IoT applications, (iv) WISe.ART Corp which focuses on trusted blockchain NFTs and operates the WISe.ART marketplace for secure NFT transactions, and (v) SEALCOIN AG which focuses on decentralized physical internet with DePIN technology and houses the development of the SEALCOIN platform.

The Company is developing a security architecture designed to protect communications, digital identities and satellite operations against both conventional cyberattacks and emerging quantum-computing threats. Its approach combines post-quantum semiconductor technologies from its sister company, SEALSQ Corp.’s (Nasdaq: LAES) with trusted digital identity and cryptographic key management across connected devices, ground infrastructure and future satellite platforms. “Security is a core differentiator in our strategy to build a satellite communications business serving governments, enterprises and critical infrastructure operators,” said Carlos Moreira, Founder and CEO of WISeSat.Space. “As satellites become increasingly critical infrastructure for our digital economy, protecting them throughout their operational lives is central to our value proposition. Our ambition is to bring trust into every layer, from the semiconductor and connected device to the ground station and satellite. By integrating post-quantum technologies across connected devices, ground infrastructure and satellites, we aim to strengthen our competitive position, address demand for secure, sovereign communications and create long-term shareholder value.” Following its October 2026 business combination and Nasdaq listing, WISeSat.Space closed a $10 million PIPE investment led by SEALSQ to accelerate the development of its quantum-resilient space architecture. WISeSat.Space’s existing network and partner infrastructure include access to 9 active low-earth-orbit satellites, supported by ground stations in Lausanne, Switzerland, and La Línea de la Concepción, Spain. This operational base supports the development of the Company’s next-generation Quantum Spatial Orbital Cloud (“QSOC”). Its long-term roadmap targets a 100-satellite sovereign constellation by 2033, subject to financing, technical development, regulatory approvals and launch availability. Integration of the next-generation PQC architecture is being advanced through planned deployments and does not imply that every satellite currently accessible through the network already carries the same post-quantum hardware. Issued on June 22, 2026, Executive Order 14412 directs the transition of federal information systems to NIST-approved post-quantum cryptography and supports migration planning for critical infrastructure owners and operators. For federal high-value assets and high-impact systems, excluding National Security Systems, the order sets migration objectives of December 31, 2030, for PQC key establishment and December 31, 2031, for PQC digital signatures. It also directs the development of proposed federal procurement requirements addressing applicable NIST standards. WISeSat.Space’s architecture is being developed to support these objectives. Regulatory alignment and compliance will be assessed for individual implementations against applicable standards, cryptographic module validation requirements and customer procurement conditions. The Company’s technology strategy draws on SEALSQ’s Quantum Shield QS7001 and QVault TPM platforms, which support NIST-standardized algorithms including: These capabilities are intended to complement hardware-based protection of cryptographic keys and trusted identities. Using standardized algorithms provides a foundation for migration; end-to-end security also depends on their implementation, integration and operation. WISeSat.Space is developing its architecture around several applications where communications security and long-term data protection are essential. Government and sovereign communications. Post-quantum key establishment and authentication can support protected satellite connectivity for government agencies, remote facilities and emergency-response teams. Combined with sovereign identity and key-management arrangements, the architecture is intended to help customers retain control over access to sensitive communications. Critical infrastructure monitoring. Satellite-connected sensors can provide telemetry from energy installations, water networks, transport corridors and other assets beyond terrestrial network coverage. Trusted device identities and authenticated messages can help operators verify the source and integrity of readings used for maintenance, incident detection and operational decisions. Satellite command and software integrity. Post-quantum signatures can support verification of satellite commands and software updates, helping protect against impersonation and unauthorized modifications. Hardware-protected keys provide a foundation for authenticating operational systems, while secure update mechanisms can support cryptographic upgrades during a satellite’s service life. Remote industrial IoT and logistics. Connected equipment, containers and monitoring devices can use satellite links to report location, condition and operational status. Authentication and protected communications are intended to help customers trust the data received from remote assets and reduce exposure to forged messages. Long-term protection of sensitive information. Government, industrial and infrastructure data may remain confidential for years. Post-quantum key establishment is intended to reduce exposure to “harvest now, decrypt later” attacks, in which adversaries collect encrypted traffic today for possible decryption using future quantum computers.
