It is an honor to participate alongside Her Excellency Rosa Villavicencio, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Colombia. I would like to thank the Government of Colombia for its ongoing cooperation with the Verification Mission and for the efforts recognized in the Secretary-General’s latest report to advance peacebuilding in the country.

It is also a pleasure to welcome Olga Quintero, a renowned peasant leader and advocate for peace in the Catatumbo region —an area that is emblematic of the complex conflict in Colombia and crucial to the consolidation of peace. She also exemplifies the important role that women have played in building peace in Colombia.
I am pleased that the Security Council is today resuming the good practice of including the voices of civil society in its meetings on Colombia.
The holding of largely peaceful and more inclusive elections has been a feature of Colombia’s positive evolution under the Peace Agreement. It is essential for the country to stay on this trajectory.

Allow me to reiterate in this regard the Secretary-General's congratulations on the peaceful participation of the Colombian people in the legislative elections held in March. Despite concerns during the campaign period over incidents of violence and the presence of illegal armed groups in conflict-affected regions, adequate measures were taken and election day was not adversely affected by security incidents — a demonstration of Colombia’s strong institutions.

I commend the role played by security forces in protecting the vote, the vigilance exercised by national and international observers, and the valuable role also played by the Office of the Ombudsperson in monitoring conditions and in promoting adherence to the Commitment to a Free and Peaceful Electoral Process.

With the presidential campaign now in full swing ahead of elections on 31 May, the Mission is adding its voice to the call for authorities and all concerned to ensure a safe and peaceful environment, free of violence and stigmatization. I reiterate my condemnation of reported threats against presidential candidates, and I call again for State authorities to guarantee the safety of all participants in the electoral process.

The Verification Mission also stands ready to contribute once again —as it did during the congressional elections— to the exercises carried out by national authorities, some of them using mechanisms of the Peace Agreement, to analyse security risks and coordinate preventive actions. Ensuring the security of candidates and voters should continue to be the utmost priority.

The latest report of the Secretary-General traces implementation across the three pillars of the mandate, as established by the Security Council in resolution 2798 of last October: reintegration of former combatants; security guarantees; and comprehensive rural reform. They are three elements at the core of the Final Peace Agreement, whose implementation contributes to peace and security in the country.

We have fully restructured the Mission to reflect the refocused mandate and streamlined further in line with UN80 reductions. This has resulted in a substantially leaner configuration, while still enabling the Mission to maintain a suitable regional field presence, which is essential for effective verification, as well as engagement with local communities, authorities and peace signatories. Receiving, now, the resources approved in the budget is essential to delivering on the mandate across Colombia.

The realities on the ground vary from region to region, and ongoing conflict dynamics are highly complex. Although security has deteriorated in some parts of the country, previously neglected areas have also been afforded with new opportunities, made possible by the Peace Accord. In visits to Mission offices across this diverse landscape, what I see is close collaboration with Colombian stakeholders and counterparts, who strongly value its unique presence in the field.

The efforts to expand access to land as part of the comprehensive rural reform are bringing hope —via the arrival of long-awaited dividends of peace— to marginalized regions and communities who suffered grievously during the armed conflict.

Behind the statistics we report on hectares delivered toward the numerical goals established in the Peace Agreement, are the people who are the beneficiaries on the ground, such as the members of a peasant community I visited in February in the Cesar Department, in northern Colombia. This was region engulfed in violence during the conflict, marked by massacres and widespread displacement of people from their land. Many members of this community I visited were direct victims, and so it was inspiring to see them recently receive a sizeable plot of land as part of the rural reform. Despite some practical challenges and security-related concerns, the community is setting down roots on this land, having established a school, begun building their own houses, and having launched fish-farming, corn and yuca growing projects. Women are prominent leaders of this community. While appreciative of the land, they still need further attention from the State to turn this opportunity into a sustainable future. This is one of 30 select cases of land adjudication in conflict-affected regions that the Mission is prioritizing in its verification.

Overall, progress has been made in recent years in providing access to land to numerous beneficiaries. However, continued efforts will be required to fulfil the objectives laid out in the rural reform. It is not only a matter of distributing land, but also ensuring its productivity, guaranteeing the safety of beneficiaries, and clarifying the legal ownership status of the plots. I wish to recognize the important step taken in this direction, with the enactment in March of a statutory law on the functioning of the Agrarian Jurisdiction. I am hopeful that this important entity —which is to address land-related disputes— will soon become fully operational through additional legislation that is pending adoption in Congress.

The rural reform also encompasses investments in local and regional development projects in conflict-affected areas known as the PDET regions —plans that were recently extended through 2037 by Congress—, as well as the implementation of sectorial plans to greatly expand state services over time, such as rural roads, education, health, irrigation, and electricity.

All told, as noted by the Secretary-General in his report, the Rural Reform is fundamental for consolidating lasting peace and security in Colombia. It aims to extend State presence and address inequalities that have fuelled conflict in the country for decades. By unlocking viable economic opportunities, it can also provide sustainable alternatives to illicit economies, thereby helping to break the cycle of violence.

The laying down of arms by Latin-America’s oldest and largest guerilla group was not only a feat in and of itself, but so is the fact that, nearly ten years later, more than 11,000 men and women from the former FARC-EP remain actively engaged in their reintegration into society. This process has been repleted with challenges, however, given the fragile socioeconomic, infrastructural, and security conditions in rural areas where many former combatants have settled.

As reported by the Secretary-General, the provision of land and housing is progressing, though more still needs to be done to complete those tasks, to strengthen security guarantees and to ensure the sustainability of reintegration. The product of the hard work carried out by former combatants can be drastically affected when security conditions deteriorate. I hope that State entities, in acknowledgement of the perseverance of former combatants, will increase all efforts to ensure the conditions that would allow them to look to the future with confidence.

The political reintegration of the former guerrilla is also an essential part of the peace process, allowing for their peaceful participation in the democratic political life of the country. Following the results of the recent congressional elections, I would like to commend the Comunes Party for the constructive role its representatives played as legislators during a transitional period in which it held guaranteed seats in the Congress under the Peace Agreement. Although that provision has now expired, the former combatants, as one of the two signatory parties of the Peace Accord, maintain all associated responsibilities and functions. I strongly welcome the clear commitments expressed by its leaders to continue abiding by the Peace Agreement, working for its full implementation, and I look forward to their active role going forward.
Mr. President, Distinguished Members of the Council,

Colombia remains today more peaceful than during peak years of the conflict. However, as we have reported extensively, a number of rural areas are still strongly impacted by the presence of illegal armed groups. Their ongoing clashes over territorial control and illicit economies are bringing violence and hardship to entire communities. We condemn, among others, their increased recruitment and use of children.

The Catatumbo region is a case in point of what is happening in such areas —its population caught in the middle of disputes by armed groups in one of the regions with the highest concentrations of coca in the country. During a visit there in January, in the aftermath of renewed clashes in the area, I visited a hamlet where homes had been heavily damaged in drone attacks between rival groups. Explosive hazards had been found near schools. Residents were fearful of landmines and raised concerns about the slow arrival of humanitarian assistance. As long as violence, territorial disputes, or governance vacuums persist in any part of the country, they risk undermining national stability and eroding the gains made elsewhere.

Through its presence and verification activities in conflict-affected regions, such as Catatumbo, the Mission is contributing to the detection of risks to communities and to the calls for timely and well-articulated responses by authorities to these risks. The Mission is also helping to give visibility to humanitarian and other needs that should be addressed under the Peace Agreement. The Mission is a regular participant in security guarantees mechanisms of, and related to, the Peace Agreement, that are important for addressing security needs of vulnerable groups in particular —including former combatants, women and those involved in the exercise of politics.
Mr. President, Distinguished Members of the Council,

When the Council meets next on Colombia in July, elections will have concluded, and a new Government will be preparing to begin its term in August. Whoever assumes the presidency will face a formidable challenge in consolidating peace and security in the regions still affected by conflict.

As the Secretary-General reminds us in his latest report, the Peace Agreement provides a comprehensive roadmap for addressing both the root causes and consequences of the conflict, for bringing inclusive development to long-neglected regions where violence is still present —impacting its ethnic communities disproportionately— and for ensuring there is justice and redress for the victims. Significant progress has occurred over the years since the Agreement was signed, yet much remains to be done, and much can be achieved through focused efforts in the coming years.

The territories where the Agreement has not been sufficiently implemented are precisely where the most acute problems persist today. Stabilizing the regions still affected by conflict requires comprehensive implementation. And as the Secretary-General has also stated in his report, peace strategies and effective security actions can and should be carried out in complement with one another in order to produce the desired results.

The Security Council has been an essential partner to Colombia in the search for lasting peace and security. The Verification Mission stands ready to continue to assist the Colombians along this path. Despite the difficulties, it remains a path that is well worth following.
I thank you, Mr. President. Download here the Report of the Secretary-General on the UN Verification Mission in Colombia S/2026/229

The United Nations Verification Mission in Colombia is a special political mission established in 2016 by the Security Council to verify the implementation of the Final Peace Agreement and support Colombia’s efforts to end conflict and build sustainable peace.

extraction.body: Miroslav Jenča, Special Representative of the Secretary-General and Head of the United Nations Verification Mission in Colombia It is my pleasure to brief the Security Council once again on Colombia. The Council’s role has been critical in supporting Colombia’s path to peace, and I deeply appreciate its constant support for the Verification Mission. I am particularly pleased that Foreign Minister Omar Bula, His Excellency, is participating for the first time in this quarterly session of the Council on Colombia. I greatly appreciate the constructive dialogue we have had with the Foreign Minister, as well as with other Government representatives, during these first two months of his term. I reiterate the commitment of the United Nations Verification Mission to continue working in close cooperation with the Colombian Government and State authorities, the High Contracting Party to the Agreement, communities —including women leaders— and all those committed to building a peaceful, secure and prosperous future. Madam President, Distinguished Members of the Council, As this Council is aware, the new Government of President Abelardo de la Espriella began its term in particularly difficult circumstances, challenged to respond on its third day in office to a devastating earthquake. The UN country team supported the national humanitarian response, with backing from the Verification Mission. I reiterate my condolences for the loss of life, injuries and damage incurred. I commend the Colombian people for their resilience in the face of adversity. The new administration also took office facing serious challenges that the Secretary-General described in his latest report: mounting insecurity due to the expansion of armed groups and illegal economies in areas still affected by conflict, and the deficits in development and state presence in those very same regions. These are key factors that have fuelled violence for decades in Colombia. The Government has identified security, the reduction of violence and the development of the territories as key objectives in this context. In our engagement with the Government we have discussed how the Verification Mission, working within its mandate fostering the continued implementation of the Peace Agreement can contribute to the realization of these objectives, especially the protection of communities and increased state presence throughout the country. At nearly ten years since its signing, the Agreement has made undeniable contributions to advancing peace in the country – ending the longest standing insurgency of the conflict, establishing policies and programs to advance development and state presence in rural areas, and the building of creative pathways -- that deserve our continued strong support -- to ensuring transitional justice and reparations to victims. Implementation over the years has also had many shortcomings, and much remains to be done to advance the Agreement in parallel with security policies that can be mutually reinforcing. The Agreement should be implemented comprehensively. And as the Secretary-General states in his report, “the years ahead will be pivotal to consolidate progress achieved to date and leverage the opportunities afforded.” The Government has stated its intention to comply with the Constitutional and legal obligations arising from the Agreement, however as the Secretary-General has also noted in his report, it has yet to fully outline its approach to implementation. We look forward to the further definition of its policies and we stand ready to support the Government in this regard, making available the Specific plans ensuring adequate financing of critical programs and peace institutions, the assignment of leadership and coordination responsibilities within the Government, and the activation of established commissions that are part of the architecture of the Agreement would provide important assurances and address the concerns raised by various stakeholders of the Agreement about the continuity of implementation. The United Nations Verification Mission has accompanied Colombia in its efforts to advance peace and security across successive administrations and stages of the peace process, always working with full respect for Colombia’s sovereignty and the principle of national ownership. Through the Mission’s regional, subregional and local offices, it has developed relationships of trust with local authorities, communities, former combatants, and civil society organizations, while accumulating valuable insight into some of Colombia's most remote and conflict-affected territories. We carry out verification with a proactive spirit of assisting the parties to overcome bottlenecks to moving forward in implementation. The Mission is also investing in digital innovation aimed at optimizing its analysis and verification in the field. Since my arrival to Colombia a year ago, I have visited almost all of the Mission's 29 territorial offices, witnessing firsthand the value of this presence on the ground. It undoubtedly constitutes one of the Mission’s key added values at this moment in time, positioning it, among others, to accompany efforts to extend the reach of state institutions bringing benefits to the population. We have observed how rapidly local dynamics can shift and how security, governance, economic opportunities, and social cohesion remain deeply interconnected. One lesson has remained constant throughout this time: sustainable peace requires security, and security requires an effective and lasting presence of State institutions. In my conversations with community representatives and local officials, they consistently emphasize the importance of sustained efforts to improve living conditions, expand sustainable economic opportunities, strengthen public services, and enhance presence of and confidence in -- local institutions. These are the main objectives of the rural reform provisions of the Peace Agreement. For example, the Development Programmes with Territorial Focus (PDET), which are monitored by the Verification Mission, foster the transformation of regions and expansion of state presence. Instruments such as the Agrarian Jurisdiction and the Multipurpose Cadaster contribute to achieving legal certainty over property that is critical for development and private-led investment and growth. Greater security and prosperity in these regions benefit not only local communities but the country as a whole. Madam President, Distinguished Members of the Council, The reintegration process remains one of the most significant achievements of the implementation of the 2016 Peace Agreement. More than eleven thousand former combatants continue to pursue their transition to civilian life. Their sustained commitment over nearly a decade reflects a steadfast determination to build peaceful and productive futures for themselves, their families, and their communities. For example, some 400 former combatants and victims – members of different associations or cooperatives – joined forces this year to launch a tourism initiative spanning six departments, aimed at stimulating economic activity in areas previously affected by conflict through a focus on nature, historical memory and reconciliation. Another example involves the production of coffee, where a commercial initiative established in 2018 with private sector support brings together some 1,300 former combatants across nine departments. These experiences demonstrate that when former combatants are connected to sustainable economic opportunities and markets, reintegration becomes a strategic investment in local development, social cohesion, and lasting peace. Unfortunately, sustainability remains a major challenge for such initiatives of former combatants. And security concerns persist in the areas where former combatants live and work. I deplore the most recent killing of a former combatant in the Department of Cesar on 22 September, which brings to 501 the total number of killings since 2016. Strengthening both protection and opportunities for those who laid down their arms must be a priority. Avoiding any return to violence remains imperative, especially as former combatants face growing pressure and heightened risks of recruitment by armed groups. Colombia has begun a new political chapter with wide ranging challenges ahead and the need for sustained international engagement in order to overcome remaining obstacles, deepen the gains achieved to date and build a more peaceful and secure future for all Colombians. The opportunity is there to make use of the instruments of the Agreement and the presence of the Mission across Colombia’s conflict-affected regions to contribute substantially toward these ends. With the support of the Council and the necessary resources to ensure that the Mission stays fit for purpose, including its territorial presences, we stand ready to continue accompanying Colombia on that path. DPPA is at the heart of United Nations efforts to prevent and resolve conflict, advance diplomacy and mediation, and build sustainable peace around the world.

extraction.body: It is a pleasure to brief the Security Council once again on the peace process in Colombia. This is an important moment in the political life of the country, following the recent holding of congressional elections and with presidential elections now only a month away. It is an honor to participate alongside Her Excellency Rosa Villavicencio, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Colombia. I would like to thank the Government of Colombia for its ongoing cooperation with the Verification Mission and for the efforts recognized in the Secretary-General’s latest report to advance peacebuilding in the country. It is also a pleasure to welcome Olga Quintero, a renowned peasant leader and advocate for peace in the Catatumbo region —an area that is emblematic of the complex conflict in Colombia and crucial to the consolidation of peace. She also exemplifies the important role that women have played in building peace in Colombia. I am pleased that the Security Council is today resuming the good practice of including the voices of civil society in its meetings on Colombia. The holding of largely peaceful and more inclusive elections has been a feature of Colombia’s positive evolution under the Peace Agreement. It is essential for the country to stay on this trajectory. Allow me to reiterate in this regard the Secretary-General's congratulations on the peaceful participation of the Colombian people in the legislative elections held in March. Despite concerns during the campaign period over incidents of violence and the presence of illegal armed groups in conflict-affected regions, adequate measures were taken and election day was not adversely affected by security incidents — a demonstration of Colombia’s strong institutions. I commend the role played by security forces in protecting the vote, the vigilance exercised by national and international observers, and the valuable role also played by the Office of the Ombudsperson in monitoring conditions and in promoting adherence to the Commitment to a Free and Peaceful Electoral Process. With the presidential campaign now in full swing ahead of elections on 31 May, the Mission is adding its voice to the call for authorities and all concerned to ensure a safe and peaceful environment, free of violence and stigmatization. I reiterate my condemnation of reported threats against presidential candidates, and I call again for State authorities to guarantee the safety of all participants in the electoral process. The Verification Mission also stands ready to contribute once again —as it did during the congressional elections— to the exercises carried out by national authorities, some of them using mechanisms of the Peace Agreement, to analyse security risks and coordinate preventive actions. Ensuring the security of candidates and voters should continue to be the utmost priority. The latest report of the Secretary-General traces implementation across the three pillars of the mandate, as established by the Security Council in resolution 2798 of last October: reintegration of former combatants; security guarantees; and comprehensive rural reform. They are three elements at the core of the Final Peace Agreement, whose implementation contributes to peace and security in the country. We have fully restructured the Mission to reflect the refocused mandate and streamlined further in line with UN80 reductions. This has resulted in a substantially leaner configuration, while still enabling the Mission to maintain a suitable regional field presence, which is essential for effective verification, as well as engagement with local communities, authorities and peace signatories. Receiving, now, the resources approved in the budget is essential to delivering on the mandate across Colombia. The realities on the ground vary from region to region, and ongoing conflict dynamics are highly complex. Although security has deteriorated in some parts of the country, previously neglected areas have also been afforded with new opportunities, made possible by the Peace Accord. In visits to Mission offices across this diverse landscape, what I see is close collaboration with Colombian stakeholders and counterparts, who strongly value its unique presence in the field. The efforts to expand access to land as part of the comprehensive rural reform are bringing hope —via the arrival of long-awaited dividends of peace— to marginalized regions and communities who suffered grievously during the armed conflict. Behind the statistics we report on hectares delivered toward the numerical goals established in the Peace Agreement, are the people who are the beneficiaries on the ground, such as the members of a peasant community I visited in February in the Cesar Department, in northern Colombia. This was region engulfed in violence during the conflict, marked by massacres and widespread displacement of people from their land. Many members of this community I visited were direct victims, and so it was inspiring to see them recently receive a sizeable plot of land as part of the rural reform. Despite some practical challenges and security-related concerns, the community is setting down roots on this land, having established a school, begun building their own houses, and having launched fish-farming, corn and yuca growing projects. Women are prominent leaders of this community. While appreciative of the land, they still need further attention from the State to turn this opportunity into a sustainable future. This is one of 30 select cases of land adjudication in conflict-affected regions that the Mission is prioritizing in its verification. Overall, progress has been made in recent years in providing access to land to numerous beneficiaries. However, continued efforts will be required to fulfil the objectives laid out in the rural reform. It is not only a matter of distributing land, but also ensuring its productivity, guaranteeing the safety of beneficiaries, and clarifying the legal ownership status of the plots. I wish to recognize the important step taken in this direction, with the enactment in March of a statutory law on the functioning of the Agrarian Jurisdiction. I am hopeful that this important entity —which is to address land-related disputes— will soon become fully operational through additional legislation that is pending adoption in Congress. The rural reform also encompasses investments in local and regional development projects in conflict-affected areas known as the PDET regions —plans that were recently extended through 2037 by Congress—, as well as the implementation of sectorial plans to greatly expand state services over time, such as rural roads, education, health, irrigation, and electricity. All told, as noted by the Secretary-General in his report, the Rural Reform is fundamental for consolidating lasting peace and security in Colombia. It aims to extend State presence and address inequalities that have fuelled conflict in the country for decades. By unlocking viable economic opportunities, it can also provide sustainable alternatives to illicit economies, thereby helping to break the cycle of violence. The laying down of arms by Latin-America’s oldest and largest guerilla group was not only a feat in and of itself, but so is the fact that, nearly ten years later, more than 11,000 men and women from the former FARC-EP remain actively engaged in their reintegration into society. This process has been repleted with challenges, however, given the fragile socioeconomic, infrastructural, and security conditions in rural areas where many former combatants have settled. As reported by the Secretary-General, the provision of land and housing is progressing, though more still needs to be done to complete those tasks, to strengthen security guarantees and to ensure the sustainability of reintegration. The product of the hard work carried out by former combatants can be drastically affected when security conditions deteriorate. I hope that State entities, in acknowledgement of the perseverance of former combatants, will increase all efforts to ensure the conditions that would allow them to look to the future with confidence. The political reintegration of the former guerrilla is also an essential part of the peace process, allowing for their peaceful participation in the democratic political life of the country. Following the results of the recent congressional elections, I would like to commend the Comunes Party for the constructive role its representatives played as legislators during a transitional period in which it held guaranteed seats in the Congress under the Peace Agreement. Although that provision has now expired, the former combatants, as one of the two signatory parties of the Peace Accord, maintain all associated responsibilities and functions. I strongly welcome the clear commitments expressed by its leaders to continue abiding by the Peace Agreement, working for its full implementation, and I look forward to their active role going forward. Mr. President, Distinguished Members of the Council, Colombia remains today more peaceful than during peak years of the conflict. However, as we have reported extensively, a number of rural areas are still strongly impacted by the presence of illegal armed groups. Their ongoing clashes over territorial control and illicit economies are bringing violence and hardship to entire communities. We condemn, among others, their increased recruitment and use of children. The Catatumbo region is a case in point of what is happening in such areas —its population caught in the middle of disputes by armed groups in one of the regions with the highest concentrations of coca in the country. During a visit there in January, in the aftermath of renewed clashes in the area, I visited a hamlet where homes had been heavily damaged in drone attacks between rival groups. Explosive hazards had been found near schools. Residents were fearful of landmines and raised concerns about the slow arrival of humanitarian assistance. As long as violence, territorial disputes, or governance vacuums persist in any part of the country, they risk undermining national stability and eroding the gains made elsewhere. Through its presence and verification activities in conflict-affected regions, such as Catatumbo, the Mission is contributing to the detection of risks to communities and to the calls for timely and well-articulated responses by authorities to these risks. The Mission is also helping to give visibility to humanitarian and other needs that should be addressed under the Peace Agreement. The Mission is a regular participant in security guarantees mechanisms of, and related to, the Peace Agreement, that are important for addressing security needs of vulnerable groups in particular —including former combatants, women and those involved in the exercise of politics. Mr. President, Distinguished Members of the Council, When the Council meets next on Colombia in July, elections will have concluded, and a new Government will be preparing to begin its term in August. Whoever assumes the presidency will face a formidable challenge in consolidating peace and security in the regions still affected by conflict. As the Secretary-General reminds us in his latest report, the Peace Agreement provides a comprehensive roadmap for addressing both the root causes and consequences of the conflict, for bringing inclusive development to long-neglected regions where violence is still present —impacting its ethnic communities disproportionately— and for ensuring there is justice and redress for the victims. Significant progress has occurred over the years since the Agreement was signed, yet much remains to be done, and much can be achieved through focused efforts in the coming years. The territories where the Agreement has not been sufficiently implemented are precisely where the most acute problems persist today. Stabilizing the regions still affected by conflict requires comprehensive implementation. And as the Secretary-General has also stated in his report, peace strategies and effective security actions can and should be carried out in complement with one another in order to produce the desired results. The Security Council has been an essential partner to Colombia in the search for lasting peace and security. The Verification Mission stands ready to continue to assist the Colombians along this path. Despite the difficulties, it remains a path that is well worth following. I thank you, Mr. President. extraction.body: Miroslav Jenča, Special Representative of the Secretary-General and Head of the United Nations Verification Mission in Colombia It is my pleasure to brief the Security Council once again on Colombia. The Council’s role has been critical in supporting Colombia’s path to peace, and I deeply appreciate its constant support for the Verification Mission. I am particularly pleased that Foreign Minister Omar Bula, His Excellency, is participating for the first time in this quarterly session of the Council on Colombia. I greatly appreciate the constructive dialogue we have had with the Foreign Minister, as well as with other Government representatives, during these first two months of his term. I reiterate the commitment of the United Nations Verification Mission to continue working in close cooperation with the Colombian Government and State authorities, the High Contracting Party to the Agreement, communities —including women leaders— and all those committed to building a peaceful, secure and prosperous future. Madam President, Distinguished Members of the Council, As this Council is aware, the new Government of President Abelardo de la Espriella began its term in particularly difficult circumstances, challenged to respond on its third day in office to a devastating earthquake. The UN country team supported the national humanitarian response, with backing from the Verification Mission. I reiterate my condolences for the loss of life, injuries and damage incurred. I commend the Colombian people for their resilience in the face of adversity. The new administration also took office facing serious challenges that the Secretary-General described in his latest report: mounting insecurity due to the expansion of armed groups and illegal economies in areas still affected by conflict, and the deficits in development and state presence in those very same regions. These are key factors that have fuelled violence for decades in Colombia. The Government has identified security, the reduction of violence and the development of the territories as key objectives in this context. In our engagement with the Government we have discussed how the Verification Mission, working within its mandate fostering the continued implementation of the Peace Agreement can contribute to the realization of these objectives, especially the protection of communities and increased state presence throughout the country. At nearly ten years since its signing, the Agreement has made undeniable contributions to advancing peace in the country – ending the longest standing insurgency of the conflict, establishing policies and programs to advance development and state presence in rural areas, and the building of creative pathways -- that deserve our continued strong support -- to ensuring transitional justice and reparations to victims. Implementation over the years has also had many shortcomings, and much remains to be done to advance the Agreement in parallel with security policies that can be mutually reinforcing. The Agreement should be implemented comprehensively. And as the Secretary-General states in his report, “the years ahead will be pivotal to consolidate progress achieved to date and leverage the opportunities afforded.” The Government has stated its intention to comply with the Constitutional and legal obligations arising from the Agreement, however as the Secretary-General has also noted in his report, it has yet to fully outline its approach to implementation. We look forward to the further definition of its policies and we stand ready to support the Government in this regard, making available the Specific plans ensuring adequate financing of critical programs and peace institutions, the assignment of leadership and coordination responsibilities within the Government, and the activation of established commissions that are part of the architecture of the Agreement would provide important assurances and address the concerns raised by various stakeholders of the Agreement about the continuity of implementation. The United Nations Verification Mission has accompanied Colombia in its efforts to advance peace and security across successive administrations and stages of the peace process, always working with full respect for Colombia’s sovereignty and the principle of national ownership. Through the Mission’s regional, subregional and local offices, it has developed relationships of trust with local authorities, communities, former combatants, and civil society organizations, while accumulating valuable insight into some of Colombia's most remote and conflict-affected territories. We carry out verification with a proactive spirit of assisting the parties to overcome bottlenecks to moving forward in implementation. The Mission is also investing in digital innovation aimed at optimizing its analysis and verification in the field. Since my arrival to Colombia a year ago, I have visited almost all of the Mission's 29 territorial offices, witnessing firsthand the value of this presence on the ground. It undoubtedly constitutes one of the Mission’s key added values at this moment in time, positioning it, among others, to accompany efforts to extend the reach of state institutions bringing benefits to the population. We have observed how rapidly local dynamics can shift and how security, governance, economic opportunities, and social cohesion remain deeply interconnected. One lesson has remained constant throughout this time: sustainable peace requires security, and security requires an effective and lasting presence of State institutions. In my conversations with community representatives and local officials, they consistently emphasize the importance of sustained efforts to improve living conditions, expand sustainable economic opportunities, strengthen public services, and enhance presence of and confidence in -- local institutions. These are the main objectives of the rural reform provisions of the Peace Agreement. For example, the Development Programmes with Territorial Focus (PDET), which are monitored by the Verification Mission, foster the transformation of regions and expansion of state presence. Instruments such as the Agrarian Jurisdiction and the Multipurpose Cadaster contribute to achieving legal certainty over property that is critical for development and private-led investment and growth. Greater security and prosperity in these regions benefit not only local communities but the country as a whole. Madam President, Distinguished Members of the Council, The reintegration process remains one of the most significant achievements of the implementation of the 2016 Peace Agreement. More than eleven thousand former combatants continue to pursue their transition to civilian life. Their sustained commitment over nearly a decade reflects a steadfast determination to build peaceful and productive futures for themselves, their families, and their communities. For example, some 400 former combatants and victims – members of different associations or cooperatives – joined forces this year to launch a tourism initiative spanning six departments, aimed at stimulating economic activity in areas previously affected by conflict through a focus on nature, historical memory and reconciliation. Another example involves the production of coffee, where a commercial initiative established in 2018 with private sector support brings together some 1,300 former combatants across nine departments. These experiences demonstrate that when former combatants are connected to sustainable economic opportunities and markets, reintegration becomes a strategic investment in local development, social cohesion, and lasting peace. Unfortunately, sustainability remains a major challenge for such initiatives of former combatants. And security concerns persist in the areas where former combatants live and work. I deplore the most recent killing of a former combatant in the Department of Cesar on 22 September, which brings to 501 the total number of killings since 2016. Strengthening both protection and opportunities for those who laid down their arms must be a priority. Avoiding any return to violence remains imperative, especially as former combatants face growing pressure and heightened risks of recruitment by armed groups. Colombia has begun a new political chapter with wide ranging challenges ahead and the need for sustained international engagement in order to overcome remaining obstacles, deepen the gains achieved to date and build a more peaceful and secure future for all Colombians. The opportunity is there to make use of the instruments of the Agreement and the presence of the Mission across Colombia’s conflict-affected regions to contribute substantially toward these ends. With the support of the Council and the necessary resources to ensure that the Mission stays fit for purpose, including its territorial presences, we stand ready to continue accompanying Colombia on that path. DPPA is at the heart of United Nations efforts to prevent and resolve conflict, advance diplomacy and mediation, and build sustainable peace around the world.

sources.title: Santa Rosa Flyers Can Skip SFO Security Starting Nov. 17 With New $55 Bus-to-Gate Service - Hoodline
passages: Santa Rosa Flyers Can Skip SFO Security Starting Nov.
Starting November 17, travelers flying out of Charles M.

Schulz–Sonoma County Airport will be able to clear security in Santa Rosa and skip the TSA line at San Francisco International Airport altogether, boarding a motorcoach that drives directly onto the SFO tarmac.
The new Straight to Gate service comes from Landline, a ground-transportation company that functions less like a shuttle and more like a connecting flight on wheels.

Checked luggage gets transferred straight to the traveler’s flight, and those with mobile boarding passes and no bags to check can walk straight to the Santa Rosa security line without even stopping at the Landline counter.
The service will run eight nonstop round trips daily, with coaches departing Santa Rosa at 5, 7, 9 and 11 a.m. and again at 1, 3, 5:30 and 8 p.m., per the same Press Democrat report.
A one-way adult fare runs $55, and kids 15 and younger ride free with a paying adult.
The history backs up the challenge of sustaining small regional flights: United began three daily Santa Rosa–SFO flights in June 2017, suspended the route in 2020, and cut it again in October 2022.
Stout said Landline gives travelers more domestic and international connection options while preserving the experience at Santa Rosa’s airport.

Southwest Airlines added to that crowding when it launched service at STS in April, becoming the airport’s third major commercial carrier with nonstop flights to San Diego, Las Vegas, Burbank and Denver — a move that designated Santa Rosa as Southwest’s 14th California destination.

extraction.body: Starting November 17, travelers flying out of Charles M. Schulz–Sonoma County Airport will be able to clear security in Santa Rosa and skip the TSA line at San Francisco International Airport altogether, boarding a motorcoach that drives directly onto the SFO tarmac. The new Straight to Gate service comes from Landline, a ground-transportation company that functions less like a shuttle and more like a connecting flight on wheels. The service was jointly announced by Landline, Sonoma County Airport and SFO, according to The Press Democrat . Passengers flying United, Alaska, Hawaiian, American or JetBlue out of SFO will be able to check in and clear TSA screening right at the Santa Rosa airport, then board a secure motorcoach at Gate A6 that arrives at SFO’s Gate A3 — entering the terminal without going through security again. Checked luggage gets transferred straight to the traveler’s flight, and those with mobile boarding passes and no bags to check can walk straight to the Santa Rosa security line without even stopping at the Landline counter. The service will run eight nonstop round trips daily, with coaches departing Santa Rosa at 5, 7, 9 and 11 a.m. and again at 1, 3, 5:30 and 8 p.m., per the same Press Democrat report. Return coaches leave SFO roughly between 8 a.m. and 11 p.m., and the drive itself takes about two hours, with Landline building in an extra 30 to 40 minutes of cushion during heavy traffic. A one-way adult fare runs $55, and kids 15 and younger ride free with a paying adult. Notably, passengers arriving at SFO on any airline — not just the five Landline currently partners with — can hop a returning coach curbside outside baggage claim at any terminal. Reservations open at sfo.landline.com, where travelers enter their flight information and receive a recommended departure time; boarding begins about 15 minutes before the coach pulls out, and Landline staff can print boarding passes and tag luggage on site. Customers book directly with Landline rather than through an airline, though the company has an agreement to pay airport fees to Sonoma County rather than the other way around — the county does not pay Landline to run the service, and instead expects added revenue from passenger fees, facility leases, parking and concessions. The appeal of the new service is rooted in a familiar North Bay headache: getting to SFO by road. Standard shuttles drop passengers landside at the curb, leaving them to navigate traffic and then clear SFO’s own TSA lines — a process the airport’s Integrated Operations Center aims to keep under 20 minutes, per SFGATE , which also notes SFO is California’s second-busiest airport and a major trans-Pacific hub for United and Alaska. Landline’s service instead carries passengers by secure motorcoach to SFO’s airside gates, rather than dropping them landside at the curb. That model isn’t unique to Sonoma County. Landline operates a similar remote terminal with Massport in Framingham, Massachusetts, roughly 20 miles outside Boston Logan, where passengers can complete check-in and TSA screening before continuing by coach to the airport. Landline also opened a remote terminal in Montreal this summer, and the Santa Rosa route marks the company’s first in the Pacific time zone. Founded in 2019, Landline has carried more than 1 million passengers and now runs more than 200 daily departures across North America, with its workforce roughly doubling to about 350 full-time employees over the past year. Sonoma County Airport manager Jon Stout said the new service will not affect the existing operations of Groome Transportation, which has run scheduled shuttles between Santa Rosa, SFO and Oakland since acquiring Airport Express in 2017 and continues to drop passengers at the SFO curb rather than airside. Stout said Landline gives travelers more domestic and international connection options while preserving the experience at Santa Rosa’s airport. Landline founder and CEO David Sunde argued that connecting Sonoma County to SFO by bus makes more practical sense than it might sound, saying that regional airplane service becomes less compelling once boarding, taxiing and flight approach times are factored in. The history backs up the challenge of sustaining small regional flights: United began three daily Santa Rosa–SFO flights in June 2017, suspended the route in 2020, and cut it again in October 2022. Delta, meanwhile, began new Santa Rosa–Salt Lake City flights earlier this month, with curbside check-in available for those passengers at the Santa Rosa airport. Nick Johnson, Landline’s vice president for commercial, said the company plans to add more airlines to the Sonoma County–SFO arrangement in the coming months. The motorcoaches themselves are outfitted with wheelchair accessibility, leather seating, extra legroom, charging outlets, restrooms and Starlink Wi-Fi, and Landline has said the coaches will not stop en route to pick up additional passengers. The timing lines up with explosive growth at the Santa Rosa airport. STS logged an all-time annual record of 780,637 passengers in 2025 — a 21.8% jump over 2023 and 60% above pre-pandemic 2019 levels — according to Sonoma County Airport , even after the airport lost low-cost carrier Avelo Airlines partway through the year. Southwest Airlines added to that crowding when it launched service at STS in April, becoming the airport’s third major commercial carrier with nonstop flights to San Diego, Las Vegas, Burbank and Denver — a move that designated Santa Rosa as Southwest’s 14th California destination. Hoodline previously covered STS's growth ahead of Southwest's arrival , and the airport has also seen operational hiccups amid the surge, including a tower technology glitch this past July that sent some flights on unexpected detours. extraction.body: North Bay travelers needing to use San Francisco International Airport soon will be able to clear airport security and check their bags in Santa Rosa before riding a bus straight onto the SFO airfield. The Landline Company, Charles M. Schulz–Sonoma County Airport (airport code STS) and SFO announced Monday that the new “Straight to Gate” connection starting Nov. 17 will offer eight nonstop round trips daily. One-way adult fares will be $55, while children 15 and younger will travel free with a paying adult. That’s the same fare quoted by Groome Transportation, a Virginia-based nationwide shuttle company that has run buses between Santa Rosa airport and SFO and Oakland International Airport (OAK) since acquiring Airport Express in 2017 . Sonoma County Airport Manager Jon Stout said the new service will not affect Groome’s existing operations, which provide the airport’s only other scheduled shuttle service. Different from Groome, which drops passengers at the SFO and OAK curb, Landline picks up passengers after they pass through security in Santa Rosa then delivers them directly to the secure side of SFO. Passengers booked on United, Alaska, Hawaiian, American or JetBlue flights departing SFO will check in and pass through Transportation Security Administration screening at Sonoma County airport, then board a secure Landline motorcoach from Gate A6. On arrival at SFO’s Gate A3, passengers enter the terminal without another security check. Under Transportation Security Administration guidelines, the buses don’t stop between the STS and SFO airfields, and the baggage compartments are locked and monitored. Checked luggage is transferred to the passengers’ flights at SFO. Travelers with mobile boarding passes and no checked bags can skip the Landline counter in Santa Rosa and go directly to security there, Nick Johnson, Landline’s vice president for commercial, told the Journal. The 36-seat wheelchair-accessible buses have leather seats, with extra legroom, Starlink Wi-Fi, charging outlets and restrooms. Landline plans to add more airlines to the Sonoma County–SFO arrangement in the coming months, founder and CEO David Sunde said. Departures from Santa Rosa are scheduled for 5, 7, 9 and 11 a.m. and 1, 3, 5:30 and 8 p.m. Return departures from SFO run from about 8 a.m. to 11 p.m. Those arriving at SFO on any airline can take a returning coach, boarding curbside outside baggage claim at any terminal. Sunde said the drive will take about two hours, with timetables allowing an extra 30 to 40 minutes during heavy traffic. Unlike conventional shuttles, the coaches will not stop to collect other passengers. Reservations are open at sfo.landline.com , and a few bookings already were made after the Monday morning announcement, Johnson said. Customers enter their flight information and receive a recommended coach departure. Unlike earlier Landline arrangements, customers book directly with the company rather than through an airline. Sunde said boarding is scheduled to begin about 15 minutes before coach departure, and staff will be able to print boarding passes and tag luggage for travelers’ final destinations. Sonoma County airport is not paying Landline to operate the service, Stout said. Instead, the company has an agreement with the county under which it pays airport fees. Stout said the airport expects additional revenue from passenger fees, facility use and leases, parking and concessions as travelers who otherwise would have driven to SFO begin their trips in Santa Rosa and visit the terminal’s concessions. Santa Rosa used to have flights to San Francisco. United began three daily flights on that route in June 2017, returning to the regional airport after a 16-year absence. The airline suspended the connection in 2020 amid the pandemic and again in October 2022. Sunde said connecting Sonoma County with SFO makes sense, but doing it with an airplane is less compelling when time required for boarding, taxiing and flight approaches are considered. “Sonoma County is a big and growing population center. It needs connectivity to an international airport,” Sunde said, referring to San Francisco. Existing and planned flights from Santa Rosa already connect to a number of international airports. The launch follows Delta Air Lines’ Oct. 6 start of Santa Rosa-Salt Lake City flights and the introduction of curbside check-in for its passengers at Sonoma County airport. Landline, which began operations in 2019, says it has carried more than 1 million passengers and operates more than 200 daily departures across North America, including several regional airports in Canada. Sunde said its workforce has doubled in a year to roughly 350 full-time employees. At STS, the company will have ticket counter agents trained in handling documents for international flights and will have its own baggage handlers. The Santa Rosa route will be its first in the Pacific time zone. The service has had some changes over time. For example, United discontinued its Landline-operated routes last year, between Denver and Fort Collins in July and between Newark, New Jersey, and Allentown, Pennsylvania, in September. But Landline still offers trips between Mile High City–area locations and the international airport. And American ended Landline routes this month between South Bend Regional Airport and Chicago O’Hare International Airport after a year, replacing it with regular regional flights, similar to the United’s former STS–SFO route. Johnson attributed that to the popularity of the secured-bus connection over its yearlong stint. The airline also ended a Landline route linking O’Hare and Chicago Rockford International Airport, without a flight replacing it. United and American returned to working with Landline with the Santa Rosa route. In Massachusetts, Landline operates with Massport at a remote terminal in Framingham, where travelers can clear security before a ride to Boston Logan International Airport. Sunde said the company also opened a remote terminal in Montreal this summer. “Landline extends that convenience by offering our travelers an incredible array of domestic and international options while still maintaining the STS experience they know and love,” Stout said. Travelers with mobile boarding passes and no checked bags can skip the Landline counter in Santa Rosa and go directly to security there, Nick Johnson, Landline’s vice president for commercial, told the Journal.
The 36-seat wheelchair-accessible buses have leather seats, with extra legroom, Starlink Wi-Fi, charging outlets and restrooms.

Stout said the airport expects additional revenue from passenger fees, facility use and leases, parking and concessions as travelers who otherwise would have driven to SFO begin their trips in Santa Rosa and visit the terminal’s concessions.

“Sonoma County is a big and growing population center. It needs connectivity to an international airport,” Sunde said, referring to San Francisco. Existing and planned flights from Santa Rosa already connect to a number of international airports.
The launch follows Delta Air Lines’ Oct. 6 start of Santa Rosa-Salt Lake City flights and the introduction of curbside check-in for its passengers at Sonoma County airport.

And American ended Landline routes this month between South Bend Regional Airport and Chicago O’Hare International Airport after a year, replacing it with regular regional flights, similar to the United’s former STS–SFO route. Schulz–Sonoma County Airport will be able to clear security in Santa Rosa and skip the TSA line at San Francisco International Airport altogether, boarding a motorcoach that drives directly onto the SFO tarmac. The new Straight to Gate service comes from Landline, a ground-transportation company that functions less like a shuttle and more like a connecting flight on wheels. The service was jointly announced by Landline, Sonoma County Airport and SFO, according to The Press Democrat . Passengers flying United, Alaska, Hawaiian, American or JetBlue out of SFO will be able to check in and clear TSA screening right at the Santa Rosa airport, then board a secure motorcoach at Gate A6 that arrives at SFO’s Gate A3 — entering the terminal without going through security again. Checked luggage gets transferred straight to the traveler’s flight, and those with mobile boarding passes and no bags to check can walk straight to the Santa Rosa security line without even stopping at the Landline counter. The service will run eight nonstop round trips daily, with coaches departing Santa Rosa at 5, 7, 9 and 11 a.m. and again at 1, 3, 5:30 and 8 p.m., per the same Press Democrat report. Return coaches leave SFO roughly between 8 a.m. and 11 p.m., and the drive itself takes about two hours, with Landline building in an extra 30 to 40 minutes of cushion during heavy traffic. A one-way adult fare runs $55, and kids 15 and younger ride free with a paying adult. Notably, passengers arriving at SFO on any airline — not just the five Landline currently partners with — can hop a returning coach curbside outside baggage claim at any terminal. Reservations open at sfo.landline.com, where travelers enter their flight information and receive a recommended departure time; boarding begins about 15 minutes before the coach pulls out, and Landline staff can print boarding passes and tag luggage on site. Customers book directly with Landline rather than through an airline, though the company has an agreement to pay airport fees to Sonoma County rather than the other way around — the county does not pay Landline to run the service, and instead expects added revenue from passenger fees, facility leases, parking and concessions. The appeal of the new service is rooted in a familiar North Bay headache: getting to SFO by road. Standard shuttles drop passengers landside at the curb, leaving them to navigate traffic and then clear SFO’s own TSA lines — a process the airport’s Integrated Operations Center aims to keep under 20 minutes, per SFGATE , which also notes SFO is California’s second-busiest airport and a major trans-Pacific hub for United and Alaska. Landline’s service instead carries passengers by secure motorcoach to SFO’s airside gates, rather than dropping them landside at the curb. That model isn’t unique to Sonoma County. Landline operates a similar remote terminal with Massport in Framingham, Massachusetts, roughly 20 miles outside Boston Logan, where passengers can complete check-in and TSA screening before continuing by coach to the airport. Landline also opened a remote terminal in Montreal this summer, and the Santa Rosa route marks the company’s first in the Pacific time zone. Founded in 2019, Landline has carried more than 1 million passengers and now runs more than 200 daily departures across North America, with its workforce roughly doubling to about 350 full-time employees over the past year. Sonoma County Airport manager Jon Stout said the new service will not affect the existing operations of Groome Transportation, which has run scheduled shuttles between Santa Rosa, SFO and Oakland since acquiring Airport Express in 2017 and continues to drop passengers at the SFO curb rather than airside. Stout said Landline gives travelers more domestic and international connection options while preserving the experience at Santa Rosa’s airport. Landline founder and CEO David Sunde argued that connecting Sonoma County to SFO by bus makes more practical sense than it might sound, saying that regional airplane service becomes less compelling once boarding, taxiing and flight approach times are factored in. The history backs up the challenge of sustaining small regional flights: United began three daily Santa Rosa–SFO flights in June 2017, suspended the route in 2020, and cut it again in October 2022. Delta, meanwhile, began new Santa Rosa–Salt Lake City flights earlier this month, with curbside check-in available for those passengers at the Santa Rosa airport. Nick Johnson, Landline’s vice president for commercial, said the company plans to add more airlines to the Sonoma County–SFO arrangement in the coming months. The motorcoaches themselves are outfitted with wheelchair accessibility, leather seating, extra legroom, charging outlets, restrooms and Starlink Wi-Fi, and Landline has said the coaches will not stop en route to pick up additional passengers. The timing lines up with explosive growth at the Santa Rosa airport. STS logged an all-time annual record of 780,637 passengers in 2025 — a 21.8% jump over 2023 and 60% above pre-pandemic 2019 levels — according to Sonoma County Airport , even after the airport lost low-cost carrier Avelo Airlines partway through the year. Southwest Airlines added to that crowding when it launched service at STS in April, becoming the airport’s third major commercial carrier with nonstop flights to San Diego, Las Vegas, Burbank and Denver — a move that designated Santa Rosa as Southwest’s 14th California destination. Hoodline previously covered STS's growth ahead of Southwest's arrival , and the airport has also seen operational hiccups amid the surge, including a tower technology glitch this past July that sent some flights on unexpected detours. It's not just the debt that many tech companies are piling on that is a concern, but as AI advances and tech is doing more for people and businesses than it did before, there are also significant risks related to automation. What could derail AI stocks is the risk that AI agents pose to both the companies that develop them and the customers relying on them.

Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

There have been multiple reports about AI agents not staying within their confines, which is a growing issue in the tech sector . One of the most high-profile events included OpenAI agents launching a cyberattack against Hugging Face a few months ago. The company is now facing a lawsuit due to that.

There are multiple issues stemming from this type of risk. First is the obvious one -- a company can face high legal costs if its agents go rogue and cause harm. In addition, OpenAI will need to spend more time and money to develop agents more carefully to ensure the risks are minimal in the future. And even then, there may still be concerns if it has done enough.

The second issue is that companies may be less willing to deploy agents if there is the potential for these types of situations. Even if an agent doesn't attack another company, it may still improperly use or share confidential data. If a company has to spend additional efforts on safeguarding its assets, it would make investments in AI even more costly. At a time when spending on AI is already under scrutiny, companies may balk at the idea, especially if there are doubts about the potential payoff.
The result could be a slowdown of demand, which could derail the bull story around not only Nvidia but also other AI stocks .

Nvidia is a top growth stock to own, so long as the AI growth story is a promising one. But if there are any cracks in it, or if there are signs that companies are beginning to pull back on AI-related spending, that can wreak havoc on Nvidia's growth and its valuation.

Currently, the stock looks cheap as it's trading at just 25 times its estimated future profits. But that's based on analyst expectations of how it will do in the future. If those expectations unravel, the stock may not look nearly as cheap and attractive anymore, and that may be the case for many other stocks as well.
Investors should consider the risks related to AI before deciding whether to buy Nvidia or any other stock, as ignoring them could prove costly down the road.

Altcoins are any cryptocurrencies aside from Bitcoin, and “altcoin season” describes a phase when traders shift funds out of Bitcoin and into smaller coins, leading to substantial gains for most altcoins. Conversely, a “Bitcoin season” occurs when Bitcoin outperforms the majority of the market.

The Altcoin Season Index formalizes this concept, declaring altcoin season only when 75% of the 50 largest coins outperform Bitcoin over a 90-day timeframe. CoinMarketCap’s version of the index showed 61 on October 1, which also falls short of the 75 threshold. Both indexes intentionally measure a 90-day period to prevent a single strong month from prematurely indicating a season.
Only NEAR (up 13%) and Cardano (up 3%) have maintained an upward trend over the past week. Meanwhile, the other six coins have experienced declines.

Uniswap has taken the biggest hit, with its UNI token still up 25% over 30 days despite a 19% drop in the past week, erasing nearly half of its earlier gains. Similarly, Hedera has slipped by 9%, while Litecoin decreased by 8%.

This quick unwind points to a temporary bounce, since the rotation reversed within the same month it began. In a lasting trend, altcoins typically continue to outperform Bitcoin week after week, but many of these coins stopped that trend before the month ended.

Still, three reasons suggest the possibility of a longer rally. First, Bitcoin also dropped 2% over the past week, suggesting the altcoin declines occurred during a broader market dip rather than a rotation back into Bitcoin. Two, two of the eight coins are still climbing. Lastly, a one-week period is a brief timeframe for assessing market trends. A coin that has lost more than 90% can still rise substantially and linger far below previous price levels, because the gain starts from a much lower base. For example, Cardano would need to increase roughly 12 times its current value to reclaim its prior record , making a 20% monthly gain seem minimal in that context. The current 30-day outlook suggests the start of an altcoin season, but the evidence leans toward a bounce. Six of the eight coins have already turned negative over the past week, and the Altcoin Season Index stands at 51, far below the 75 threshold needed for a season call. A genuine altcoin season requires sustained outperformance across the 50 largest coins over several months, and a handful of coins showing short-term gains does not provide enough support for such a declaration.

For holders of these coins, the index serves as a vital indicator. A reading of 75 or higher would contradict the bounce scenario and signal the first altcoin season in 379 days. coreStoryFacts.text: Litecoin (CRYPTO: LTC) rose 20.7% in the 30 days leading up to October 12, 2026, while Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) rose a more modest 8%.
This shift presents a significant change in the Litecoin vs.
Bitcoin comparison, especially since Litecoin had been on a downward trajectory for much of the year.
Litecoin's price reached as high as $80 in September before pulling back.
Litecoin outpaced Bitcoin by 13 points over 30 days, but its three prior leads from 2017, 2021, and 2023 all ultimately faded.
Traders looking for larger gains often shift their money from Bitcoin into altcoins — any cryptocurrency that isn't Bitcoin.
For Litecoin holders, two key changes need to happen for its lead to seem sustainable.
First, Litecoin must stop decreasing faster than Bitcoin during downturns.
Second, it needs to rise above its September high of $80—about 23% above its current price—while Bitcoin either remains flat or increases.
If Litecoin's 30-day gains slip below Bitcoin's before it breaks the $80 mark, this rally may mirror its previous attempts to outshine Bitcoin.

Three previous instances followed a similar pattern: Litecoin surged in December 2017, again in spring 2021, and rallied ahead of its 2023 halving.
However, each time, Litecoin eventually surrendered its lead over Bitcoin.
Yet Litecoin fell 7%, while Bitcoin fell 3.2%.
It's still too soon to tell whether Litecoin's recent success signals lasting demand or just a temporary trend.
Historically, Litecoin has outperformed Bitcoin before, but its lead has consistently faded over time.
The key question is whether Litecoin can maintain its current advantage over Bitcoin this time.
Litecoin still has a long way to go to reclaim its record high compared to Bitcoin.
In contrast, Litecoin would need to climb 6.3 times, meaning even a 21% rise over the month barely dents its recovery.
Although the fund and upcoming halving are promising developments, they still haven't given Litecoin enough stability to withstand drops as well as Bitcoin.

passages: This week, on 13 October, Apple is hosting a "Welcome Home" event that will represent a major attempt to break into the smart home .
The headline of the launch event is rumoured to be the "HomeView", a new screen meant to be placed around people's houses that will allow them to interact with Siri and see information .
In recent months, reports have suggested they have actually been finished for some time, but that Apple was waiting until its redesign of Siri was ready.

The home products are presumably part of the same strategy: giving people different ways to both give and receive information from that digital assistant, distributed through a network of different Apple-branded products.

The iPhone will still sit at the heart of it – as well as being the device that is with people wherever they are, rumours suggest that the HomeView will be able to connect to phones for authentication and to share data – but Apple looks set to try and put Siri wherever you need it, in whatever form works best.
It launched its HomeKit framework in 2014, to allow different devices to work together, and in 2016 released a devoted Home app for controlling those devices.
He pointed out that a version of this product designed from the ground-up would require a powerful processor, a display, sensors such as cameras and more – exactly like an iPhone, in short.
But that will also decide the future for the rest of us, too, changing the role that technology takes in our lives.
But it represents not just a new kind of product for Apple, in a new category.
Now, however, Apple says that it has fixed Siri, with a new version announced in summer that arrived last month .
That update completely overhauled the voice assistant, adding new artificial intelligence features in an attempt to catch up with rivals such as Google.
The updated virtual assistant – which Apple has branded as Siri AI – is not simply an improvement to the user experience, and a complete overhaul of the technology to allow that improvement.
Many of those rival companies present their products as ways of moving past the phone, which some have even suggested could be under threat entirely.
