extraction.body: Ask your smart speaker to play K C B S Radio on Audacy WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal agents on Monday searched the home of Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar , a startling escalation in a criminal investigation that brings renewed focus to the frequent target of Trump administration derision in the final weeks of her reelection bid . The search of the Minnesota congresswoman's home so close to next month's midterm contests that will determine control of the House and the Senate was swiftly condemned by top Democrats in Congress, who raised questions about the timing given longstanding Justice Department protocol to avoid overt investigative steps involving political candidates in the direct run-up to an election. Omar, an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, said she was being targeted as one of the Republican's “political enemies.” The scope of the investigation was unclear, though Trump and officials in his administration have repeatedly referred in recent months to the existence of an inquiry into Omar, a Somali-born Democrat whose status as an immigrant to the U.S. and left-wing views have drawn scrutiny from the White House and other Republicans. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin last month cited an “ongoing investigation” that he suggested was examining potential fraud in her family's immigration paperwork. “Something's going to happen,” he said in a potential foreshadowing of the search. In a statement on X on Monday, Omar called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said. “I will not be silenced.” Though the Republican focus on Omar's background dates back years, the search notably took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking reelection. The Justice Department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election. Top Democrats seized on the timing as the latest instance in what they said was the “continued corrupt weaponization” against Trump's perceived adversaries. “For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations,” said a joint statement from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and other top congressional Democrats. “Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.” The search was carried out by agents with Homeland Security Investigations, which is part of the Department of Homeland Security. A DHS spokesperson referred questions to the Justice Department, which said in a statement that HSI agents had executed a judicially authorized search warrant in the Washington, D.C., area related to an ongoing federal criminal investigation but provided no other details. The street around Omar's home was blocked off Monday morning as some HSI agents removed boxes labeled “Seized Property Evidence.” The operation came just days after Trump referred pejoratively to Omar at a rally in Tennessee as coming from a country of “crime and squalor" and suggested that Vice President JD Vance “and our people” were investigating her. Hours after the search, Trump told reporters he had “nothing to do” with it and it's “really up to the DOJ.” Vance has in the past accused Omar of committing immigration fraud, an allegation she has denied, and has said the administration was looking for pathways to investigate her. Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota’s 5th District, including Minneapolis. She is part of The Squad of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim-American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress. When Republicans swept control of the House in 2023, they voted to oust Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee, citing her anti-Israel remarks. In January, Trump lashed out at Omar during a rally in Iowa hours before an assailant sprayed the congresswoman during her own town hall meeting in Minneapolis with a substance that turned out to be vinegar. The attacker was sentenced to 14 months in prison. Omar has repeatedly refuted allegations about her marriage and immigration status raised by conservative critics, even before she joined Congress. According to her House biography, Omar has said she and her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was 8: “The family spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya before coming to the United States in 1990s. In 1997, she moved to Minneapolis with her family.” Conservative online sites have alleged that Omar married a brother to commit immigration fraud. Omar has broadly denied the allegations as “disgusting lies" and called the insinuation “absurd and offensive.” “It certainly seems like something fishy is there, but everybody's entitled to equal justice under the laws,” Vance told reporters in May. “So we're going to investigate it. We're going to take a look at it. If we think there's a crime, we're going to prosecute that crime. And that's something the Department of Justice is looking at right now." In an interview last March with conservative podcaster Benny Johnson, Vance said without offering evidence that “we actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud against the United States of America.” Omar’s office at the time dismissed Vance’s claims as fabricated and defamatory. Last month, when the podcaster Johnson reminded Mullin about Vance's comments on Omar and asked whether anything would happen from that investigation, the Homeland Security secretary responded, “Something's going to happen.” He cited an “ongoing investigation” that he suggested was examining potential fraud in the family's immigration paperwork. “If we actually move a case forward, it's not a political case. It's actually a case because they did things wrong,” Mullin said. “If you decided to break the law or lie on the information that you gave to the United States, to be able to come into the United States ... there's no expiration to that.”

“For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations,” said a joint statement from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and other top congressional Democrats. “Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.”

A DHS spokesperson referred questions to the Justice Department, which said in a statement that HSI agents had executed a judicially authorized search warrant in the Washington, D.C., area related to an ongoing federal criminal investigation but provided no other details.
The street around Omar's home was blocked off Monday morning as some HSI agents removed boxes labeled “Seized Property Evidence.”

The operation came just days after Trump referred pejoratively to Omar at a rally in Tennessee as coming from a country of “crime and squalor" and suggested that Vice President JD Vance “and our people” were investigating her. Hours after the search, Trump told reporters he had “nothing to do” with it and it's “really up to the DOJ.”
Vance has in the past accused Omar of committing immigration fraud, an allegation she has denied, and has said the administration was looking for pathways to investigate her.

Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota’s 5th District, including Minneapolis. She is part of The Squad of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim-American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress.
When Republicans swept control of the House in 2023, they voted to oust Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee, citing her anti-Israel remarks.

In January, Trump lashed out at Omar during a rally in Iowa hours before an assailant sprayed the congresswoman during her own town hall meeting in Minneapolis with a substance that turned out to be vinegar. The attacker was sentenced to 14 months in prison.
Omar has repeatedly refuted allegations about her marriage and immigration status raised by conservative critics, even before she joined Congress.

According to her House biography, Omar has said she and her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was 8: “The family spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya before coming to the United States in 1990s. In 1997, she moved to Minneapolis with her family.”

Conservative online sites have alleged that Omar married a brother to commit immigration fraud. Omar has broadly denied the allegations as “disgusting lies" and called the insinuation “absurd and offensive.”

“It certainly seems like something fishy is there, but everybody's entitled to equal justice under the laws,” Vance told reporters in May. “So we're going to investigate it. We're going to take a look at it. If we think there's a crime, we're going to prosecute that crime. And that's something the Department of Justice is looking at right now."

In an interview last March with conservative podcaster Benny Johnson, Vance said without offering evidence that “we actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud against the United States of America.” Omar’s office at the time dismissed Vance’s claims as fabricated and defamatory.

Last month, when the podcaster Johnson reminded Mullin about Vance's comments on Omar and asked whether anything would happen from that investigation, the Homeland Security secretary responded, “Something's going to happen.”
He cited an “ongoing investigation” that he suggested was examining potential fraud in the family's immigration paperwork.

“If we actually move a case forward, it's not a political case. It's actually a case because they did things wrong,” Mullin said. “If you decided to break the law or lie on the information that you gave to the United States, to be able to come into the United States ... there's no expiration to that.”

Omar derived citizenship from a father who may have been ineligible to obtain naturalized status." extraction.body: On Monday, CBS News reported that federal agents searched the Washington, D.C., home of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar (D–Minn.), as part of an ongoing investigation that "centers on Omar's immigration paperwork." In a statement to the Associated Press, the Justice Department said agents from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI)—an office within the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) that conducts federal criminal investigations into immigration fraud and identity and benefits fraud—"executed a judicially authorized search warrant" as "part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation." The search warrant reportedly "lists a series of potential immigration crimes under investigation, including false statements and fraud in immigration paperwork, as well as a general conspiracy charge," according to The New York Times . The Times reported that federal officials are also investigating "whether Ms. Omar derived citizenship from a father who may have been ineligible to obtain naturalized status." In a statement, Omar called the investigation an "outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies," stating she did "nothing wrong." Omar has been in the Justice Department's crosshairs since January, when President Donald Trump announced that the department and Congress were "looking at 'Congresswoman' Illhan Omar, who left Somalia with NOTHING, and is now reportedly worth more than 44 Million Dollars." Trump was referencing an investigation by the House Ethics Committee, based on a 2025 financial disclosure form showing she and her husband held assets worth between $6 million and $30 million, a notable increase from her previous filings. Omar later filed an amended disclosure form that showed the assets were worth $18,004 to $95,000 after accounting for liabilities. However, in September, the Wall Street Journal reported that the Office of Congressional Conduct—which reviews allegations against House members and their staff—voted 5–1 to recommend that the House Ethics Committee dismiss the allegations. Per the Journal , investigators found no "substantial reason to believe that Rep. Omar reported false or incomplete information in her financial disclosures." Omar's office told the Journal she didn't catch the errors, which stemmed from erroneous valuations of her husband's businesses, because she "isn't involved in her husband's businesses and trusted the accountant involved." The investigation into Omar appears to be part and parcel of the Trump administration's weaponization of government—which the president vowed to end—adding to a list of cases that includes former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson , former FBI Director James Comey , and former National Security Adviser John Bolton . Omar's opposition to the Trump administration's immigration enforcement efforts, particularly in her home state of Minnesota, and her Somali heritage have made her a frequent target of the president and his allies. Last December, a federal indictment revealed a nearly $9 billion fraud scandal in Minnesota, much of it tied to the state's Somali immigrants. In March, Vice President J.D. Vance—who leads the Trump administration's anti-fraud task force — told right-wing commentator Benny Johnson that Omar "definitely committed immigration fraud against the United States of America." Vance accused Omar of "being at the center of a lot of the worst fraudsters in the Somali community." Vance doubled down in May, telling White House reporters the immigration fraud allegations were "something that the Department of Justice is looking at right now." He appeared to pull back from his March claim that he was certain Omar had committed immigration fraud, instead stating that while he didn't want to "prejudge an investigation," it "certainly seems like something fishy is there." In September, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin told Johnson that the investigation into Omar was still "ongoing," and that the department knew she had "married her brother to try to bring him into the United States." Omar's office has denied the accusations, which were first levied against her in 2016. Mullin claims the investigation into Omar is "not political." He could be telling the truth; federal investigators have scrutinized Omar before. In 2024, the Biden administration's Justice Department opened an investigation into Omar's "finances, campaign spending and interactions with a foreign citizen," according to The New York Times . Per the Times , the investigation eventually "stalled for lack of evidence." But Mullin's words are also hard to take at face value. Despite denying accusations of weaponizing the justice system, the Trump administration has time and again used dubious legal reasoning to investigate the president's political enemies. This includes New York Attorney General Letitia James, who, after successfully suing Trump for financial fraud, was indicted for mortgage fraud by Trump's Justice Department, which used the same petty justification on her. The president has also continued a campaign to indict Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, announcing last week that the White House would hold in-person hearings to look into claims she committed mortgage fraud. Ousting Cook would ostensibly allow the president to install a Fed governor aligned with his priorities. It's a tactic that failed Trump once before, when his Justice Department opened a criminal investigation into former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell for his handling of renovations at the central bank's headquarters. Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, dropped the probe in April, and the department ultimately found nothing criminal in Powell's conduct. An investigation will reveal whether Omar broke the law. Still, if it's anything like the Trump administration's previous efforts, the investigation is likely driven by political animus, not criminal behavior. Start your day with Reason . Get a daily brief of the most important stories and trends every weekday morning when you subscribe to Reason Roundup . NEXT: Are Warrantless Phone Searches at the Border Constitutional? The Supreme Court May Soon Decide. Tosin Akintola is an assistant editor at Reason . Celebrate your independence with a subscription to Reason magazine, your most trusted source of honest, insightful news and analysis. Omar, an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, said she was being targeted as one of the Republican's “political enemies.” The scope of the investigation was unclear, though Trump and officials in his administration have repeatedly referred in recent months to the existence of an inquiry into Omar, a Somali-born Democrat whose status as an immigrant to the U.S. and left-wing views have drawn scrutiny from the White House and other Republicans. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin last month cited an “ongoing investigation” that he suggested was examining potential fraud in her family's immigration paperwork. “Something's going to happen,” he said in a potential foreshadowing of the search. In a statement on X on Monday, Omar called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said. “I will not be silenced.” Though the Republican focus on Omar's background dates back years, the search notably took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking reelection. The Justice Department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election. Top Democrats seized on the timing as the latest instance in what they said was the “continued corrupt weaponization” against Trump's perceived adversaries. “For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations,” said a joint statement from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and other top congressional Democrats. “Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.” The search was carried out by agents with Homeland Security Investigations, which is part of the Department of Homeland Security. A DHS spokesperson referred questions to the Justice Department, which said in a statement that HSI agents had executed a judicially authorized search warrant in the Washington, D.C., area related to an ongoing federal criminal investigation but provided no other details. The street around Omar's home was blocked off Monday morning as some HSI agents removed boxes labeled “Seized Property Evidence.” The operation came just days after Trump referred pejoratively to Omar at a rally in Tennessee as coming from a country of “crime and squalor" and suggested that Vice President JD Vance “and our people” were investigating her. Hours after the search, Trump told reporters he had “nothing to do” with it and it's “really up to the DOJ.” Vance has in the past accused Omar of committing immigration fraud, an allegation she has denied, and has said the administration was looking for pathways to investigate her. Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota’s 5th District, including Minneapolis. She is part of The Squad of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim-American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress. When Republicans swept control of the House in 2023, they voted to oust Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee, citing her anti-Israel remarks. In January, Trump lashed out at Omar during a rally in Iowa hours before an assailant sprayed the congresswoman during her own town hall meeting in Minneapolis with a substance that turned out to be vinegar. The attacker was sentenced to 14 months in prison. Omar has repeatedly refuted allegations about her marriage and immigration status raised by conservative critics, even before she joined Congress. According to her House biography, Omar has said she and her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was 8: “The family spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya before coming to the United States in 1990s. In 1997, she moved to Minneapolis with her family.” Conservative online sites have alleged that Omar married a brother to commit immigration fraud. Omar has broadly denied the allegations as “disgusting lies" and called the insinuation “absurd and offensive.” “It certainly seems like something fishy is there, but everybody's entitled to equal justice under the laws,” Vance told reporters in May. “So we're going to investigate it. We're going to take a look at it. If we think there's a crime, we're going to prosecute that crime. And that's something the Department of Justice is looking at right now." In an interview last March with conservative podcaster Benny Johnson, Vance said without offering evidence that “we actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud against the United States of America.” Omar’s office at the time dismissed Vance’s claims as fabricated and defamatory. WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal agents on Monday searched the home of Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar , a startling escalation in a criminal investigation that brings renewed focus to the frequent target of Trump administration derision in the final weeks of her reelection bid .

The search of the Minnesota congresswoman's home so close to next month's midterm contests that will determine control of the House and the Senate was swiftly condemned by top Democrats in Congress, who raised questions about the timing given longstanding Justice Department protocol to avoid overt investigative steps involving political candidates in the direct run-up to an election. Omar, an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, said she was being targeted as one of the Republican's “political enemies.”

The scope of the investigation was unclear, though Trump and officials in his administration have repeatedly referred in recent months to the existence of an inquiry into Omar, a Somali-born Democrat whose status as an immigrant to the U.S. and left-wing views have drawn scrutiny from the White House and other Republicans.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin last month cited an “ongoing investigation” that he suggested was examining potential fraud in her family's immigration paperwork. “Something's going to happen,” he said in a potential foreshadowing of the search.
In a statement on X on Monday, Omar called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”
“For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said. “I will not be silenced.”

Though the Republican focus on Omar's background dates back years, the search notably took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking reelection. The Justice Department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election. Top Democrats seized on the timing as the latest instance in what they said was the “continued corrupt weaponization” against Trump's perceived adversaries.

“For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations,” said a joint statement from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and other top congressional Democrats. “Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.”
The search was carried out by agents with Homeland Security Investigations, which is part of the Department of Homeland Security.

A DHS spokesperson referred questions to the Justice Department, which said in a statement that HSI agents had executed a judicially authorized search warrant in the Washington, D.C., area related to an ongoing federal criminal investigation but provided no other details.
The street around Omar's home was blocked off Monday morning as some HSI agents removed boxes labeled “Seized Property Evidence.”

The operation came just days after Trump referred pejoratively to Omar at a rally in Tennessee as coming from a country of “crime and squalor" and suggested that Vice President JD Vance “and our people” were investigating her. Hours after the search, Trump told reporters he had “nothing to do” with it and it's “really up to the DOJ.”
Vance has in the past accused Omar of committing immigration fraud, an allegation she has denied, and has said the administration was looking for pathways to investigate her.

Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota’s 5th District, including Minneapolis. She is part of The Squad of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim-American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress.
When Republicans swept control of the House in 2023, they voted to oust Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee, citing her anti-Israel remarks.

In January, Trump lashed out at Omar during a rally in Iowa hours before an assailant sprayed the congresswoman during her own town hall meeting in Minneapolis with a substance that turned out to be vinegar. The attacker was sentenced to 14 months in prison.
Omar has repeatedly refuted allegations about her marriage and immigration status raised by conservative critics, even before she joined Congress.

According to her House biography, Omar has said she and her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was 8: “The family spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya before coming to the United States in 1990s. In 1997, she moved to Minneapolis with her family.”

Conservative online sites have alleged that Omar married a brother to commit immigration fraud. Omar has broadly denied the allegations as “disgusting lies" and called the insinuation “absurd and offensive.”

“It certainly seems like something fishy is there, but everybody's entitled to equal justice under the laws,” Vance told reporters in May. “So we're going to investigate it. We're going to take a look at it. If we think there's a crime, we're going to prosecute that crime. And that's something the Department of Justice is looking at right now."

In an interview last March with conservative podcaster Benny Johnson, Vance said without offering evidence that “we actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud against the United States of America.” Omar’s office at the time dismissed Vance’s claims as fabricated and defamatory.

Last month, when the podcaster Johnson reminded Mullin about Vance's comments on Omar and asked whether anything would happen from that investigation, the Homeland Security secretary responded, “Something's going to happen.”
He cited an “ongoing investigation” that he suggested was examining potential fraud in the family's immigration paperwork.

“If we actually move a case forward, it's not a political case. It's actually a case because they did things wrong,” Mullin said. “If you decided to break the law or lie on the information that you gave to the United States, to be able to come into the United States ... there's no expiration to that.”

Ilhan Omar , a startling escalation in a criminal investigation that brings renewed focus to the frequent target of Trump administration derision in the final weeks of her reelection bid .
The street around Omar's home was blocked off Monday morning as some HSI agents removed boxes labeled “Seized Property Evidence.”

In a statement on X on Monday, Omar called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin last month cited an “ongoing investigation” that he suggested was examining potential fraud in her family's immigration paperwork.

Additionally, FFR and FFAI will host a joint new product launch event on October 14, 2026, featuring four major launches focused on embodied AI robotics, Physical AI education, and developer enablement. The event will feature FF Nova, FF's first embodied AI humanoid robot designed for developers and educational institutions, through an exclusive, invitation-only launch. FFAI has also announced that FF will introduce FF Nova Mini, a humanoid robot designed for foundational Physical AI education, along with the EAI Education Ecosystem Brain and Curriculum Skills 2.0. In addition, FF will launch the FF Nova Developer Reinforcement Learning Platform and open exclusive early access to the developer community. FF EAI Robotics Ecosystem Inc. (NASDAQ: FFR ) is a U.S.-based Embodied AI (EAI) robotics company that is in the process of acquiring the FF EAI Robotics business. Upon completion of the acquisition, the Company will focus on the research and development, manufacturing, commercialization, and deployment of intelligent robotic technologies, products, and industry solutions. The Company is committed to building a "Four-Core Full-Stack" AI ecosystem covering the full lifecycle of robotics, consisting of EAI Brain & Developer Platform, EAI Devices, Industry Productivity Solutions, and EAI Data Factory. Guided by the technology and product philosophy of "One Brain, Multi-forms, Multi-capabilities," the Company aims to empower humanoid, biomimetic, and other robotic form factors through a unified EAI Brain, while continuously expanding their multi-task and multi-scenario capabilities. The ecosystem is designed to support the full robotics lifecycle, including R&D, deployment, data collection and training, operations, and commercial applications. The FF EAI Robotics business has already achieved commercial deliveries of humanoid and biomimetic robotic products. Through its multi-form-factor robotic products, EAI technology platform, closed-loop data capabilities, and industry solutions, the business continues to advance the scaled adoption of robotics across real-world applications. The Company also operates RoboShare, a robot-sharing and services platform designed to connect robotic assets, service capabilities, customer demand, and ecosystem partners, further strengthening its robotics commercialization and service ecosystem. The event will feature FF Nova, FF's first embodied AI humanoid robot designed for developers and educational institutions, through an exclusive, invitation-only launch.
FFAI has also announced that FF will introduce FF Nova Mini, a humanoid robot designed for foundational Physical AI education, along with the EAI Education Ecosystem Brain and Curriculum Skills 2.0.
In addition, FF will launch the FF Nova Developer Reinforcement Learning Platform and open exclusive early access to the developer community.

FF EAI Robotics Ecosystem Inc. (NASDAQ: FFR ) is a U.S.-based Embodied AI (EAI) robotics company that is in the process of acquiring the FF EAI Robotics business. Upon completion of the acquisition, the Company will focus on the research and development, manufacturing, commercialization, and deployment of intelligent robotic technologies, products, and industry solutions.

The Company is committed to building a "Four-Core Full-Stack" AI ecosystem covering the full lifecycle of robotics, consisting of EAI Brain & Developer Platform, EAI Devices, Industry Productivity Solutions, and EAI Data Factory. Guided by the technology and product philosophy of "One Brain, Multi-forms, Multi-capabilities," the Company aims to empower humanoid, biomimetic, and other robotic form factors through a unified EAI Brain, while continuously expanding their multi-task and multi-scenario capabilities. The ecosystem is designed to support the full robotics lifecycle, including R&D, deployment, data collection and training, operations, and commercial applications.

The FF EAI Robotics business has already achieved commercial deliveries of humanoid and biomimetic robotic products. Through its multi-form-factor robotic products, EAI technology platform, closed-loop data capabilities, and industry solutions, the business continues to advance the scaled adoption of robotics across real-world applications. The Company also operates RoboShare, a robot-sharing and services platform designed to connect robotic assets, service capabilities, customer demand, and ecosystem partners, further strengthening its robotics commercialization and service ecosystem.

extraction.body: LOS ANGELES , Oct. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- FF EAI Robotics Ecosystem Inc. (NASDAQ: FFR ), a U.S.-based Embodied AI ("EAI") robotics company that has proposed to acquire Faraday Future Intelligent Electric Inc.'s (NASDAQ: FFAI ) EAI Robotics business, today highlighted FFAI's announcement that this week's Investor Weekly Report from Faraday Future ("FF") Founder and Global CEO YT Jia has been rescheduled to October 14. Additionally, FFR and FFAI will host a joint new product launch event on October 14, 2026, featuring four major launches focused on embodied AI robotics, Physical AI education, and developer enablement. The event will feature FF Nova, FF's first embodied AI humanoid robot designed for developers and educational institutions, through an exclusive, invitation-only launch. FFAI has also announced that FF will introduce FF Nova Mini, a humanoid robot designed for foundational Physical AI education, along with the EAI Education Ecosystem Brain and Curriculum Skills 2.0. In addition, FF will launch the FF Nova Developer Reinforcement Learning Platform and open exclusive early access to the developer community. FF EAI Robotics Ecosystem Inc. (NASDAQ: FFR ) is a U.S.-based Embodied AI (EAI) robotics company that is in the process of acquiring the FF EAI Robotics business. Upon completion of the acquisition, the Company will focus on the research and development, manufacturing, commercialization, and deployment of intelligent robotic technologies, products, and industry solutions. The Company is committed to building a "Four-Core Full-Stack" AI ecosystem covering the full lifecycle of robotics, consisting of EAI Brain & Developer Platform, EAI Devices, Industry Productivity Solutions, and EAI Data Factory. Guided by the technology and product philosophy of "One Brain, Multi-forms, Multi-capabilities," the Company aims to empower humanoid, biomimetic, and other robotic form factors through a unified EAI Brain, while continuously expanding their multi-task and multi-scenario capabilities. The ecosystem is designed to support the full robotics lifecycle, including R&D, deployment, data collection and training, operations, and commercial applications. The FF EAI Robotics business has already achieved commercial deliveries of humanoid and biomimetic robotic products. Through its multi-form-factor robotic products, EAI technology platform, closed-loop data capabilities, and industry solutions, the business continues to advance the scaled adoption of robotics across real-world applications. The Company also operates RoboShare, a robot-sharing and services platform designed to connect robotic assets, service capabilities, customer demand, and ecosystem partners, further strengthening its robotics commercialization and service ecosystem. extraction.body: Without a cause of death, it’s unclear if Russia’s precautions were the right ones. Over the weekend, the World Health Organization released a disease outbreak report on the events surrounding the death of a Russian infectious disease researcher earlier this month, highlighting that Russia has yet to report a confirmed cause of death. With that “key uncertainty,” the United Nations health agency said it remains impossible to assess the risk of the event or whether the public health measures Russia took were adequate to prevent spread of the unknown disease. The WHO reported that, so far, it has seen no evidence of ongoing transmission of the mystery disease. “However, confidence in the assessment remains limited by the absence of a confirmed etiological diagnosis, and the remaining uncertainty regarding the source and mode of exposure,” the agency wrote in its report. The agency laid out the order of events as information trickled out from Russian authorities, noting that it only became aware of the death via media reports on October 2. The WHO subsequently made contact with Russian authorities and requested information on October 3, 6, 7, and 8. Early media reports indicated that the lab worker had become ill on September 29, possibly following an incident at the lab, the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute (APRI) of Siberia and the Far East. Some early reports suggested that the researcher—who was identified by media as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova—died of the plague after breaking a test tube. On October 2, the Irkutsk branch of Russian health agency Rospotrebnadzor (RPN) said in a statement that a “special sanitary-epidemiological expert commission” had already met over a suspected case of a high-threat pathogen. Sanitary and epidemic control measures were put in place, including identifying, monitoring, and testing all contacts. At the time, RPN said that all contacts had tested negative for high-threat pathogens. On October 6, Russia’s National Focal Point for the International Health Regulations (NFP) first responded to the WHO’s information requests, saying that no case of plague had been recorded in Irkutsk Oblast. The NFP confirmed that an APRI lab worker had died from a severe case of pneumonia after developing symptoms compatible with an acute respiratory viral infection. The worker was tested for a number of high-threat pathogens, but all the tests had come back negative. Doctors categorized the cause of death as being from pneumonia of undetermined etiology. The NFP also reiterated information from RPN about the public health measures taken and that people in contact with the lab worker all tested negative for high-threat pathogens. The NFP added that the widest range of possible contacts were identified and tested in accordance with Russia’s public health laws. In follow-up responses, the NFP gave more details about testing and some results that weren’t concerning. It said authorities conducted 5,500 laboratory tests on contacts. Over the weekend, the World Health Organization released a disease outbreak report on the events surrounding the death of a Russian infectious disease researcher earlier this month, highlighting that Russia has yet to report a confirmed cause of death. With that “key uncertainty,” the United Nations health agency said it remains impossible to assess the risk of the event or whether the public health measures Russia took were adequate to prevent spread of the unknown disease.

The WHO reported that, so far, it has seen no evidence of ongoing transmission of the mystery disease. “However, confidence in the assessment remains limited by the absence of a confirmed etiological diagnosis, and the remaining uncertainty regarding the source and mode of exposure,” the agency wrote in its report.

The agency laid out the order of events as information trickled out from Russian authorities, noting that it only became aware of the death via media reports on October 2. The WHO subsequently made contact with Russian authorities and requested information on October 3, 6, 7, and 8.

Early media reports indicated that the lab worker had become ill on September 29, possibly following an incident at the lab, the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute (APRI) of Siberia and the Far East. Some early reports suggested that the researcher—who was identified by media as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova—died of the plague after breaking a test tube.

On October 2, the Irkutsk branch of Russian health agency Rospotrebnadzor (RPN) said in a statement that a “special sanitary-epidemiological expert commission” had already met over a suspected case of a high-threat pathogen. Sanitary and epidemic control measures were put in place, including identifying, monitoring, and testing all contacts. At the time, RPN said that all contacts had tested negative for high-threat pathogens.

On October 6, Russia’s National Focal Point for the International Health Regulations (NFP) first responded to the WHO’s information requests, saying that no case of plague had been recorded in Irkutsk Oblast. The NFP confirmed that an APRI lab worker had died from a severe case of pneumonia after developing symptoms compatible with an acute respiratory viral infection. The worker was tested for a number of high-threat pathogens, but all the tests had come back negative. Doctors categorized the cause of death as being from pneumonia of undetermined etiology.

The NFP also reiterated information from RPN about the public health measures taken and that people in contact with the lab worker all tested negative for high-threat pathogens. The NFP added that the widest range of possible contacts were identified and tested in accordance with Russia’s public health laws.

In follow-up responses, the NFP gave more details about testing and some results that weren’t concerning. It said authorities conducted 5,500 laboratory tests on contacts. They tested for a range of pathogens, including influenza, SARS-CoV-2, other respiratory infections, and bacterial infections, including plague and Streptococcus. Among the contacts, they identified two cases of COVID-19, three cases of rhinovirus, and one case of Haemophilus spp., a common bacteria group that includes those that can cause respiratory infections and pneumonia. They also found a few opportunistic infections.

As of October 9, Russian authorities told WHO that they had not detected any high-threat pathogens in the laboratory’s research portfolio in any of the contacts, and they were no longer being monitored. The monitoring period was set for seven days for all the contacts.

Authorities also added that the worker who died was not infected with plague bacteria, Yersinia pestis, and the worker had been vaccinated against the infection due to the occupational hazard. They added that no lab biosafety or biosecurity incident had occurred at APRI, and the deceased worker had not traveled outside the region within the two weeks before becoming ill.

Reviewing all the information coming out of Russia, the WHO was largely at a loss as to what happened and what risk the event posed, concluding: “A key uncertainty for this event is the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker.” Without the cause of death, the agency can’t “independently assess whether the duration of the reported monitoring period for contacts was sufficient to exclude all plausible causes of the fatal illness.” They also aren’t ruling out the possibility of a laboratory-associated exposure.

The global health body has not confirmed plague as the cause of death and says it has not identified evidence of ongoing transmission associated with the event. Pneumonia Of Unknown Etiology According to information provided by Russian authorities, testing did not identify plague or other tested high-threat pathogens. The death has been classified as pneumonia of undetermined etiology, while WHO says it has not received information identifying the causative agent responsible for the fatal illness. 'No Confirmation On Cause' A key uncertainty in the assessment is the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the dead laboratory worker. WHO has stated that it cannot independently assess whether the reported monitoring period for contacts was sufficient to exclude all plausible causes of the fatal illness without a confirmed diagnosis. The absence of an identified pathogen means that the source of the illness remains unclear, and further clinical, epidemiological and laboratory information is needed to establish the cause. Lab-Associated Exposure Cannot Be Ruled Out The occupational background of the dead remains an important consideration. The laboratory worker was employed at an institution that handles high-consequence pathogens, and precautionary public health measures were reportedly implemented because of the individual's professional activities. Although the information provided by Russian authorities does not indicate infection with the tested high-threat pathogens or identify additional linked cases, WHO has cautioned that a laboratory-associated exposure cannot be fully excluded at this stage. No Evidence Of Ongoing Transmission Yet WHO has stated that it has not identified evidence of ongoing transmission associated with the event. However, the organisation has emphasised that confidence in its risk assessment remains limited because the cause of the fatal illness has not been confirmed and uncertainty persists regarding the source and mode of exposure. Confirmatory testing by reference laboratories, where appropriate, may help identify the causative agent. Over the weekend, the World Health Organization released a disease outbreak report on the events surrounding the death of a Russian infectious disease researcher earlier this month, highlighting that Russia has yet to report a confirmed cause of death. With that “key uncertainty,” the United Nations health agency said it remains impossible to assess the risk of the event or whether the public health measures Russia took were adequate to prevent spread of the unknown disease.

The WHO reported that, so far, it has seen no evidence of ongoing transmission of the mystery disease. “However, confidence in the assessment remains limited by the absence of a confirmed etiological diagnosis, and the remaining uncertainty regarding the source and mode of exposure,” the agency wrote in its report.

The agency laid out the order of events as information trickled out from Russian authorities, noting that it only became aware of the death via media reports on October 2. The WHO subsequently made contact with Russian authorities and requested information on October 3, 6, 7, and 8.

Early media reports indicated that the lab worker had become ill on September 29, possibly following an incident at the lab, the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute (APRI) of Siberia and the Far East. Some early reports suggested that the researcher—who was identified by media as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova—died of the plague after breaking a test tube.

On October 2, the Irkutsk branch of Russian health agency Rospotrebnadzor (RPN) said in a statement that a “special sanitary-epidemiological expert commission” had already met over a suspected case of a high-threat pathogen. Sanitary and epidemic control measures were put in place, including identifying, monitoring, and testing all contacts. At the time, RPN said that all contacts had tested negative for high-threat pathogens.

On October 6, Russia’s National Focal Point for the International Health Regulations (NFP) first responded to the WHO’s information requests, saying that no case of plague had been recorded in Irkutsk Oblast. The NFP confirmed that an APRI lab worker had died from a severe case of pneumonia after developing symptoms compatible with an acute respiratory viral infection. The worker was tested for a number of high-threat pathogens, but all the tests had come back negative. Doctors categorized the cause of death as being from pneumonia of undetermined etiology.

The NFP also reiterated information from RPN about the public health measures taken and that people in contact with the lab worker all tested negative for high-threat pathogens. The NFP added that the widest range of possible contacts were identified and tested in accordance with Russia’s public health laws.

In follow-up responses, the NFP gave more details about testing and some results that weren’t concerning. It said authorities conducted 5,500 laboratory tests on contacts. They tested for a range of pathogens, including influenza, SARS-CoV-2, other respiratory infections, and bacterial infections, including plague and Streptococcus. Among the contacts, they identified two cases of COVID-19, three cases of rhinovirus, and one case of Haemophilus spp., a common bacteria group that includes those that can cause respiratory infections and pneumonia. They also found a few opportunistic infections.

As of October 9, Russian authorities told WHO that they had not detected any high-threat pathogens in the laboratory’s research portfolio in any of the contacts, and they were no longer being monitored. The monitoring period was set for seven days for all the contacts.

Authorities also added that the worker who died was not infected with plague bacteria, Yersinia pestis, and the worker had been vaccinated against the infection due to the occupational hazard. They added that no lab biosafety or biosecurity incident had occurred at APRI, and the deceased worker had not traveled outside the region within the two weeks before becoming ill.

Reviewing all the information coming out of Russia, the WHO was largely at a loss as to what happened and what risk the event posed, concluding: “A key uncertainty for this event is the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker.” Without the cause of death, the agency can’t “independently assess whether the duration of the reported monitoring period for contacts was sufficient to exclude all plausible causes of the fatal illness.” They also aren’t ruling out the possibility of a laboratory-associated exposure.

The World Health Organisation (WHO) says it has found no evidence of ongoing transmission linked to the death of a laboratory worker in Russia, following reports that pneumonic plague was suspected as the cause.

In a Disease Outbreak News update published on Saturday, 10 October 2026, the WHO said it was informed of the death of an employee of the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East on 2 October.

According to reports, the worker died on the same day after being hospitalised on 29 September with severe pneumonia. Pneumonic plague was suspected following possible occupational exposure in a laboratory setting.

However, the Russian Federation’s National Focal Point for the International Health Regulations confirmed the death to the WHO and reported that no recent cases of plague had been registered in Irkutsk Oblast.
The authorities also said investigations found no evidence of a laboratory biosecurity incident, contrary to media reports.

The WHO said laboratory tests conducted on the deceased worker and contacts were negative for the high-threat pathogens tested, while no additional cases of severe pneumonia linked to the incident had been reported.
All identified contacts were medically monitored in healthcare facilities or at home and remained asymptomatic throughout the follow-up period.
Quarantine measures were also introduced at the hospital where the worker had been treated.
“Based on the information provided by NFP, WHO has not identified evidence of ongoing transmission associated with this event,” the organisation said.
However, the global health agency noted that a key uncertainty remained because the cause of the worker’s death had not been conclusively established.
The WHO said it would continue monitoring the situation and assess any potential public health implications as further information becomes available.
Pneumonic plague is a severe form of plague that affects the lungs and can spread between people through infectious respiratory droplets.
However, the suspected diagnosis in this case has not been confirmed.
The WHO’s update is based on information supplied by Russian health authorities and does not establish a confirmed plague outbreak.

extraction.body: Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks have been soaring in value in recent years, with Nvidia ( NVDA -1.29% ) leading the charge. The chip giant is worth a massive $5.4 trillion, as its products are crucial for many tech companies looking to stay ahead of the competition. The opportunities are enormous, but what doesn't get nearly as much attention are the risks. It's not just the debt that many tech companies are piling on that is a concern, but as AI advances and tech is doing more for people and businesses than it did before, there are also significant risks related to automation. What could derail AI stocks is the risk that AI agents pose to both the companies that develop them and the customers relying on them. There have been multiple reports about AI agents not staying within their confines, which is a growing issue in the tech sector . One of the most high-profile events included OpenAI agents launching a cyberattack against Hugging Face a few months ago. The company is now facing a lawsuit due to that. There are multiple issues stemming from this type of risk. First is the obvious one -- a company can face high legal costs if its agents go rogue and cause harm. In addition, OpenAI will need to spend more time and money to develop agents more carefully to ensure the risks are minimal in the future. And even then, there may still be concerns if it has done enough. The second issue is that companies may be less willing to deploy agents if there is the potential for these types of situations. Even if an agent doesn't attack another company, it may still improperly use or share confidential data. If a company has to spend additional efforts on safeguarding its assets, it would make investments in AI even more costly. At a time when spending on AI is already under scrutiny, companies may balk at the idea, especially if there are doubts about the potential payoff. The result could be a slowdown of demand, which could derail the bull story around not only Nvidia but also other AI stocks . Nvidia is a top growth stock to own, so long as the AI growth story is a promising one. But if there are any cracks in it, or if there are signs that companies are beginning to pull back on AI-related spending, that can wreak havoc on Nvidia's growth and its valuation. Currently, the stock looks cheap as it's trading at just 25 times its estimated future profits. But that's based on analyst expectations of how it will do in the future. If those expectations unravel, the stock may not look nearly as cheap and attractive anymore, and that may be the case for many other stocks as well. Investors should consider the risks related to AI before deciding whether to buy Nvidia or any other stock, as ignoring them could prove costly down the road. With stocks like Nvidia ( Nasdaq: NVDA ) posting moonshot growth over the past year, Canadian investors are no doubt wondering — should I be investing in “AI stocks?” It’s easy to lose sight of this in all the buzz, but artificial intelligence (AI) stocks are simply tech companies that are making incredibly smart machines. Whether it’s using face recognition to unlock your phone or “auto-correcting” your grammatical errors, artificial intelligence has already infiltrated our daily lives. And the technology is only getting started: The worldwide AI market is forecasted to grow immensely before the end of this decade. PWC sees AI technology contributing up to $15.7 trillion to the global economy by 2030. 1 So if you believe artificial intelligence will play a growing role in our lives, investing in AI stocks could be a smart way to benefit from that prediction. Here, we’ll break down the ins and outs of AI investing in Canada to help you decide if it’s the right investment for you in 2026. When our analyst team has a stock tip, it can pay to listen. After all, Stock Advisor Canada's total average return is 103% - a market-crushing outperformance compared to 88% for the S&P/TSX Composite Index. Artificial intelligence (AI) is a branch of computer science tasked with making machines that emulate human intelligence. These machines make decisions without human interference, and they can learn from past experiences to make better decisions in the future. Generally speaking, AI stocks can be broken down into two groups This list of Canadian AI stocks to invest in will no doubt evolve as the technology continues to grow at a furious pace. Already, there are dozens of startups that could one day hit the public markets. For now, let’s look at a few of the top artificial intelligence companies already trading on the Toronto Stock Exchange . Kinaxis ( TSX: KXS ) remains one of the most compelling Canadian names at the intersection of SaaS (software-as-a-service) and AI, offering mission-critical supply chain management tools that global enterprises rely on daily. Its RapidResponse platform enables real-time simulation, planning, and problem detection across complex logistics networks – capabilities that became indispensable during the pandemic and remain essential amid ongoing supply disruptions and the shift toward AI-driven efficiency. While the stock doesn’t pay a dividend, its value proposition lies squarely in growth, recurring revenue, and long-term compounding. The company continues to post strong momentum though 2025. In its most recent quarter, SaaS recurring revenue grew more than 17%, supporting a broader trend of consistent double-digit annual revenue gains. Net profit jumped 150% year over year, highlighting the scalability of its model. Despite these results, the share price has remained in a relatively tight range, suggesting the market hasn’t yet fully recognized the company’s strength. What sets Kinaxis apart is the “stickiness” of its customer base. With blue-chip clients in sectors like automotive, healthcare, and consumer goods, multi-year contracts and mission-critical integrations create a high barrier to switching. This stability fuels predictable subscription income, strong gross margins, and a healthy flow of cash that Kinaxis uses to reinvest in innovation rather than risky expansion. The company also maintains a debt-free balance sheet, an advantage few tech peers can claim. With enterprise demand rising for AI-enhanced planning tools this year, and financial performance strengthening quarter after quarter, Kinaxis looks well positioned for a breakout if sentiment shifts. For investors seeking high-quality, profitable tech exposure into 2026, this remains a standout candidate. Celestica ( TSX: CLS ) has emerged as one of Canada’s most explosive growth stories in 2025, powered by its deep exposure to AI data-center hardware and hyperscaler infrastructure. Once known primarily as a contract manufacturer, the company has transformed into a central supplier for next-generation compute and cloud systems. That shift has unlocked extraordinary shareholder returns: Celestica is up more than 350% over the past year and nearly 3,000% since late 2022, making it the best-performing large-cap tech stock in the country. Momentum remains strong this year. In Q3 2025, Celestica delivered 28% revenue growth, a record operating margin, and rising contributions from hyperscaler clients—its most important growth engine as AI/ML compute demand accelerates. With cloud providers racing to expand capacity for high-performance servers, networking gear, and storage systems, Celestica has secured a multiyear runway of orders tied directly to the global AI buildout. Analysts now expect the company’s earnings to more than double by 2028, reflecting both margin expansion and aggressive production scaling. Celestica’s positioning within the AI hardware stack is what sets it apart. The company supplies critical components needed for AI workloads, training clusters, and massive cloud deployments, making it a direct beneficiary of capex cycles led by Meta, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and other hyperscalers. Demand for compute and storage capacity continues to climb sharply in 2025 as AI rollouts intensify, driving consistently strong backlogs and repeated quarterly earnings beats. OpenText ( TSX: OTEX ) is one of the more intriguing value opportunities in Canadian tech heading into 2025, with its transformation efforts now gaining traction after several reset years. The Waterloo-based enterprise software company focuses on information management, cybersecurity, and AI-enhanced cloud solutions. Its Aviator platform — which integrates generative AI, predictive analytics, and conversational search — has become central to its strategy as customers shift toward higher-margin cloud subscriptions. After a difficult start to last year, OpenText has staged a meaningful rebound. Shares have climbed more than 40% over the past six months, boosted by improving financial execution and clearer integration progress following the Micro Focus acquisition. In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025, revenue rose 4.5% sequentially to US$1.3 billion, while adjusted EBITDA jumped more than 12% to US$443.9 million. That pushed the EBITDA margin to 33.9%, up from 32.7% a year earlier. The stock offers a dividend yield near 2.8%, making it a rare total-return play within Canada’s AI sector. A key driver of the recent rally has been OpenText’s strategic shift toward cloud and AI, supported by a multiyear effort to streamline operations. To reduce debt and concentrate capital on cloud innovation, the OpenText divested non-core assets including the AMC business in 2024 and just recently, eDOCS. With fresh guidance calling for 1–2% revenue growth in fiscal 2026, investors have taken the return to forward visibility as a sign that the balance-sheet cleanup and product consolidation are working. Momentum into late 2025 remains strong, with the stock breaking above the $50 level for the first time since early 2024. For investors seeking a stable, cash-flow-rich way to participate in the rise of AI and enterprise cloud, OTEX stands out as a compelling, under-the-radar option. Another SaaS company, Docebo ( TSX: DCBO ) remains one of the more compelling long-term growth stories in Canada’s tech sector, even if its recent share-price performance suggests otherwise. The stock has fallen sharply in 2025 pressured by leadership turnover, tougher competition, and a broader market debate around the profitability of AI-aligned software firms. As a pure growth name, the company does not pay a dividend, so returns are entirely tied to business execution and share-price appreciation. Operationally, the company continues to deliver. Docebo’s most recent quarterly report showed revenue up 11% to more than $61 million, ahead of expectations, with profitability rising more than 20% year over year. Earlier quarters also exceeded guidance, including second-quarter increases of 14.5% in revenue and 15.4% in adjusted EPS. Multi-year customer agreements help support revenue stability, even as the broader learning-software landscape becomes more competitive. Instead, the focus for 2026 is on companies with established competitive moats and proprietary data. Canada’s AI landscape offers diverse opportunities beyond the global mega-caps. Conservative investors can look to blue-chip giants like CGI Inc. and OpenText, which provide stability by integrating AI into massive existing service contracts. Growth-focused investors may prefer specialized SaaS leaders like Kinaxis or Docebo, which are leveraging AI to dominate supply chain and e-learning niches. This list of Canadian AI stocks to invest in will no doubt evolve as the technology continues to grow at a furious pace. Already, there are dozens of startups that could one day hit the public markets.
For now, let’s look at a few of the top artificial intelligence companies already trading on the Toronto Stock Exchange .

Kinaxis ( TSX: KXS ) remains one of the most compelling Canadian names at the intersection of SaaS (software-as-a-service) and AI, offering mission-critical supply chain management tools that global enterprises rely on daily. Its RapidResponse platform enables real-time simulation, planning, and problem detection across complex logistics networks – capabilities that became indispensable during the pandemic and remain essential amid ongoing supply disruptions and the shift toward AI-driven efficiency. While the stock doesn’t pay a dividend, its value proposition lies squarely in growth, recurring revenue, and long-term compounding.

The company continues to post strong momentum though 2025. In its most recent quarter, SaaS recurring revenue grew more than 17%, supporting a broader trend of consistent double-digit annual revenue gains. Net profit jumped 150% year over year, highlighting the scalability of its model. Despite these results, the share price has remained in a relatively tight range, suggesting the market hasn’t yet fully recognized the company’s strength.

What sets Kinaxis apart is the “stickiness” of its customer base. With blue-chip clients in sectors like automotive, healthcare, and consumer goods, multi-year contracts and mission-critical integrations create a high barrier to switching. This stability fuels predictable subscription income, strong gross margins, and a healthy flow of cash that Kinaxis uses to reinvest in innovation rather than risky expansion. The company also maintains a debt-free balance sheet, an advantage few tech peers can claim.

With enterprise demand rising for AI-enhanced planning tools this year, and financial performance strengthening quarter after quarter, Kinaxis looks well positioned for a breakout if sentiment shifts. For investors seeking high-quality, profitable tech exposure into 2026, this remains a standout candidate.

Celestica ( TSX: CLS ) has emerged as one of Canada’s most explosive growth stories in 2025, powered by its deep exposure to AI data-center hardware and hyperscaler infrastructure. Once known primarily as a contract manufacturer, the company has transformed into a central supplier for next-generation compute and cloud systems. That shift has unlocked extraordinary shareholder returns: Celestica is up more than 350% over the past year and nearly 3,000% since late 2022, making it the best-performing large-cap tech stock in the country.

Momentum remains strong this year. In Q3 2025, Celestica delivered 28% revenue growth, a record operating margin, and rising contributions from hyperscaler clients—its most important growth engine as AI/ML compute demand accelerates. With cloud providers racing to expand capacity for high-performance servers, networking gear, and storage systems, Celestica has secured a multiyear runway of orders tied directly to the global AI buildout. Analysts now expect the company’s earnings to more than double by 2028, reflecting both margin expansion and aggressive production scaling.

Celestica’s positioning within the AI hardware stack is what sets it apart. The company supplies critical components needed for AI workloads, training clusters, and massive cloud deployments, making it a direct beneficiary of capex cycles led by Meta, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and other hyperscalers. Demand for compute and storage capacity continues to climb sharply in 2025 as AI rollouts intensify, driving consistently strong backlogs and repeated quarterly earnings beats.

OpenText ( TSX: OTEX ) is one of the more intriguing value opportunities in Canadian tech heading into 2025, with its transformation efforts now gaining traction after several reset years. The Waterloo-based enterprise software company focuses on information management, cybersecurity, and AI-enhanced cloud solutions. Its Aviator platform — which integrates generative AI, predictive analytics, and conversational search — has become central to its strategy as customers shift toward higher-margin cloud subscriptions.

After a difficult start to last year, OpenText has staged a meaningful rebound. Shares have climbed more than 40% over the past six months, boosted by improving financial execution and clearer integration progress following the Micro Focus acquisition. In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025, revenue rose 4.5% sequentially to US$1.3 billion, while adjusted EBITDA jumped more than 12% to US$443.9 million. That pushed the EBITDA margin to 33.9%, up from 32.7% a year earlier. The stock offers a dividend yield near 2.8%, making it a rare total-return play within Canada’s AI sector.

A key driver of the recent rally has been OpenText’s strategic shift toward cloud and AI, supported by a multiyear effort to streamline operations. To reduce debt and concentrate capital on cloud innovation, the OpenText divested non-core assets including the AMC business in 2024 and just recently, eDOCS. With fresh guidance calling for 1–2% revenue growth in fiscal 2026, investors have taken the return to forward visibility as a sign that the balance-sheet cleanup and product consolidation are working.

Momentum into late 2025 remains strong, with the stock breaking above the $50 level for the first time since early 2024. For investors seeking a stable, cash-flow-rich way to participate in the rise of AI and enterprise cloud, OTEX stands out as a compelling, under-the-radar option.

Another SaaS company, Docebo ( TSX: DCBO ) remains one of the more compelling long-term growth stories in Canada’s tech sector, even if its recent share-price performance suggests otherwise. The stock has fallen sharply in 2025 pressured by leadership turnover, tougher competition, and a broader market debate around the profitability of AI-aligned software firms. That decline has pushed Docebo’s valuation down to appealing levels, with its forward earnings multiple now below 20. As a pure growth name, the company does not pay a dividend, so returns are entirely tied to business execution and share-price appreciation.

Operationally, the company continues to deliver. Docebo’s most recent quarterly report showed revenue up 11% to more than $61 million, ahead of expectations, with profitability rising more than 20% year over year. Earlier quarters also exceeded guidance, including second-quarter increases of 14.5% in revenue and 15.4% in adjusted EPS. Multi-year customer agreements help support revenue stability, even as the broader learning-software landscape becomes more competitive.

The AI market has evolved from the “hype” phase of previous years into a period of massive commercial deployment. By the start of 2026, AI has become a fundamental driver of corporate earnings, with the Canadian AI market projected to surpass $40 billion (USD) in revenue this year.
While the sector offers immense growth, the investment landscape has become more discerning:

Canadian investors should remain cautious of micro-cap “pure-play” AI stocks, which often exhibit extreme volatility. Instead, the focus for 2026 is on companies with established competitive moats and proprietary data.

Canada’s AI landscape offers diverse opportunities beyond the global mega-caps. Conservative investors can look to blue-chip giants like CGI Inc. and OpenText, which provide stability by integrating AI into massive existing service contracts. Growth-focused investors may prefer specialized SaaS leaders like Kinaxis or Docebo, which are leveraging AI to dominate supply chain and e-learning niches. For high-reward infrastructure plays, Celestica remains a standout, benefiting from the global surge in demand for AI data center hardware.

The Bottom Line: AI stocks remain a strong buy for those with a long-term horizon. However, success in 2026 requires moving past the buzzwords to evaluate a company’s fundamental business model and its ability to turn AI integration into bottom-line profit.

If you don’t want to invest in individual AI stocks, you can always buy an AI-focused exchange-traded fund (ETF) . ETFs are an easy way to invest in a bunch of companies at the same time, so you get more diversification and potentially take on less risk than you would by investing in any single stock.

extraction.body: Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks have been soaring in value in recent years, with Nvidia ( NVDA -1.29% ) leading the charge. The chip giant is worth a massive $5.4 trillion, as its products are crucial for many tech companies looking to stay ahead of the competition. The opportunities are enormous, but what doesn't get nearly as much attention are the risks. It's not just the debt that many tech companies are piling on that is a concern, but as AI advances and tech is doing more for people and businesses than it did before, there are also significant risks related to automation. What could derail AI stocks is the risk that AI agents pose to both the companies that develop them and the customers relying on them. There have been multiple reports about AI agents not staying within their confines, which is a growing issue in the tech sector . One of the most high-profile events included OpenAI agents launching a cyberattack against Hugging Face a few months ago. The company is now facing a lawsuit due to that. There are multiple issues stemming from this type of risk. First is the obvious one -- a company can face high legal costs if its agents go rogue and cause harm. In addition, OpenAI will need to spend more time and money to develop agents more carefully to ensure the risks are minimal in the future. And even then, there may still be concerns if it has done enough. The second issue is that companies may be less willing to deploy agents if there is the potential for these types of situations. Even if an agent doesn't attack another company, it may still improperly use or share confidential data. If a company has to spend additional efforts on safeguarding its assets, it would make investments in AI even more costly. At a time when spending on AI is already under scrutiny, companies may balk at the idea, especially if there are doubts about the potential payoff. The result could be a slowdown of demand, which could derail the bull story around not only Nvidia but also other AI stocks . Nvidia is a top growth stock to own, so long as the AI growth story is a promising one. But if there are any cracks in it, or if there are signs that companies are beginning to pull back on AI-related spending, that can wreak havoc on Nvidia's growth and its valuation. Currently, the stock looks cheap as it's trading at just 25 times its estimated future profits. But that's based on analyst expectations of how it will do in the future. If those expectations unravel, the stock may not look nearly as cheap and attractive anymore, and that may be the case for many other stocks as well. Investors should consider the risks related to AI before deciding whether to buy Nvidia or any other stock, as ignoring them could prove costly down the road. extraction.body: “No more hand-written code” or AI-free art for delayed Marvel/Star Wars shooter. Epic Games is shifting to an “AI first” development strategy for its collaboration with the Walt Disney Company, letting AI models write all the code and guide all the artwork for an upcoming shooter. That’s according to a Bloomberg report , which cites unnamed people familiar with the project who commented on the significant pivot in internal development at the Unreal Engine maker. Human developers will be tasked with managing and guiding code and art assets generated by models such as Anthropic’s Claude, according to internal Epic employee messages viewed by Bloomberg. That means “no more hand-written code” and art assets “generated with full AI workflows,” according to the report. The $1.5 billion collaboration between Epic and Disney, announced in early 2024 , was slated to release a Marvel- and Star Wars-themed shooter in March 2027. That project has now been delayed indefinitely amid the AI-related shakeup and understaffed, slower-than-expected development thus far, according to the report. “We’re embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do,” an Epic spokesperson said in a statement. “We have a huge pivot underway here at Epic, moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration,” Epic CEO Tim Sweeney wrote on social media shortly after the Bloomberg story was posted. “The aim isn’t to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal.” Sweeney and Epic have long been bullish on what they see as an impending game development revolution spurred by AI. In an interview with IGN in June , Sweeney saw the technology resulting in games with “the possibility of infinite dialogue with a really simple setup for creators,” leading to situations where “small teams will be able to create games with immense amounts of characters and immense and interactive worlds.” Sweeney said last November that AI usage disclosure tags such as those required by Valve’s Steam platform “make no sense” because AI tools “will be involved in nearly all future production.” Epic laid off over 1,000 employees in March , citing a “downturn in Fortnite engagement” as the main reason behind the move. Months later, Fortnite Senior External Development Manager Stephanie Arnette said that “I know everyone’s biggest fear is, ‘Oh my god, AI is going to take all our jobs.’ That’s not our goal. The goal is to make us more efficient.” Last May, Epic and Disney faced some embarrassment when an AI-voiced Darth Vader character added to Fortnite started repeating curse words and uttering some baffling opinions before a hotfix was rolled out. A survey of over 2,300 game industry professionals ahead of this year’s Game Developers Conference found that 36 percent used generative AI tools as part of their jobs, including 30 percent of those at game development studios. But those AI tools were used for tasks like research and brainstorming (by 81 percent of AI-using respondents) much more than for code assistance (47 percent) and prototyping (35 percent).
