Epic Games is shifting to an “AI first” development strategy for its collaboration with the Walt Disney Company, letting AI models write all the code and guide all the artwork for an upcoming shooter. That’s according to a Bloomberg report , which cites unnamed people familiar with the project who commented on the significant pivot in internal development at the Unreal Engine maker.

Human developers will be tasked with managing and guiding code and art assets generated by models such as Anthropic’s Claude, according to internal Epic employee messages viewed by Bloomberg. That means “no more hand-written code” and art assets “generated with full AI workflows,” according to the report.

The $1.5 billion collaboration between Epic and Disney, announced in early 2024 , was slated to release a Marvel- and Star Wars-themed shooter in March 2027. That project has now been delayed indefinitely amid the AI-related shakeup and understaffed, slower-than-expected development thus far, according to the report.
“We’re embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do,” an Epic spokesperson said in a statement.

“We have a huge pivot underway here at Epic, moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration,” Epic CEO Tim Sweeney wrote on social media shortly after the Bloomberg story was posted. “The aim isn’t to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal.”

Sweeney and Epic have long been bullish on what they see as an impending game development revolution spurred by AI. In an interview with IGN in June , Sweeney saw the technology resulting in games with “the possibility of infinite dialogue with a really simple setup for creators,” leading to situations where “small teams will be able to create games with immense amounts of characters and immense and interactive worlds.”
Sweeney said last November that AI usage disclosure tags such as those required by Valve’s Steam platform “make no sense” because AI tools “will be involved in nearly all future production.”

The game, a multiplayer shooter built around Marvel and Star Wars characters, was slated for a March release. That date is gone, and Epic has not named a replacement. The story lands at an awkward moment for the games industry, which is already bracing for a wave of AI-driven production changes. Epic is not a scrappy startup experimenting on a side project. It is the company behind Fortnite, the Unreal Engine that powers a huge share of AAA development, and a decade of public fights over app store economics. When Epic changes how it builds games, other studios take notice, and this delay is becoming a case study in what “AI first” actually means when it collides with a licensed, high-profile project tied to two of the most valuable entertainment brands on the planet. The project in question is described across multiple outlets, including GamesIndustry.biz , as a multiplayer shooter drawing characters and settings from Marvel and Star Wars, two franchises Disney owns outright. It had been positioned internally for a March launch. That timeline has now slipped, and as of October 12, 2026, Epic has not communicated a new date publicly or internally, according to the reporting reviewed for this story. What makes this delay different from a routine schedule slip is the instruction that reportedly came with it. Developers on the project were told to adopt an AI first production model, a phrase that, per the internal messaging described in the reporting, meant leaning on generative tools for both code and art rather than treating AI as a supplementary tool. One of the game’s directors reportedly wrote in an internal message that there would be “no more hand-written code,” and that the game’s art would be “generated with full AI workflows.” Those are striking lines for a licensed project built on characters as tightly controlled as Spider-Man or Darth Vader, where visual consistency with decades of established designs typically matters as much as gameplay feel. Epic’s communications director, Jake Jones, addressed the shift in a statement to Ars Technica , saying the company is “embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do.” The framing is deliberate: Epic wants the story to read as developers directing AI tools, not AI tools replacing developers. Whether that distinction holds up once the game actually ships is a separate question, and one the industry will be watching closely. Human developers were still instructed to manage and guide the AI-generated output rather than being removed from the loop entirely, based on the available reporting. That detail matters because it suggests Epic is not attempting to automate the project end to end without oversight, but rather restructuring what human developers spend their time doing, shifting them from production tasks toward direction, curation, and quality control. It is tempting to draw a straight line from “AI first mandate” to “project delayed,” but the reporting does not actually confirm that causation. Alongside the AI shift, reports also point to underestimated staffing needs and development time as contributing factors, a far more ordinary explanation that shows up in postmortems for licensed games going back decades. Disney properties come with extensive approval processes, legal review, and brand guidelines that can slow any studio regardless of its tooling. Still, the optics are hard to ignore. A studio pivots to AI-generated art and code on a project, and the same project misses its date. Readers and competitors will draw their own conclusions, and some of those conclusions will be unfair to the engineers and artists who had no say in the production strategy. The more useful question is whether retooling a project mid-development around generative tools is itself a schedule risk, independent of whether the underlying technology works. Switching pipelines partway through any game’s production cycle has historically been one of the most reliable ways to blow a deadline, long before generative AI entered the picture. There is also a simpler explanation worth taking seriously: Epic may have concluded that shipping in March with the original pipeline would have produced a worse game than shipping later with a retooled one. Delays framed around quality are common in games marketing, but they are not automatically false. Without an official release date or a direct comment from Epic on root cause, both readings remain live possibilities, and this article treats them as such rather than asserting one as fact. “AI first” is quickly becoming one of those phrases every tech company wants to claim and few define consistently. For Epic’s Disney project, the reporting indicates it meant generative tools, including Anthropic’s Claude, handling first-pass code generation and full AI workflows producing art assets, with human staff reviewing, directing, and refining the output rather than originating it from scratch. That is a meaningfully different workflow from using AI as autocomplete inside an IDE, which is how most studios have deployed these tools so far. Claude’s presence in a flagship Epic production is notable on its own. Anthropic has spent much of 2026 pushing its models deeper into coding and agentic workflows, and Claude Opus 5.5’s expanded context window has made it a popular choice for large, sprawling codebases, exactly the kind a live-service multiplayer shooter accumulates. Using it for both code and creative asset direction on a Disney-licensed title signals a level of institutional confidence from Epic that goes beyond a pilot program. The internal line about “no more hand-written code” is the most quoted detail from the reporting, and for good reason. Most studios that have adopted AI coding assistants still describe the tools as accelerants, something that drafts boilerplate or suggests fixes while engineers remain the primary authors. A directive suggesting the reverse, that AI generates the code and engineers primarily review and steer it, represents a different division of labor. It is closer to how some teams already use Claude Code for scaffolding entire features, just scaled up to a full production title rather than a side project or prototype. Art generation carries its own set of complications that code generation does not. Marvel and Star Wars characters are governed by brand bibles that specify exact silhouettes, color palettes, and proportions. Generative art tools are good at producing plausible-looking content quickly, but matching decades-old brand guidelines with pixel-level consistency across hundreds of assets is a harder bar to clear than writing functional code. If Disney’s approval process rejected early AI-generated assets for failing to match established character designs, that alone could account for schedule slippage independent of any coding issues. Epic did not arrive at this decision in a vacuum. The broader game engine market has been racing toward AI-assisted tooling for more than a year. Google and Unity launched Spark, an AI game maker aimed at adult creators , and Unity’s own roadmap for Unity 7 includes AI-assisted shader work promising dramatic speed gains. Capcom has gone even further on the content side, building a suite of six internal AI programs under its REX initiative to help remake assets in its RE Engine. Reaction across gaming press and developer communities, including outlets like Dexerto , has split along predictable lines. Some read the delay as validation that AI-generated code and art still need more runway before they can anchor a major licensed release. Others see it as evidence that studios willing to absorb short-term schedule pain for structural workflow change will come out ahead once the tools mature. Both camps are, in effect, making predictions about technology that is evolving month to month, which is exactly why a single delayed game should not be treated as definitive proof of either position. A high-profile stumble on a Disney collaboration, even one eventually resolved, gives ammunition to studios weighing whether to commit to Epic’s AI-forward production philosophy for their own licensed projects. The bigger risk for Disney is not the delay itself but the possibility that AI-generated likenesses of Spider-Man, Darth Vader, or other closely guarded characters drift even slightly from established designs in ways fans notice immediately. Brand consistency, not ship dates, is typically Disney’s highest priority in licensing deals of this scale. For Anthropic, the exposure is reputational in the opposite direction, a positive one if the eventual game ships well, a negative one if critics trace production problems back to AI-generated code or art. Anthropic has been aggressively marketing Claude’s coding capabilities throughout 2026, and a visible win inside a Disney-branded, Epic-published title would be a significant proof point for enterprise and studio customers evaluating whether to adopt similar workflows. For engineers and artists working inside Epic or watching from competing studios, the practical question is what “managing and guiding AI-generated work” actually looks like day to day. Reviewing AI output at scale, catching subtle art inconsistencies, and debugging code you did not write yourself are different skills than originating that work from scratch, and they are not skills every studio has systematically trained its staff to use. Studios considering a similar pivot would be wise to treat this less as a tooling swap and more as a role redefinition that needs its own onboarding and quality assurance processes. Developers who spent months building systems for a shooter under one production model, then were told midstream to shift toward reviewing AI output instead of writing it, are absorbing a significant change in how they spend their working hours. Jones’s statement that Epic developers remain “the visionaries and creative drivers” is Epic’s attempt to reassure that workforce, but whether that framing matches the day-to-day experience on the ground is something only the people on the project can really judge. Strip away the Disney and Marvel names, and this story is really about whether “AI first” is a production philosophy mature enough to survive contact with a real, dated, high-stakes commercial release. Plenty of studios have used AI tools successfully on smaller, lower-visibility features. Far fewer have attempted to rebuild an entire project’s code and art pipeline around generative tools mid-development, on a licensed product, with a named external partner watching the outcome. Epic’s experience, whatever the eventual verdict, will be one of the most closely studied case studies the industry has for judging that question. Some read the delay as validation that AI-generated code and art still need more runway before they can anchor a major licensed release. Others see it as evidence that studios willing to absorb short-term schedule pain for structural workflow change will come out ahead once the tools mature. Both camps are, in effect, making predictions about technology that is evolving month to month, which is exactly why a single delayed game should not be treated as definitive proof of either position.

The comparison makes Epic’s situation look distinct for one reason: it is the only entry on this list where AI tooling was applied directly to a specific, dated, licensed product rather than to an engine feature, an internal catalog project, or a standalone consumer app. That distinction is exactly why the delay carries more weight than it otherwise would. A missed internal roadmap milestone is routine. A missed date on a co-branded Marvel and Star Wars title, attached publicly to an AI production method, becomes a referendum on the method itself, fairly or not.

Generative AI’s march into game production did not start with Epic’s Disney project, and it is worth placing this story on a timeline rather than treating it as an isolated event. Jagex leaned on modern engine tooling, including a jump to Unreal Engine, for its RS4 relaunch of RuneScape, a title reportedly ending a 25-year wait for a new entry in the MMO’s core lineage . Rocket League’s developers took an even bigger technical leap, skipping two engine generations entirely to jump from Unreal Engine 3 straight to Unreal Engine 6 , a move that reflects how aggressively studios are willing to overhaul foundational tooling when the payoff looks big enough.

What distinguishes this moment is the specificity of the claim: not “we upgraded our engine” or “we built an AI tool,” but “we rebuilt our production process around AI mid-development on a named, dated, licensed product.” That is a much higher-stakes bet than anything on the list above, and it is why the Disney delay is drawing more scrutiny than a typical engine migration story would.

For Epic, the immediate financial exposure from a single delayed title is limited. Epic is privately held and does not disclose per-project revenue, so there is no stock reaction to track the way there would be for a public company. The bigger stake is reputational and strategic: Epic has spent years positioning Unreal Engine as the technically superior choice for AAA and licensed development, competing directly against Unity for engine market share. A high-profile stumble on a Disney collaboration, even one eventually resolved, gives ammunition to studios weighing whether to commit to Epic’s AI-forward production philosophy for their own licensed projects.

For Disney, the calculus is different. Disney licenses its characters across dozens of partners every year and has weathered delays on games before without major fallout, provided the eventual product meets brand standards. The bigger risk for Disney is not the delay itself but the possibility that AI-generated likenesses of Spider-Man, Darth Vader, or other closely guarded characters drift even slightly from established designs in ways fans notice immediately. Brand consistency, not ship dates, is typically Disney’s highest priority in licensing deals of this scale.

For Anthropic, the exposure is reputational in the opposite direction, a positive one if the eventual game ships well, a negative one if critics trace production problems back to AI-generated code or art. Anthropic has been aggressively marketing Claude’s coding capabilities throughout 2026, and a visible win inside a Disney-branded, Epic-published title would be a significant proof point for enterprise and studio customers evaluating whether to adopt similar workflows.

For engineers and artists working inside Epic or watching from competing studios, the practical question is what “managing and guiding AI-generated work” actually looks like day to day. Reviewing AI output at scale, catching subtle art inconsistencies, and debugging code you did not write yourself are different skills than originating that work from scratch, and they are not skills every studio has systematically trained its staff to use. Studios considering a similar pivot would be wise to treat this less as a tooling swap and more as a role redefinition that needs its own onboarding and quality assurance processes.

There is also a morale dimension that rarely shows up in corporate statements. Developers who spent months building systems for a shooter under one production model, then were told midstream to shift toward reviewing AI output instead of writing it, are absorbing a significant change in how they spend their working hours. Jones’s statement that Epic developers remain “the visionaries and creative drivers” is Epic’s attempt to reassure that workforce, but whether that framing matches the day-to-day experience on the ground is something only the people on the project can really judge.

Strip away the Disney and Marvel names, and this story is really about whether “AI first” is a production philosophy mature enough to survive contact with a real, dated, high-stakes commercial release. Plenty of studios have used AI tools successfully on smaller, lower-visibility features. Far fewer have attempted to rebuild an entire project’s code and art pipeline around generative tools mid-development, on a licensed product, with a named external partner watching the outcome. Epic’s experience, whatever the eventual verdict, will be one of the most closely studied case studies the industry has for judging that question.

The takeaway: this delay is not proof that AI-first game development fails, nor is it proof that it works. It is one data point from one studio on one project, wrapped in a licensing relationship that adds pressure the typical AI pilot program never faces. The next real signal will come when Epic actually sets, and hits or misses, a new date, and when players finally get to judge whether “full AI workflows” produced art that looks and feels like the Marvel and Star Wars they already know.

sources.title: Epic Delays Disney Game, Goes AI First [2026] - shattered.io
passages: Epic Games has pushed back the release of its long-awaited collaboration with Walt Disney Co., and the reason has nothing to do with a bug list or a missing boss fight.

According to reporting from Bloomberg and GamesIndustry.biz, Epic told the development team working on the project to rebuild its workflow around an “AI first” model, trading hand-written code and traditional art pipelines for generative tools including Anthropic’s Claude.
Claude’s presence in a flagship Epic production is notable on its own.

Anthropic has spent much of 2026 pushing its models deeper into coding and agentic workflows, and Claude Opus 5.5’s expanded context window has made it a popular choice for large, sprawling codebases, exactly the kind a live-service multiplayer shooter accumulates.
Using it for both code and creative asset direction on a Disney-licensed title signals a level of institutional confidence from Epic that goes beyond a pilot program.

Epic’s own engine business has repeatedly used technical superiority as a competitive weapon against Unity, and the two companies have traded market share in recent quarters, with Unreal Engine 6 reportedly holding roughly 42% share against Unity’s 30% .
An AI-first production pipeline, if it proves faster without compromising quality, would be another point Epic could use to recruit studios away from competing engines.

If it instead produces a visibly rough, delayed game built on one of the most recognizable entertainment properties in the world, it becomes a cautionary tale that rival engine makers will be happy to cite.

For Anthropic, the exposure is reputational in the opposite direction, a positive one if the eventual game ships well, a negative one if critics trace production problems back to AI-generated code or art.
The takeaway: this delay is not proof that AI-first game development fails, nor is it proof that it works.
It had been positioned internally for a March launch.
That timeline has now slipped, and as of October 12, 2026, Epic has not communicated a new date publicly or internally, according to the reporting reviewed for this story.
Did Epic confirm the AI shift caused the delay?

Against that backdrop, Epic retooling a flagship Disney collaboration around generative workflows looks less like an outlier bet and more like catching up to an industry-wide shift that is already underway.
For Epic, the immediate financial exposure from a single delayed title is limited.

There is also a simpler explanation worth taking seriously: Epic may have concluded that shipping in March with the original pipeline would have produced a worse game than shipping later with a retooled one.

What distinguishes this moment is the specificity of the claim: not “we upgraded our engine” or “we built an AI tool,” but “we rebuilt our production process around AI mid-development on a named, dated, licensed product.” That is a much higher-stakes bet than anything on the list above, and it is why the Disney delay is drawing more scrutiny than a typical engine migration story would.
Disney licenses its characters across dozens of partners every year and has weathered delays on games before without major fallout, provided the eventual product meets brand standards.

extraction.body: Epic Games has pushed back the release of its long-awaited collaboration with Walt Disney Co., and the reason has nothing to do with a bug list or a missing boss fight. According to reporting from Bloomberg and GamesIndustry.biz, Epic told the development team working on the project to rebuild its workflow around an “AI first” model, trading hand-written code and traditional art pipelines for generative tools including Anthropic’s Claude. The game, a multiplayer shooter built around Marvel and Star Wars characters, was slated for a March release. That date is gone, and Epic has not named a replacement. The story lands at an awkward moment for the games industry, which is already bracing for a wave of AI-driven production changes. Epic is not a scrappy startup experimenting on a side project. It is the company behind Fortnite, the Unreal Engine that powers a huge share of AAA development, and a decade of public fights over app store economics. When Epic changes how it builds games, other studios take notice, and this delay is becoming a case study in what “AI first” actually means when it collides with a licensed, high-profile project tied to two of the most valuable entertainment brands on the planet. The project in question is described across multiple outlets, including GamesIndustry.biz , as a multiplayer shooter drawing characters and settings from Marvel and Star Wars, two franchises Disney owns outright. It had been positioned internally for a March launch. That timeline has now slipped, and as of October 12, 2026, Epic has not communicated a new date publicly or internally, according to the reporting reviewed for this story. What makes this delay different from a routine schedule slip is the instruction that reportedly came with it. Developers on the project were told to adopt an AI first production model, a phrase that, per the internal messaging described in the reporting, meant leaning on generative tools for both code and art rather than treating AI as a supplementary tool. One of the game’s directors reportedly wrote in an internal message that there would be “no more hand-written code,” and that the game’s art would be “generated with full AI workflows.” Those are striking lines for a licensed project built on characters as tightly controlled as Spider-Man or Darth Vader, where visual consistency with decades of established designs typically matters as much as gameplay feel. Epic’s communications director, Jake Jones, addressed the shift in a statement to Ars Technica , saying the company is “embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do.” The framing is deliberate: Epic wants the story to read as developers directing AI tools, not AI tools replacing developers. Whether that distinction holds up once the game actually ships is a separate question, and one the industry will be watching closely. Human developers were still instructed to manage and guide the AI-generated output rather than being removed from the loop entirely, based on the available reporting. That detail matters because it suggests Epic is not attempting to automate the project end to end without oversight, but rather restructuring what human developers spend their time doing, shifting them from production tasks toward direction, curation, and quality control. It is tempting to draw a straight line from “AI first mandate” to “project delayed,” but the reporting does not actually confirm that causation. Alongside the AI shift, reports also point to underestimated staffing needs and development time as contributing factors, a far more ordinary explanation that shows up in postmortems for licensed games going back decades. Disney properties come with extensive approval processes, legal review, and brand guidelines that can slow any studio regardless of its tooling. Still, the optics are hard to ignore. A studio pivots to AI-generated art and code on a project, and the same project misses its date. Readers and competitors will draw their own conclusions, and some of those conclusions will be unfair to the engineers and artists who had no say in the production strategy. The more useful question is whether retooling a project mid-development around generative tools is itself a schedule risk, independent of whether the underlying technology works. Switching pipelines partway through any game’s production cycle has historically been one of the most reliable ways to blow a deadline, long before generative AI entered the picture. There is also a simpler explanation worth taking seriously: Epic may have concluded that shipping in March with the original pipeline would have produced a worse game than shipping later with a retooled one. Delays framed around quality are common in games marketing, but they are not automatically false. Without an official release date or a direct comment from Epic on root cause, both readings remain live possibilities, and this article treats them as such rather than asserting one as fact. “AI first” is quickly becoming one of those phrases every tech company wants to claim and few define consistently. For Epic’s Disney project, the reporting indicates it meant generative tools, including Anthropic’s Claude, handling first-pass code generation and full AI workflows producing art assets, with human staff reviewing, directing, and refining the output rather than originating it from scratch. That is a meaningfully different workflow from using AI as autocomplete inside an IDE, which is how most studios have deployed these tools so far. Claude’s presence in a flagship Epic production is notable on its own. Anthropic has spent much of 2026 pushing its models deeper into coding and agentic workflows, and Claude Opus 5.5’s expanded context window has made it a popular choice for large, sprawling codebases, exactly the kind a live-service multiplayer shooter accumulates. Using it for both code and creative asset direction on a Disney-licensed title signals a level of institutional confidence from Epic that goes beyond a pilot program. The internal line about “no more hand-written code” is the most quoted detail from the reporting, and for good reason. Most studios that have adopted AI coding assistants still describe the tools as accelerants, something that drafts boilerplate or suggests fixes while engineers remain the primary authors. A directive suggesting the reverse, that AI generates the code and engineers primarily review and steer it, represents a different division of labor. It is closer to how some teams already use Claude Code for scaffolding entire features, just scaled up to a full production title rather than a side project or prototype. Art generation carries its own set of complications that code generation does not. Marvel and Star Wars characters are governed by brand bibles that specify exact silhouettes, color palettes, and proportions. Generative art tools are good at producing plausible-looking content quickly, but matching decades-old brand guidelines with pixel-level consistency across hundreds of assets is a harder bar to clear than writing functional code. If Disney’s approval process rejected early AI-generated assets for failing to match established character designs, that alone could account for schedule slippage independent of any coding issues. Epic did not arrive at this decision in a vacuum. The broader game engine market has been racing toward AI-assisted tooling for more than a year. Google and Unity launched Spark, an AI game maker aimed at adult creators , and Unity’s own roadmap for Unity 7 includes AI-assisted shader work promising dramatic speed gains. Capcom has gone even further on the content side, building a suite of six internal AI programs under its REX initiative to help remake assets in its RE Engine. Against that backdrop, Epic retooling a flagship Disney collaboration around generative workflows looks less like an outlier bet and more like catching up to an industry-wide shift that is already underway. Epic’s own engine business has repeatedly used technical superiority as a competitive weapon against Unity, and the two companies have traded market share in recent quarters, with Unreal Engine 6 reportedly holding roughly 42% share against Unity’s 30% . An AI-first production pipeline, if it proves faster without compromising quality, would be another point Epic could use to recruit studios away from competing engines. If it instead produces a visibly rough, delayed game built on one of the most recognizable entertainment properties in the world, it becomes a cautionary tale that rival engine makers will be happy to cite. Reaction across gaming press and developer communities, including outlets like Dexerto , has split along predictable lines. Some read the delay as validation that AI-generated code and art still need more runway before they can anchor a major licensed release. Others see it as evidence that studios willing to absorb short-term schedule pain for structural workflow change will come out ahead once the tools mature. Both camps are, in effect, making predictions about technology that is evolving month to month, which is exactly why a single delayed game should not be treated as definitive proof of either position. The comparison makes Epic’s situation look distinct for one reason: it is the only entry on this list where AI tooling was applied directly to a specific, dated, licensed product rather than to an engine feature, an internal catalog project, or a standalone consumer app. That distinction is exactly why the delay carries more weight than it otherwise would. A missed internal roadmap milestone is routine. A missed date on a co-branded Marvel and Star Wars title, attached publicly to an AI production method, becomes a referendum on the method itself, fairly or not. Generative AI’s march into game production did not start with Epic’s Disney project, and it is worth placing this story on a timeline rather than treating it as an isolated event. Jagex leaned on modern engine tooling, including a jump to Unreal Engine, for its RS4 relaunch of RuneScape, a title reportedly ending a 25-year wait for a new entry in the MMO’s core lineage . Rocket League’s developers took an even bigger technical leap, skipping two engine generations entirely to jump from Unreal Engine 3 straight to Unreal Engine 6 , a move that reflects how aggressively studios are willing to overhaul foundational tooling when the payoff looks big enough. What distinguishes this moment is the specificity of the claim: not “we upgraded our engine” or “we built an AI tool,” but “we rebuilt our production process around AI mid-development on a named, dated, licensed product.” That is a much higher-stakes bet than anything on the list above, and it is why the Disney delay is drawing more scrutiny than a typical engine migration story would. For Epic, the immediate financial exposure from a single delayed title is limited. Epic is privately held and does not disclose per-project revenue, so there is no stock reaction to track the way there would be for a public company. The bigger stake is reputational and strategic: Epic has spent years positioning Unreal Engine as the technically superior choice for AAA and licensed development, competing directly against Unity for engine market share. A high-profile stumble on a Disney collaboration, even one eventually resolved, gives ammunition to studios weighing whether to commit to Epic’s AI-forward production philosophy for their own licensed projects. For Disney, the calculus is different. Disney licenses its characters across dozens of partners every year and has weathered delays on games before without major fallout, provided the eventual product meets brand standards. The bigger risk for Disney is not the delay itself but the possibility that AI-generated likenesses of Spider-Man, Darth Vader, or other closely guarded characters drift even slightly from established designs in ways fans notice immediately. Brand consistency, not ship dates, is typically Disney’s highest priority in licensing deals of this scale. For Anthropic, the exposure is reputational in the opposite direction, a positive one if the eventual game ships well, a negative one if critics trace production problems back to AI-generated code or art. Anthropic has been aggressively marketing Claude’s coding capabilities throughout 2026, and a visible win inside a Disney-branded, Epic-published title would be a significant proof point for enterprise and studio customers evaluating whether to adopt similar workflows. The project in question is described across multiple outlets, including GamesIndustry.biz , as a multiplayer shooter drawing characters and settings from Marvel and Star Wars, two franchises Disney owns outright. Developers on the project were told to adopt an AI first production model, a phrase that, per the internal messaging described in the reporting, meant leaning on generative tools for both code and art rather than treating AI as a supplementary tool. Epic’s communications director, Jake Jones, addressed the shift in a statement to Ars Technica , saying the company is “embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do.” The framing is deliberate: Epic wants the story to read as developers directing AI tools, not AI tools replacing developers. Human developers were still instructed to manage and guide the AI-generated output rather than being removed from the loop entirely, based on the available reporting. That detail matters because it suggests Epic is not attempting to automate the project end to end without oversight, but rather restructuring what human developers spend their time doing, shifting them from production tasks toward direction, curation, and quality control.

It is tempting to draw a straight line from “AI first mandate” to “project delayed,” but the reporting does not actually confirm that causation. Alongside the AI shift, reports also point to underestimated staffing needs and development time as contributing factors, a far more ordinary explanation that shows up in postmortems for licensed games going back decades. Disney properties come with extensive approval processes, legal review, and brand guidelines that can slow any studio regardless of its tooling.

Delays framed around quality are common in games marketing, but they are not automatically false. “AI first” is quickly becoming one of those phrases every tech company wants to claim and few define consistently. That is a meaningfully different workflow from using AI as autocomplete inside an IDE, which is how most studios have deployed these tools so far.

Claude’s presence in a flagship Epic production is notable on its own. Anthropic has spent much of 2026 pushing its models deeper into coding and agentic workflows, and Claude Opus 5.5’s expanded context window has made it a popular choice for large, sprawling codebases, exactly the kind a live-service multiplayer shooter accumulates. Using it for both code and creative asset direction on a Disney-licensed title signals a level of institutional confidence from Epic that goes beyond a pilot program.

The internal line about “no more hand-written code” is the most quoted detail from the reporting, and for good reason. Google and Unity launched Spark, an AI game maker aimed at adult creators , and Unity’s own roadmap for Unity 7 includes AI-assisted shader work promising dramatic speed gains. passages: SEALSQ Corp has announced a $10 million private investment in public equity (PIPE) in WISeSat.Space Holdings Corp, aimed at advancing next-generation satellite technology and integrating post-quantum security measures across space and ground infrastructure.

The investment, which closed on October 1, 2026, will enable WISeSat.Space to expand its satellite infrastructure and develop quantum-resilient communications to bolster cybersecurity against future quantum computing threats.
Both companies, part of the WISeQey Corp group, share a commitment to enhancing secure communications in the emerging space economy.

SEALSQ's involvement is expected to facilitate the delivery of quantum and post-quantum services, ultimately contributing to a more trusted and secure space infrastructure for transactions among different systems.

John O’Hara, CFO of SEALSQ, added, “This investment supports SEALSQ’s strategy to extend the application of our secure semiconductor, cryptographic and trusted identity technologies into space-based communications.
Our focus is on translating this collaboration into commercial opportunities that support long-term value for SEALSQ shareholders.”
WISeSat is a space technology company focused on secure satellite communications for Internet of Things applications.
Its approach combines satellite infrastructure with cybersecurity and digital identity technologies to support trusted communications between connected devices and ground-based systems.

The Subscription Agreement includes a price-protection mechanism that may result in the issuance of additional WISeSat Ordinary Shares to SEALSQ under certain conditions if the volume-weighted average price of WISeSat Ordinary Shares for the 10 consecutive trading days ending on the 60th calendar day after Closing is below the purchase price, subject to a maximum issuance of an additional 1,073,216 shares.
About SEALSQ: SEALSQ is a leading innovator in Post-Quantum Technology hardware and software solutions.
As quantum computers advance, traditional cryptographic methods like RSA and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) are increasingly vulnerable.
By embedding Post-Quantum Cryptography into our semiconductor solutions, SEALSQ ensures that organizations stay protected against quantum threats.

passages: Geneva, Switzerland – May 5, 2026 — WISeKey International Holding Ltd (SIX: WIHN; NASDAQ: WKEY ), a global leader in cybersecurity, digital identity and IoT, today provides an update on the strategic progress of its space subsidiary WISeSat.Space ("WISeSat"), from its initial secure satellite communications pilot missions launched in 2021 to advancing its positioning as "WISE Space Advanced Technologies," a European quantum-secure space-technology company.

By integrating post‑quantum payloads developed with SEALSQ and aligning with its QSOC roadmap, WISeSat is building a differentiated, defensible platform that can support new revenue streams in secure data services, edge processing, and trusted connectivity for both governmental and commercial customers.

The subsidiaries include (i) SEALSQ Corp (Nasdaq: LAES), which focuses on semiconductors, PKI, and post-quantum technology products, (ii) WISeKey SA, which specializes in RoT and PKI solutions for secure authentication and identification in IoT, blockchain, and AI, (iii) WISeSat AG which focuses on space technology for secure satellite communication, specifically for IoT applications, (iv) WISe.ART Corp which focuses on trusted blockchain NFTs and operates the WISe.ART marketplace for secure NFT transactions, and (v) SEALCOIN AG which focuses on decentralized physical internet with DePIN technology and houses the development of the SEALCOIN platform.

This positioning is designed to make WISeSat's positioning and name reference to be purpose accessible to U.S. and European institutional investors and other interested persons, and as a focused space-and-quantum platform, distinct from generic satellite operators or chip-only cybersecurity companies.

WISeSat began its space program as a focused industrial initiative inside the WISeKey Group, with the conviction that the world's connected infrastructure would require a sovereign, quantum-resilient communications layer delivered from orbit.

From its first pilot missions, WISeSat has progressively developed satellite-related capabilities and partner-operated mission experience, providing technical learning and flight heritage for its planned transition toward larger, next-generation satellite infrastructure.
Each subsidiary contributes to WISeKey's mission of securing the internet while focusing on their respective areas of research and expertise.
For more information on WISeKey's strategic direction and its subsidiary companies, please visit www.wisekey.com.
WISeSat develops, procures, and operates small satellites infrastructure, rights-of-use arrangements, and runs the associated ground-segment capabilities in LEO.

extraction.body: PRESS RELEASE — WISeSat.Space (Nasdaq: SAIQ) (“WISeSat.Space” or the “Company”) today outlined its strategy to integrate post-quantum cryptography (“PQC”) into its next-generation satellite communications and Internet of Things (“IoT”) architecture, supporting the migration objectives established by U.S. Executive Order 14412, Securing the Nation Against Advanced Cryptographic Attacks. The Company is developing a security architecture designed to protect communications, digital identities and satellite operations against both conventional cyberattacks and emerging quantum-computing threats. Its approach combines post-quantum semiconductor technologies from its sister company, SEALSQ Corp.’s (Nasdaq: LAES) with trusted digital identity and cryptographic key management across connected devices, ground infrastructure and future satellite platforms. “Security is a core differentiator in our strategy to build a satellite communications business serving governments, enterprises and critical infrastructure operators,” said Carlos Moreira, Founder and CEO of WISeSat.Space. “As satellites become increasingly critical infrastructure for our digital economy, protecting them throughout their operational lives is central to our value proposition. Our ambition is to bring trust into every layer, from the semiconductor and connected device to the ground station and satellite. By integrating post-quantum technologies across connected devices, ground infrastructure and satellites, we aim to strengthen our competitive position, address demand for secure, sovereign communications and create long-term shareholder value.” Following its October 2026 business combination and Nasdaq listing, WISeSat.Space closed a $10 million PIPE investment led by SEALSQ to accelerate the development of its quantum-resilient space architecture. WISeSat.Space’s existing network and partner infrastructure include access to 9 active low-earth-orbit satellites, supported by ground stations in Lausanne, Switzerland, and La Línea de la Concepción, Spain. This operational base supports the development of the Company’s next-generation Quantum Spatial Orbital Cloud (“QSOC”). Its long-term roadmap targets a 100-satellite sovereign constellation by 2033, subject to financing, technical development, regulatory approvals and launch availability. Integration of the next-generation PQC architecture is being advanced through planned deployments and does not imply that every satellite currently accessible through the network already carries the same post-quantum hardware. Issued on June 22, 2026, Executive Order 14412 directs the transition of federal information systems to NIST-approved post-quantum cryptography and supports migration planning for critical infrastructure owners and operators. For federal high-value assets and high-impact systems, excluding National Security Systems, the order sets migration objectives of December 31, 2030, for PQC key establishment and December 31, 2031, for PQC digital signatures. It also directs the development of proposed federal procurement requirements addressing applicable NIST standards. WISeSat.Space’s architecture is being developed to support these objectives. Regulatory alignment and compliance will be assessed for individual implementations against applicable standards, cryptographic module validation requirements and customer procurement conditions. The Company’s technology strategy draws on SEALSQ’s Quantum Shield QS7001 and QVault TPM platforms, which support NIST-standardized algorithms including: These capabilities are intended to complement hardware-based protection of cryptographic keys and trusted identities. Using standardized algorithms provides a foundation for migration; end-to-end security also depends on their implementation, integration and operation. WISeSat.Space is developing its architecture around several applications where communications security and long-term data protection are essential. Government and sovereign communications. Post-quantum key establishment and authentication can support protected satellite connectivity for government agencies, remote facilities and emergency-response teams. Combined with sovereign identity and key-management arrangements, the architecture is intended to help customers retain control over access to sensitive communications. Critical infrastructure monitoring. Satellite-connected sensors can provide telemetry from energy installations, water networks, transport corridors and other assets beyond terrestrial network coverage. Trusted device identities and authenticated messages can help operators verify the source and integrity of readings used for maintenance, incident detection and operational decisions. Satellite command and software integrity. Post-quantum signatures can support verification of satellite commands and software updates, helping protect against impersonation and unauthorized modifications. Hardware-protected keys provide a foundation for authenticating operational systems, while secure update mechanisms can support cryptographic upgrades during a satellite’s service life. Remote industrial IoT and logistics. Connected equipment, containers and monitoring devices can use satellite links to report location, condition and operational status. Authentication and protected communications are intended to help customers trust the data received from remote assets and reduce exposure to forged messages. Long-term protection of sensitive information. Government, industrial and infrastructure data may remain confidential for years. Post-quantum key establishment is intended to reduce exposure to “harvest now, decrypt later” attacks, in which adversaries collect encrypted traffic today for possible decryption using future quantum computers. Our focus is on translating this collaboration into commercial opportunities that support long-term value for SEALSQ shareholders.”

Geneva, Switzerland – May 5, 2026 — WISeKey International Holding Ltd (SIX: WIHN; NASDAQ: WKEY ), a global leader in cybersecurity, digital identity and IoT, today provides an update on the strategic progress of its space subsidiary WISeSat.Space ("WISeSat"), from its initial secure satellite communications pilot missions launched in 2021 to advancing its positioning as "WISE Space Advanced Technologies," a European quantum-secure space-technology company.

By integrating post‑quantum payloads developed with SEALSQ and aligning with its QSOC roadmap, WISeSat is building a differentiated, defensible platform that can support new revenue streams in secure data services, edge processing, and trusted connectivity for both governmental and commercial customers.

This positioning is designed to make WISeSat's positioning and name reference to be purpose accessible to U.S. and European institutional investors and other interested persons, and as a focused space-and-quantum platform, distinct from generic satellite operators or chip-only cybersecurity companies.

passages: Geneva, Switzerland – May 5, 2026 — WISeKey International Holding Ltd (SIX: WIHN; NASDAQ: WKEY ), a global leader in cybersecurity, digital identity and IoT, today provides an update on the strategic progress of its space subsidiary WISeSat.Space ("WISeSat"), from its initial secure satellite communications pilot missions launched in 2021 to advancing its positioning as "WISE Space Advanced Technologies," a European quantum-secure space-technology company.

By integrating post‑quantum payloads developed with SEALSQ and aligning with its QSOC roadmap, WISeSat is building a differentiated, defensible platform that can support new revenue streams in secure data services, edge processing, and trusted connectivity for both governmental and commercial customers.

The subsidiaries include (i) SEALSQ Corp (Nasdaq: LAES), which focuses on semiconductors, PKI, and post-quantum technology products, (ii) WISeKey SA, which specializes in RoT and PKI solutions for secure authentication and identification in IoT, blockchain, and AI, (iii) WISeSat AG which focuses on space technology for secure satellite communication, specifically for IoT applications, (iv) WISe.ART Corp which focuses on trusted blockchain NFTs and operates the WISe.ART marketplace for secure NFT transactions, and (v) SEALCOIN AG which focuses on decentralized physical internet with DePIN technology and houses the development of the SEALCOIN platform.

This positioning is designed to make WISeSat's positioning and name reference to be purpose accessible to U.S. and European institutional investors and other interested persons, and as a focused space-and-quantum platform, distinct from generic satellite operators or chip-only cybersecurity companies.

WISeSat began its space program as a focused industrial initiative inside the WISeKey Group, with the conviction that the world's connected infrastructure would require a sovereign, quantum-resilient communications layer delivered from orbit.

From its first pilot missions, WISeSat has progressively developed satellite-related capabilities and partner-operated mission experience, providing technical learning and flight heritage for its planned transition toward larger, next-generation satellite infrastructure.
Each subsidiary contributes to WISeKey's mission of securing the internet while focusing on their respective areas of research and expertise.
For more information on WISeKey's strategic direction and its subsidiary companies, please visit www.wisekey.com.
WISeSat develops, procures, and operates small satellites infrastructure, rights-of-use arrangements, and runs the associated ground-segment capabilities in LEO.

extraction.body: PRESS RELEASE — WISeSat.Space (Nasdaq: SAIQ) (“WISeSat.Space” or the “Company”) today outlined its strategy to integrate post-quantum cryptography (“PQC”) into its next-generation satellite communications and Internet of Things (“IoT”) architecture, supporting the migration objectives established by U.S. Executive Order 14412, Securing the Nation Against Advanced Cryptographic Attacks. The Company is developing a security architecture designed to protect communications, digital identities and satellite operations against both conventional cyberattacks and emerging quantum-computing threats. Its approach combines post-quantum semiconductor technologies from its sister company, SEALSQ Corp.’s (Nasdaq: LAES) with trusted digital identity and cryptographic key management across connected devices, ground infrastructure and future satellite platforms. “Security is a core differentiator in our strategy to build a satellite communications business serving governments, enterprises and critical infrastructure operators,” said Carlos Moreira, Founder and CEO of WISeSat.Space. “As satellites become increasingly critical infrastructure for our digital economy, protecting them throughout their operational lives is central to our value proposition. Our ambition is to bring trust into every layer, from the semiconductor and connected device to the ground station and satellite. By integrating post-quantum technologies across connected devices, ground infrastructure and satellites, we aim to strengthen our competitive position, address demand for secure, sovereign communications and create long-term shareholder value.” Following its October 2026 business combination and Nasdaq listing, WISeSat.Space closed a $10 million PIPE investment led by SEALSQ to accelerate the development of its quantum-resilient space architecture. WISeSat.Space’s existing network and partner infrastructure include access to 9 active low-earth-orbit satellites, supported by ground stations in Lausanne, Switzerland, and La Línea de la Concepción, Spain. This operational base supports the development of the Company’s next-generation Quantum Spatial Orbital Cloud (“QSOC”). Its long-term roadmap targets a 100-satellite sovereign constellation by 2033, subject to financing, technical development, regulatory approvals and launch availability. Integration of the next-generation PQC architecture is being advanced through planned deployments and does not imply that every satellite currently accessible through the network already carries the same post-quantum hardware. Issued on June 22, 2026, Executive Order 14412 directs the transition of federal information systems to NIST-approved post-quantum cryptography and supports migration planning for critical infrastructure owners and operators. For federal high-value assets and high-impact systems, excluding National Security Systems, the order sets migration objectives of December 31, 2030, for PQC key establishment and December 31, 2031, for PQC digital signatures. It also directs the development of proposed federal procurement requirements addressing applicable NIST standards. WISeSat.Space’s architecture is being developed to support these objectives. Regulatory alignment and compliance will be assessed for individual implementations against applicable standards, cryptographic module validation requirements and customer procurement conditions. The Company’s technology strategy draws on SEALSQ’s Quantum Shield QS7001 and QVault TPM platforms, which support NIST-standardized algorithms including: These capabilities are intended to complement hardware-based protection of cryptographic keys and trusted identities. Using standardized algorithms provides a foundation for migration; end-to-end security also depends on their implementation, integration and operation. WISeSat.Space is developing its architecture around several applications where communications security and long-term data protection are essential. Government and sovereign communications. Post-quantum key establishment and authentication can support protected satellite connectivity for government agencies, remote facilities and emergency-response teams. Combined with sovereign identity and key-management arrangements, the architecture is intended to help customers retain control over access to sensitive communications. Critical infrastructure monitoring. Satellite-connected sensors can provide telemetry from energy installations, water networks, transport corridors and other assets beyond terrestrial network coverage. Trusted device identities and authenticated messages can help operators verify the source and integrity of readings used for maintenance, incident detection and operational decisions. Satellite command and software integrity. Post-quantum signatures can support verification of satellite commands and software updates, helping protect against impersonation and unauthorized modifications. Hardware-protected keys provide a foundation for authenticating operational systems, while secure update mechanisms can support cryptographic upgrades during a satellite’s service life. Remote industrial IoT and logistics. Connected equipment, containers and monitoring devices can use satellite links to report location, condition and operational status. Authentication and protected communications are intended to help customers trust the data received from remote assets and reduce exposure to forged messages. Long-term protection of sensitive information. Government, industrial and infrastructure data may remain confidential for years. Post-quantum key establishment is intended to reduce exposure to “harvest now, decrypt later” attacks, in which adversaries collect encrypted traffic today for possible decryption using future quantum computers. Leveraging post-quantum cryptography and quantum key distribution, WISeSat.Space addresses the need for resilient, trusted digital infrastructure in the era of quantum threats. Its solutions emphasize easy deployment, global coverage, and integration with existing systems, supporting critical operations in remote and high-security environments. facts.text: SEALSQ Corp has announced a $10 million private investment in public equity (PIPE) in WISeSat.Space Holdings Corp, aimed at advancing next-generation satellite technology and integrating post-quantum security measures across space and ground infrastructure.

The investment, which closed on October 1, 2026, will enable WISeSat.Space to expand its satellite infrastructure and develop quantum-resilient communications to bolster cybersecurity against future quantum computing threats.
Both companies, part of the WISeQey Corp group, share a commitment to enhancing secure communications in the emerging space economy.

SEALSQ's involvement is expected to facilitate the delivery of quantum and post-quantum services, ultimately contributing to a more trusted and secure space infrastructure for transactions among different systems.

John O’Hara, CFO of SEALSQ, added, “This investment supports SEALSQ’s strategy to extend the application of our secure semiconductor, cryptographic and trusted identity technologies into space-based communications.
Our focus is on translating this collaboration into commercial opportunities that support long-term value for SEALSQ shareholders.”
WISeSat is a space technology company focused on secure satellite communications for Internet of Things applications.
Its approach combines satellite infrastructure with cybersecurity and digital identity technologies to support trusted communications between connected devices and ground-based systems.

The Subscription Agreement includes a price-protection mechanism that may result in the issuance of additional WISeSat Ordinary Shares to SEALSQ under certain conditions if the volume-weighted average price of WISeSat Ordinary Shares for the 10 consecutive trading days ending on the 60th calendar day after Closing is below the purchase price, subject to a maximum issuance of an additional 1,073,216 shares.
About SEALSQ: SEALSQ is a leading innovator in Post-Quantum Technology hardware and software solutions.
As quantum computers advance, traditional cryptographic methods like RSA and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) are increasingly vulnerable.
By embedding Post-Quantum Cryptography into our semiconductor solutions, SEALSQ ensures that organizations stay protected against quantum threats.

The company focuses on providing global satellite-based communications for asset monitoring and device-to-device data transfer, targeting industries such as logistics, agriculture, energy, and defense.

The Company is developing a security architecture designed to protect communications, digital identities and satellite operations against both conventional cyberattacks and emerging quantum-computing threats.
WISeSat.Space is developing its architecture around several applications where communications security and long-term data protection are essential.

WISeSat.Space’s existing network and partner infrastructure include access to 9 active low-earth-orbit satellites, supported by ground stations in Lausanne, Switzerland, and La Línea de la Concepción, Spain.

Following its October 2026 business combination and Nasdaq listing, WISeSat.Space closed a $10 million PIPE investment led by SEALSQ to accelerate the development of its quantum-resilient space architecture.
The Quantum Insider (TQI) is the leading source for the latest quantum technology news, market intelligence, industry analysis, and data covering the global quantum ecosystem.

Federal officers raided Minnesota Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home early Monday morning, reportedly related to an investigation into the lawmaker’s immigration paperwork, filed by a relative when Omar was a child.

The search was conducted by Homeland Security Investigations, a branch of the Department of Homeland Security that manages criminal investigations, and, according to a Justice Department spokesperson, “executed a judicially authorized search warrant” the agency secured. An anonymous source reportedly “familiar with the situation” alleged to NBC News that the raid was part of a yearslong investigation involving whistleblowers. CNN also reported that a federal judge approved the search warrant but did not name the judge.

White House border czar Tom Homan, the acting head of ICE, stated on Fox News last month that Homeland Security was investigating Omar for alleged unspecified “criminal” conduct, but claimed he couldn’t “give the specifics of what’s happening.”

“If someone committed an immigration violation, if someone committed marriage fraud or anything like that, regardless if they’re a congressman or not, no one’s above the law,” Homan said at the time. “So, I’ll leave it at that. We’ll let HSI, Homeland Security Investigations, continue the investigation.”
In a Monday morning Fox interview, Homan confirmed that the search had taken place.

Omar immigrated to the US from Somalia in 1995, when she was 12, amid the ongoing civil war in the country. She became a naturalized US citizen in 2000. President Donald Trump and his administration have regularly racially targeted Omar —a progressive Democrat and frequent critic of the administration’s policies—fueling further violent threats against her and other lawmakers of color, and people from Somalia living in Minnesota .

Trump and other White House officials have repeatedly cited the Feeding Our Future fraud scandal that involved members of the state’s Somali American community to justify the mass violence by immigration officers in the area as part of ICE’s Operation Metro Surge in late 2025.

The timing of the raid on Omar’s Washington-area home—22 days before the November midterms, in which she is a heavy favorite for reelection—adds additional scrutiny, as Justice Department policy prohibits federal prosecutors and agents from timing investigations or charges to affect election outcomes. While not a binding rule, the Justice Department has historically complied by pausing all related actions in the 60 days before an election. (Trump and the wider MAGA movement have repeatedly targeted former FBI head James Comey, and that agency as a whole, in part over the timing and supposed political motivations of the FBI’s own investigations under Comey into both Trump and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton.)

“Americans see this for what it is,” Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, a Democrat who the Trump administration has also targeted , wrote on social media. “President ​Trump is abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election.”

“I’m ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar posted on social media Monday afternoon. “This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.”

And a bipartisan group of senators is calling on the Trump administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia despite a U.S. sanctions law. extraction.body: The Fitbit Edge may not be Google’s best-kept fitness-tracking secret, but as of today, its existence is official. The tracker sits smack-dab between the recently launched Fitbit Air and the more powerful Google Pixel Watch 5 in the company’s current wearable lineup. Basically, if you have smartwatch fatigue but don’t want to give up notifications, this is Google’s answer to the aging Fitbit Charge 6. Much of the Edge’s specs were previously leaked, but the tracker has a 46 percent larger OLED display compared to the Charge 6, a physical side button, and is a smidge thicker at 11.5mm. The tracker uses the same proprietary charger as the Air, and can also get about a day’s worth of battery in five minutes. (A full charge takes 90 minutes.) For health tracking, the Edge has an EKG sensor for atrial fibrillation detection, a skin temperature sensor, SpO2 and optical heart rate sensors, plus your typical motion tracking sensors. The Edge doesn’t have a mic or speaker, so you can’t take calls from the wrist even though you can see who’s calling on the screen. The latter is a bit disappointing, given that the Edge essentially replaces the Charge 6 and is $20 more expensive at $179.99. The new Fitbit offers improved automatic workout tracking and GPS compared to the Charge 6. The former is a revised motion model that’ll also come to the Air. Google says the new model means auto activity tracking is twice as accurate and supports over 100 activities. extraction.body: Amazon recently followed Microsoft’s lead and said it will no longer use nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) while negotiating with local governments over data centers. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Sean O’Kane, Rebecca Bellan, and I discussed Amazon’s announcement, which came in the middle of a longer blog post making the case that data centers are actually good for communities. Rebecca was a bit skeptical that the recent spate of data center moratoriums will have a lasting effect, especially since the moratoriums only last for a year or two and “these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years,” though I countered that data center backers definitely seem worried. Sean, meanwhile, suggested that a big reason for the backlash is the industry’s poor communication. “We’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them,” he said. Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Sean: It’s an interesting thing that it was sort of buried in the blog post and part of a larger story that Amazon’s clearly trying to tell. I guess I understand why they weren’t putting it in the foreground, but to me, this is at the root of so many of the problems that the tech industry currently faces when it comes to AI broadly, but data centers in particular. There are so many things that could be said about whether or not people should be worried about the effect that data centers have on their property values, on their electricity bills, on their water usage in the area, and whether or not those things are real problems, inflated problems, etc. I think so much of that just really goes back to the fact that a lot of these projects are being negotiated essentially in secret. Sometimes they’re being negotiated [with the public knowing] that it’s a data center, but just not knowing who’s actually going to use it or occupy it at any point. This is a long-standing issue with the tech industry. I always go back to the mid-2010s when Uber was expanding really fast. Uber was one of the companies that really used this tactic a ton when it came to working with local governments. In particular, I remember I was working at The Verge at the time and we had a freelancer write a story about a city outside of Orlando where Uber was trying to negotiate tax subsidies to subsidize rides for people to use public transit after the Uber trip. The whole thing was negotiated in secret. And not only that, which was frustrating on its face, but also, because of the secrecy, you could just see Uber getting really comfortable with asking for a lot of other stuff, too. So there needs to be more of this. I’m glad Amazon’s doing this. We’ll see if it actually does have any positive effect, but people are pretty entrenched right now. Rebecca: Yeah, I’m curious about what effect this will have and whether it will lead to communities successfully delaying or or killing any infrastructure that the companies need to build. What I’ve heard from some people I’ve spoken to, who deal with data centers every day, a lot of these moratoriums that are getting passed — and there are a significant number of them, including one recently in San Francisco , which is pretty ironic — but they’re only for like a year or two years. But these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years. All of the buildouts are going to be massively delayed for a number of reasons from zoning to funding. Of course, if the pushback keeps going, then it might have an effect, but I often wonder just how much of an effect this political pushback is having on this. Anthony: The moratorium I’m most familiar with is the one in New York . I believe it’s a one-year moratorium, and that’s on permits for large projects. [Technically, it’s until the state finalizes an environmental review process, which is expected to take a year.] So already, there’s some wiggle room within that. And often, they’re framed as: “It’s not like we think [data centers are] bad, let’s not do this. It’s [that] we need to take the time to study this.” Which gives them a lot of room to say later on, “Actually, we’ve decided this is great. We love it.” But you can tell that the people trying to build these data centers are worried, which is why you have these unhinged tweets from people like Trump or David Sacks. Only time will tell in terms of how long and how deep that [community] resistance is, but I do think they are worried. It’s also noteworthy that Microsoft, earlier this year, made a similar announcement about not using NDAs. I don’t think that getting rid of the NDAs automatically is going to make the people who opposed these data centers be like, “Great, let’s let’s do it. I’m in.” But I think the beginning of that conversation is, “Well, we don’t even know what the heck you’re doing, because you’ve negotiated all this stuff in secret.” So it does seem like a good first step. Sean: The larger problem here is just a communication problem, right? This is a problem I think that goes across the entire tech industry, but it’s especially acute now, because we’re living in the era of “going direct” and “you don’t need to talk to the media, the media is dead,” etc. And I’m not trying to beat that horse, because we’re in the media and [we] think we’re still relevant. But we’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them. And that’s because, a lot of time, the [technological] ability’s not there, and in part because they’re just not explaining it well. I wrote a story last week about how it’s been a year since we’ve really heard Tesla beating its own drum about building towards what it originally was calling “sustainable abundance” and is now “amazing abundance” as its mission statement. It’s just wild to me that we’re a year into that, and the company still doesn’t have a very good definition of it, especially considering that they released this whole multi-page PDF laying it out when they announced this, and even Tesla’s biggest fans criticized Elon Musk and Tesla for how unspecific it was. It read like LLM nonsense. Anthony: One of the things this has made me think about is just the narrative and this sense that for a while, it really felt like it was being pushed down our throats — this idea of, “This is inevitable, this AI-driven future, and get on board or you’re just going to be left behind.” Obviously that future is barreling ahead in a lot of ways, but in a few key ways, there have been these obstacles. What I’ve really liked about that is this sense of “No, you actually have to make the case for it.” You can’t just say, “This is the future, shut up.” And then specifically about Tesla and the abundance thing, what was shocking to me is not so much that they haven’t come up with a definition of abundance, but that that was a promise that they were making in the first place. I think [that] speaks to how strange our relationship to Tesla, and particularly the people who are invested and ride-or-die for Elon, [has become.] It’s not about, is this company going to sell a lot of cars? It’s about this vision for remaking society. Or at least, that’s what they’re being sold.
